Before we proceed any further, hear me speak.
Before we go any further, listen to me.
You are all resolved rather to die than to famish?
Are you all determined to die rather than starve?
First, you know Caius Marcius is chief enemy to the people.
First of all, you know Caius Marcius is the people's worst enemy.
We know it, we know it.
Let us kill him, and we'll have corn at our own price. Is't a / verdict?
Let's kill him, and then we'll have grain at a price we set ourselves. Are we agreed?
No more talking on't; let it be done: away, away!
No more talk about it; let's do it. Come on, come on!

We are accounted poor citizens; the patricians good. / What authority surfeits on would relieve us; if they would yield / us but the superfluity, while it were wholesome, we might guess / they relieved us humanely; but they think we are too dear: the / leanness that afflicts us, the object of our misery, is as an / inventory to particularize their abundance; our sufferance is a / gain to them.—Let us revenge this with our pikes ere we become / rakes: for the gods know I speak this in hunger for bread, not in / thirst for revenge.

We're counted the poor citizens; the patricians are the "good" ones. What the rulers stuff themselves with would be enough to feed us. If they gave us only their leftovers while they were still fresh, we might think they were helping us out of humanity; but they think we cost too much. Our thinness, the sight of our misery, works like a list that spells out how rich they are; our suffering is their profit. Let's get revenge with our pikes before we're as thin as rakes. The gods know I say this because I'm hungry for bread, not thirsty for revenge.
Would you proceed especially against Caius Marcius?
Do you mean to go after Caius Marcius in particular?
Against him first: he's a very dog to the commonalty.
Him first. He's a real dog to the common people.
Consider you what services he has done for his country?
Have you thought about what he has done for his country?
Very well; and could be content to give him good report for't, / but that he pays himself with being proud.
Very much, and I'd gladly praise him for it, except that he pays himself back by being proud.
Come on, don't speak out of spite.

I say unto you, what he hath done famously he did it to that end: / though soft-conscienced men can be content to say it was for his / country, he did it to please his mother, and to be partly proud; / which he is, even to the altitude of his virtue.

I tell you, the famous things he has done he did for that reason. Soft-hearted people may say it was for his country, but he did it to please his mother and partly out of pride, and his pride is as great as his courage.
What he cannot help in his nature you account a vice in him. You / must in no way say he is covetous.
You're calling something he can't help in his own nature a vice. At least you can't say he's greedy.

If I must not, I need not be barren of accusations; he hath / faults, with surplus, to tire in repetition. [Shouts within] / What shouts are these? The other side o' the city is risen: why / stay we prating here? to the Capitol!

If I can't say that, I'm still not short of accusations; he has faults enough to tire you out listing them. (Shouts offstage) What's that shouting? The other side of the city has risen. Why are we standing here chattering? To the Capitol!
Worthy Menenius Agrippa; one that hath always loved the people.
The worthy Menenius Agrippa, a man who has always loved the people.
He's one honest enough; would all the rest were so!
He's honest enough. I wish all the rest were like him!
What work's, my countrymen, in hand? where go you / With bats and clubs? the matter? speak, I pray you.
What work have you got in hand, my countrymen? Where are you going with bats and clubs? What's the matter? Tell me, please.

Our business is not unknown to the senate; they have had inkling / this fortnight what we intend to do, which now we'll show 'em in / deeds. They say poor suitors have strong breaths; they shall know / we have strong arms too.

The senate knows all about our business; they've had a hint of what we mean to do for two weeks, and now we'll show them in action. They say poor petitioners have strong breath; they'll find out we have strong arms too.
Why, masters, my good friends, mine honest neighbours, / Will you undo yourselves?
Why, sirs, my good friends, my honest neighbours, do you want to ruin yourselves?
We cannot, sir; we are undone already.
We can't, sir; we're ruined already.

I tell you, friends, most charitable care / Have the patricians of you. For your wants, / Your suffering in this dearth, you may as well / Strike at the heaven with your staves as lift them / Against the Roman state; whose course will on / The way it takes, cracking ten thousand curbs / Of more strong link asunder than can ever / Appear in your impediment: for the dearth, / The gods, not the patricians, make it; and / Your knees to them, not arms, must help. Alack, / You are transported by calamity / Thither where more attends you; and you slander / The helms o' th' state, who care for you like fathers, / When you curse them as enemies.

I tell you, friends, the patricians look after you with the kindest care. As for your needs and your suffering in this famine, you might as well hit the sky with your sticks as raise them against the Roman state. The state will go on its way, snapping ten thousand chains far stronger than any you could put in its path. As for the famine, the gods make it, not the patricians, and you need to kneel to the gods, not take up arms. Oh dear, your misery is carrying you towards worse trouble, and you slander the men who steer the state, who care for you like fathers, when you curse them as enemies.

Care for us! True, indeed! They ne'er cared for us yet. Suffer us / to famish, and their storehouses crammed with grain; make edicts / for usury, to support usurers; repeal daily any wholesome act / established against the rich, and provide more piercing statutes / daily to chain up and restrain the poor. If the wars eat us not / up, they will; and there's all the love they bear us.

Care for us! Oh yes, really! They've never cared for us yet. They let us starve while their storehouses are crammed with grain; they make laws for moneylenders' interest to support the moneylenders; every day they repeal some good law made against the rich, and every day they bring in harsher laws to chain up and restrain the poor. If the wars don't eat us up, they will; and that's all the love they have for us.

Either you must / Confess yourselves wondrous malicious, / Or be accus'd of folly. I shall tell you / A pretty tale: it may be you have heard it; / But, since it serves my purpose, I will venture / To stale't a little more.
You must either admit you're amazingly malicious or be accused of foolishness. I'll tell you a pretty story. Maybe you've heard it, but since it suits my purpose I'll risk making it a little staler.
Well, I'll hear it, sir; yet you must not think to fob off our / disgrace with a tale: but, an't please you, deliver.
Well, I'll listen, sir; but don't think you can brush off our wrongs with a story. Go on, if you please.

There was a time when all the body's members / Rebell'd against the belly; thus accus'd it:— / That only like a gulf it did remain / I' the midst o' the body, idle and unactive, / Still cupboarding the viand, never bearing / Like labour with the rest; where th' other instruments / Did see and hear, devise, instruct, walk, feel, / And, mutually participate, did minister / Unto the appetite and affection common / Of the whole body. The belly answered,—

Once upon a time all the parts of the body rebelled against the belly and accused it like this: that it just sat like a pit in the middle of the body, idle and doing nothing, always storing away the food, never doing its share of the work like the rest, while the other organs saw and heard, planned, taught, walked, felt, and, working together, served the desires and needs of the whole body. The belly answered—
Well, sir, what answer made the belly?
Well, sir, what answer did the belly give?

Sir, I shall tell you.—With a kind of smile, / Which ne'er came from the lungs, but even thus,— / For, look you, I may make the belly smile / As well as speak,—it tauntingly replied / To the discontented members, the mutinous parts / That envied his receipt; even so most fitly / As you malign our senators for that / They are not such as you.

I'll tell you, sir. With a sort of smile that didn't come from the lungs, just like this (for you see, I can make the belly smile as well as speak), it answered mockingly to the discontented parts, the rebels who envied what it took in, exactly as you resent our senators because they aren't like you.

Your belly's answer? What! / The kingly crowned head, the vigilant eye, / The counsellor heart, the arm our soldier, / Our steed the leg, the tongue our trumpeter, / With other muniments and petty helps / Is this our fabric, if that they,—

The belly's answer? What! The royal crowned head, the watchful eye, the heart that advises, the arm that's our soldier, the leg that's our horse, the tongue our trumpeter, and all the other defences and little helpers in our body, if they—
What then?— / 'Fore me, this fellow speaks!—what then? what then?
What then? Goodness me, this fellow can talk! What then? What then?
Should by the cormorant belly be restrain'd, / Who is the sink o' the body,—
Should be held back by the greedy belly, the sewer of the body—
The former agents, if they did complain, / What could the belly answer?
If those working parts complained, what could the belly say back?
I will tell you; / If you'll bestow a small,—of what you have little,— / Patience awhile, you'll hear the belly's answer.
I'll tell you. If you'll spare me a little of what you're short of, patience, for a while, you'll hear the belly's answer.
You're taking a long time about it.

Note me this, good friend; / Your most grave belly was deliberate, / Not rash like his accusers, and thus answer'd: / 'True is it, my incorporate friends,' quoth he, / 'That I receive the general food at first / Which you do live upon; and fit it is, / Because I am the storehouse and the shop / Of the whole body: but, if you do remember, / I send it through the rivers of your blood, / Even to the court, the heart,—to the seat o' the brain; / And, through the cranks and offices of man, / The strongest nerves and small inferior veins / From me receive that natural competency / Whereby they live: and though that all at once / You, my good friends,'—this says the belly,—mark me,—

Take note of this, my good friend. Your very serious belly took its time, unlike its rash accusers, and answered like this: "It's true, my friends who make up one body with me," it said, "that I take in all the food first, which you live on, and that's right, because I'm the storehouse and the workshop of the whole body. But remember, I send it through the rivers of your blood all the way to the court, which is the heart, and to the throne, which is the brain; and through all the winding passages and rooms of the body, the strongest sinews and smallest veins get from me the natural supply they live on. And though all of you at once, my good friends"—this is the belly speaking, listen to me—
'Though all at once cannot / See what I do deliver out to each, / Yet I can make my audit up, that all / From me do back receive the flour of all, / And leave me but the bran.' What say you to't?
"Though you can't all see at once what I hand out to each of you, I can prove by my accounts that you all get the best flour from me and leave me only the bran." What do you say to that?
It was an answer: how apply you this?
It was an answer. How do you apply it?

The senators of Rome are this good belly, / And you the mutinous members; for, examine / Their counsels and their cares; digest things rightly / Touching the weal o' the common; you shall find / No public benefit which you receive / But it proceeds or comes from them to you, / And no way from yourselves.—What do you think, / You, the great toe of this assembly?

The senators of Rome are this good belly, and you are the rebellious parts. Examine their discussions and their worries, think properly about the common welfare, and you'll find there's no public benefit you receive that doesn't come from them to you, and none from yourselves. What do you think, you, the big toe of this crowd?
I the great toe? why the great toe?
Me, the big toe? Why the big toe?

For that, being one o' the lowest, basest, poorest, / Of this most wise rebellion, thou go'st foremost: / Thou rascal, that art worst in blood to run, / Lead'st first to win some vantage.— / But make you ready your stiff bats and clubs: / Rome and her rats are at the point of battle; / The one side must have bale.—

Because, though you're one of the lowest, meanest, poorest members of this very wise rebellion, you go first. You scoundrel, the worst-bred to run with the pack, you lead the way to get some advantage for yourself. Still, get your stiff bats and clubs ready: Rome and her rats are about to fight, and one side must come to harm.
Thanks.—What's the matter, you dissentious rogues / That, rubbing the poor itch of your opinion, / Make yourselves scabs?
Thanks. What's going on, you quarrelsome rascals, scratching the poor itch of your opinions until you turn yourselves into scabs?
We have ever your good word.
We always get kind words from you.

He that will give good words to thee will flatter / Beneath abhorring.—What would you have, you curs, / That like nor peace nor war? The one affrights you, / The other makes you proud. He that trusts to you, / Where he should find you lions, finds you hares; / Where foxes, geese: you are no surer, no, / Than is the coal of fire upon the ice, / Or hailstone in the sun. Your virtue is / To make him worthy whose offence subdues him, / And curse that justice did it. Who deserves greatness / Deserves your hate; and your affections are / A sick man's appetite, who desires most that / Which would increase his evil. He that depends / Upon your favours swims with fins of lead, / And hews down oaks with rushes. Hang ye! Trust ye! / With every minute you do change a mind; / And call him noble that was now your hate, / Him vile that was your garland. What's the matter, / That in these several places of the city / You cry against the noble senate, who, / Under the gods, keep you in awe, which else / Would feed on one another?—What's their seeking?

Anyone who gives you kind words is a disgusting flatterer. What do you want, you dogs, who like neither peace nor war? War frightens you, peace makes you arrogant. Whoever trusts you finds hares where he wanted lions, geese where he wanted foxes. You're no more reliable than hot coals on ice or a hailstone in the sun. Your great skill is to honour a criminal brought down by his crime and curse the justice that did it. Whoever deserves greatness deserves your hatred, and your desires are like a sick man's appetite, wanting most what will make him worse. Anyone who depends on your favour is swimming with lead fins and chopping down oaks with reeds. Hang you! Trust you! You change your minds every minute, calling a man noble who was just now hateful to you, and calling the man you crowned with garlands vile. What's the matter, that all over the city you're shouting against the noble senate, who, under the gods, keep you in check, when otherwise you'd eat each other? What are they after?
For corn at their own rates; whereof they say / The city is well stor'd.
Grain at prices they set, and they say the city has plenty.

Hang 'em! They say! / They'll sit by th' fire and presume to know / What's done i' the Capitol; who's like to rise, / Who thrives and who declines; side factions, and give out / Conjectural marriages; making parties strong, / And feebling such as stand not in their liking / Below their cobbled shoes. They say there's grain enough! / Would the nobility lay aside their ruth / And let me use my sword, I'd make a quarry / With thousands of these quarter'd slaves, as high / As I could pick my lance.

Hang them! "They say"! They sit by the fire and claim to know what goes on in the Capitol: who's likely to rise, who's thriving and who's in decline. They take sides, gossip about who'll marry whom, build up one party and run down those they don't like until they're lower than their patched shoes. "They say there's grain enough"! If the nobility would put aside their pity and let me use my sword, I'd make a heap of these chopped-up slaves as high as I could throw my lance.
Nay, these are almost thoroughly persuaded; / For though abundantly they lack discretion, / Yet are they passing cowardly. But, I beseech you, / What says the other troop?
No, this lot are almost won round, because though they're badly short of sense, they're extremely cowardly. But please tell me, what does the other crowd say?

They are dissolved: hang 'em! / They said they were an-hungry; sigh'd forth proverbs,— / That hunger broke stone walls, that dogs must eat, / That meat was made for mouths, that the gods sent not / Corn for the rich men only:—with these shreds / They vented their complainings; which being answer'd, / And a petition granted them,—a strange one, / To break the heart of generosity, / And make bold power look pale,—they threw their caps / As they would hang them on the horns o' the moon, / Shouting their emulation.

They've broken up, hang them! They said they were hungry and sighed out proverbs: that hunger breaks through stone walls, that dogs must eat, that food was made for mouths, that the gods didn't send grain for the rich alone. With these scraps they let out their complaints. When they were answered and given what they asked, a strange demand fit to break the heart of the nobility and make power go pale, they threw their caps up as if to hang them on the horns of the moon, shouting to outdo each other.

Five tribunes, to defend their vulgar wisdoms, / Of their own choice: one's Junius Brutus, / Sicinius Velutus, and I know not.—'Sdeath! / The rabble should have first unroof'd the city / Ere so prevail'd with me: it will in time / Win upon power, and throw forth greater themes / For insurrection's arguing.

Five tribunes of their own choosing, to stand up for their common wisdom. One is Junius Brutus, one Sicinius Velutus, and I don't know who else. Damn it! The mob should have torn the roofs off the city before they got that from me. In time it will eat away at power and throw up bigger causes for rebellion to argue over.
Go get you home, you fragments!
The news is, sir, the Volsces are in arms.
The news is, sir, that the Volscians are up in arms.
I am glad on't: then we shall ha' means to vent / Our musty superfluity.—See, our best elders.
I'm glad of it. Now we'll have a way to get rid of our mouldy surplus. Look, here come our chief elders.
Marcius, 'tis true that you have lately told us:— / The Volsces are in arms.
Marcius, what you told us recently is true: the Volscians are in arms.
They have a leader, / Tullus Aufidius, that will put you to't. / I sin in envying his nobility; / And were I anything but what I am, / I would wish me only he.
They have a leader, Tullus Aufidius, who will test you. It's a sin, but I envy his nobility, and if I were anyone but myself, I'd wish to be him.
Were half to half the world by the ears, and he / Upon my party, I'd revolt, to make / Only my wars with him: he is a lion / That I am proud to hunt.
If half the world were fighting the other half and he were on my side, I'd change sides just to fight him. He's a lion I'm proud to hunt.
Then, worthy Marcius, / Attend upon Cominius to these wars.
Then, worthy Marcius, go with Cominius to these wars.
Sir, it is; / And I am constant.—Titus Lartius, thou / Shalt see me once more strike at Tullus' face. / What, art thou stiff? stand'st out?
Yes, sir, I did, and I keep my word. Titus Lartius, you'll see me strike at Tullus's face once more. What, are you stiff? Will you stay out of it?
No, Caius Marcius; / I'll lean upon one crutch and fight with the other / Ere stay behind this business.
No, Caius Marcius. I'd lean on one crutch and fight with the other before I'd be left out of this.
Your company to the Capitol; where, I know, / Our greatest friends attend us.
Come with us to the Capitol, where I know our chief friends are waiting.
Lead you on. / Follow, Cominius; we must follow you; / Right worthy your priority.
(To Cominius) You lead on. (To Marcius) Follow Cominius; we must follow you, you who fully deserve to go first.
Hence to your homes; be gone!
Go to your homes; be off!
Nay, let them follow: / The Volsces have much corn; take these rats thither / To gnaw their garners.—Worshipful mutineers, / Your valour puts well forth: pray follow.
No, let them come along. The Volscians have plenty of grain; take these rats there to gnaw their granaries. Honourable rebels, your courage is blooming nicely. Please, follow.
Was ever man so proud as is this Marcius?
Was there ever a man as proud as this Marcius?
When we were chosen tribunes for the people,—
When we were chosen as tribunes for the people—
Mark'd you his lip and eyes?
Did you see his lip and his eyes?
Being mov'd, he will not spare to gird the gods.
When he's angry, he won't hesitate to mock the gods.
To sneer at the chaste moon.
The present wars devour him: he is grown / Too proud to be so valiant.
These wars will swallow him up; he's grown too proud to be so brave.
Such a nature, / Tickled with good success, disdains the shadow / Which he treads on at noon: but I do wonder / His insolence can brook to be commanded / Under Cominius.
A nature like his, flattered by success, scorns the very shadow he walks on at noon. But I'm amazed his arrogance can stand being under Cominius's command.

Fame, at the which he aims,— / In whom already he is well grac'd,—cannot / Better be held, nor more attain'd, than by / A place below the first: for what miscarries / Shall be the general's fault, though he perform / To th' utmost of a man; and giddy censure / Will then cry out of Marcius 'O, if he / Had borne the business!'

Fame is what he's after, and he's already well endowed with it. He can't keep it better, or win more, than by being second in command. Whatever goes wrong will be the general's fault, even if the general does all a man can, and fickle public opinion will cry out about Marcius, "Oh, if only he had been in charge!"
Besides, if things go well, / Opinion, that so sticks on Marcius, shall / Of his demerits rob Cominius.
Besides, if things go well, public opinion, which is so attached to Marcius, will rob Cominius of the credit he deserves.
Come: / Half all Cominius' honours are to Marcius, / Though Marcius earn'd them not; and all his faults / To Marcius shall be honours, though, indeed, / In aught he merit not.
Come on: half of Cominius's honours will go to Marcius, though Marcius didn't earn them, and all Cominius's faults will turn into honours for Marcius, even if he doesn't deserve them at all.
Let's hence and hear / How the dispatch is made; and in what fashion, / More than in singularity, he goes / Upon this present action.
Let's go and hear how the orders are drawn up and in what manner, apart from his usual style, he goes off on this campaign.
So, your opinion is, Aufidius, / That they of Rome are enter'd in our counsels / And know how we proceed.
So your view, Aufidius, is that the Romans have got into our secret plans and know what we're doing.

Is it not yours? / What ever have been thought on in this state, / That could be brought to bodily act ere Rome / Had circumvention! 'Tis not four days gone / Since I heard thence; these are the words: I think / I have the letter here; yes, here it is:

Isn't that your view too? What has ever been planned in this state that Rome didn't block before it could be carried out? It's not four days since I heard from there. These are the words; I think I have the letter here. Yes, here it is.

'They have pressed a power, but it is not known / Whether for east or west: the dearth is great; / The people mutinous: and it is rumour'd, / Cominius, Marcius your old enemy,— / Who is of Rome worse hated than of you,— / And Titus Lartius, a most valiant Roman, / These three lead on this preparation / Whither 'tis bent: most likely 'tis for you: / Consider of it.'

"They have raised an army, but nobody knows whether it's for east or west. The famine is severe, the people rebellious, and there's a rumour that Cominius, Marcius your old enemy (who is more hated in Rome than by you), and Titus Lartius, a very brave Roman, these three lead this force wherever it's heading. Most likely it's against you. Think about it."
Our army's in the field: / We never yet made doubt but Rome was ready / To answer us.
Our army is in the field. We never doubted Rome would be ready to answer us.

Nor did you think it folly / To keep your great pretences veil'd till when / They needs must show themselves; which in the hatching, / It seem'd, appear'd to Rome. By the discovery / We shall be shorten'd in our aim; which was, / To take in many towns ere, almost, Rome / Should know we were afoot.

And you didn't think it foolish to keep your great plans hidden until they had to come out, yet it seems Rome saw them while they were still hatching. Because they've been discovered, we'll fall short of our aim, which was to capture many towns before Rome even knew we were on the move.

Noble Aufidius, / Take your commission; hie you to your bands; / Let us alone to guard Corioli: / If they set down before's, for the remove / Bring up your army; but I think you'll find / They've not prepared for us.

Noble Aufidius, take your command and hurry to your troops. Leave it to us to guard Corioli. If they lay siege to us, bring up your army to lift it; but I think you'll find they haven't prepared for us.

O, doubt not that; / I speak from certainties. Nay, more, / Some parcels of their power are forth already, / And only hitherward. I leave your honours. / If we and Caius Marcius chance to meet, / 'Tis sworn between us we shall ever strike / Till one can do no more.

Oh, don't doubt that; I speak from what I know for certain. More than that, some of their forces are already out and heading only this way. I take my leave of you. If Caius Marcius and I happen to meet, we've sworn to keep striking until one of us can't go on.
And keep you safe, my lords!

I pray you, daughter, sing, or express yourself in a more / comfortable sort; if my son were my husband, I should freelier / rejoice in that absence wherein he won honour than in the / embracements of his bed where he would show most love. When yet / he was but tender-bodied, and the only son of my womb; when youth / with comeliness pluck'd all gaze his way; when, for a day of / kings' entreaties, a mother should not sell him an hour from her / beholding; I,—considering how honour would become such a person; / that it was no better than picture-like to hang by th' wall if / renown made it not stir;—was pleased to let him seek danger / where he was to find fame. To a cruel war I sent him; from whence / he returned his brows bound with oak. I tell thee, daughter, I / sprang not more in joy at first hearing he was a man-child than / now in first seeing he had proved himself a man.

Please, daughter, sing, or at least cheer up a bit. If my son were my husband, I'd be happier about him being away winning honour than about him embracing me in bed, where he'd show most love. When he was still a soft-bodied boy, my only son, when his youth and good looks drew every eye to him, when a mother wouldn't let him out of her sight for an hour even if kings begged her for a whole day, I thought how honour would suit a man like him, that without fame to bring him to life he'd be no better than a picture hanging on the wall. So I was glad to let him look for danger where he'd find fame. I sent him to a cruel war, and he came back with an oak-leaf wreath on his brow. I tell you, daughter, I didn't leap for joy more when I first heard I'd given birth to a boy than I did when I first saw he'd proved himself a man.
But had he died in the business, madam? how then?
But if he'd died doing it, madam? What then?

Then his good report should have been my son; I therein / would have found issue. Hear me profess sincerely,—had I a dozen / sons, each in my love alike, and none less dear than thine and my / good Marcius, I had rather had eleven die nobly for their country / than one voluptuously surfeit out of action.

Then his good name would have been my son; I would have found my descendants in that. Let me tell you honestly: if I had a dozen sons, all loved equally, none less dear than your Marcius and mine, I'd rather eleven died nobly for their country than one stuffed himself with pleasure, doing nothing.
Madam, the Lady Valeria is come to visit you.
Madam, Lady Valeria has come to visit you.
Beseech you, give me leave to retire myself.
Please, let me go to my room.

Indeed you shall not. / Methinks I hear hither your husband's drum; / See him pluck Aufidius down by the hair; / As children from a bear, the Volsces shunning him: / Methinks I see him stamp thus, and call thus:— / 'Come on, you cowards! you were got in fear / Though you were born in Rome:' his bloody brow / With his mail'd hand then wiping, forth he goes, / Like to a harvest-man that's tasked to mow / Or all, or lose his hire.

You certainly won't. I think I can hear your husband's drum from here. I can see him dragging Aufidius down by the hair, the Volscians running from him like children from a bear. I can see him stamping like this and shouting like this: "Come on, you cowards! You were conceived in fear, even if you were born in Rome!" Then, wiping his bloody brow with his armoured hand, he goes forward like a harvester who has to mow the whole field or lose his pay.
His bloody brow! O Jupiter, no blood!
His bloody brow! Oh Jupiter, no blood!

Away, you fool! It more becomes a man / Than gilt his trophy: the breasts of Hecuba, / When she did suckle Hector, looked not lovelier / Than Hector's forehead when it spit forth blood / At Grecian swords contending.—Tell Valeria / We are fit to bid her welcome.

Get away, you fool! Blood suits a man better than gold suits his monument. Hecuba's breasts, when she was nursing Hector, didn't look lovelier than Hector's forehead spitting blood as he fought Greek swords. Tell Valeria we're ready to welcome her.
Heavens bless my lord from fell Aufidius!
Heavens protect my husband from cruel Aufidius!
He'll beat Aufidius' head below his knee, / And tread upon his neck.
He'll beat Aufidius's head down below his knee and stamp on his neck.
My ladies both, good-day to you.
Good day to you both, my ladies.
I am glad to see your ladyship.
I'm glad to see your ladyship.
How do you both? you are manifest housekeepers. What are / you sewing here? A fine spot, in good faith.—How does your / little son?
How are you both? You're real stay-at-homes. What are you sewing? A pretty pattern, honestly. How is your little son?
I thank your ladyship; well, good madam.
Thank you, your ladyship; he's well, good madam.
He had rather see the swords and hear a drum than look upon his / schoolmaster.
He'd rather see swords and hear a drum than look at his schoolmaster.

O' my word, the father's son: I'll swear 'tis a very pretty boy. / O' my troth, I looked upon him o' Wednesday, half an hour / together: has such a confirmed countenance. I saw him run after a / gilded butterfly; and when he caught it he let it go again; and / after it again; and over and over he comes, and up again; catched / it again; or whether his fall enraged him, or how 'twas, he did / so set his teeth and tear it; O, I warrant, how he mammocked it!

Upon my word, he's his father's son. I swear he's a very pretty boy. Honestly, I watched him on Wednesday for half an hour on end; he has such a determined face. I saw him run after a golden butterfly; when he caught it he let it go, and ran after it again, and fell head over heels, and got up again, and caught it again. And whether the fall made him angry or what, he gritted his teeth and tore it apart. Oh, I promise you, how he shredded it!
Come, lay aside your stitchery; I must have you play the idle / huswife with me this afternoon.
Come, put away your needlework. I want you to play the idle housewife with me this afternoon.
No, good madam; I will not out of doors.
No, good madam, I won't go out of the house.
Not go out of the house!
Indeed, no, by your patience; I'll not over the threshold till my / lord return from the wars.
Really, no, if you'll excuse me. I won't cross the doorstep until my husband comes back from the wars.
Fie, you confine yourself most unreasonably; come, you must go / visit the good lady that lies in.
Shame on you, you shut yourself up quite unreasonably. Come, you must visit the good lady who's just had her baby.
I will wish her speedy strength, and visit her with my prayers; / but I cannot go thither.
I'll wish her a quick recovery and visit her with my prayers, but I can't go there.
'Tis not to save labour, nor that I want love.
It's not to save effort, and it's not that I don't care.

You would be another Penelope; yet they say all the yarn she spun / in Ulysses' absence did but fill Ithaca full of moths. Come; I / would your cambric were sensible as your finger, that you might / leave pricking it for pity.—Come, you shall go with us.

You want to be another Penelope; yet they say all the yarn she spun while Ulysses was away only filled Ithaca with moths. Come on. I wish your linen could feel like your finger, so you'd stop pricking it out of pity. Come, you're coming with us.
No, good madam, pardon me; indeed I will not forth.
No, good madam, forgive me; I really won't go out.
In truth, la, go with me; and I'll tell you excellent news / of your husband.
Honestly, come with me, and I'll tell you excellent news about your husband.
O, good madam, there can be none yet.
Oh, good madam, there can't be any yet.
Verily, I do not jest with you; there came news from him last / night.
Truly, I'm not joking; news came from him last night.

In earnest, it's true; I heard a senator speak it. Thus it / is:—the Volsces have an army forth; against whom Cominius the / general is gone, with one part of our Roman power: your lord and / Titus Lartius are set down before their city Corioli; they / nothing doubt prevailing, and to make it brief wars. This is / true, on mine honour; and so, I pray, go with us.

Seriously, it's true; I heard a senator say it. It's like this: the Volscians have an army out, and the general Cominius has gone against it with part of our Roman forces. Your husband and Titus Lartius are besieging their city of Corioli. They have no doubt they'll win and make it a short war. This is true, on my honour; so please, come with us.
Give me excuse, good madam; I will obey you in everything / hereafter.
Excuse me, good madam; I'll do what you say in everything else from now on.
Let her alone, lady; as she is now, she will but disease our / better mirth.
Leave her alone, lady. In her present mood she'd only spoil our fun.
In troth, I think she would.—Fare you well, then.—Come, / good sweet lady.—Pr'ythee, Virgilia, turn thy solemness out o' / door and go along with us.
Honestly, I think she would. Goodbye, then. Come, dear lady. Please, Virgilia, throw your gloom out of the door and come along with us.
No, at a word, madam; indeed I must not. I wish you much mirth.
No, once and for all, madam, I really mustn't. I hope you have a lot of fun.
Yonder comes news:—a wager they have met.
Here comes news. I bet they've met in battle.
My horse against yours that they haven't.
Say, has our general met the enemy?
Tell me, has our general met the enemy?
They lie in view; but have not spoke as yet.
They're in sight of each other but haven't engaged yet.
So, the good horse is mine.
So the good horse is mine.
No, I'll nor sell nor give him: lend you him I will / For half a hundred years.—Summon the town.
No, I won't sell him or give him away; but I'll lend him to you for fifty years. Call on the town to talk.
How far off lie these armies?
How far off are these armies?
Within a mile and a half.

Then shall we hear their 'larum, and they ours.— / Now, Mars, I pr'ythee, make us quick in work, / That we with smoking swords may march from hence / To help our fielded friends!—Come, blow thy blast.

Then we'll hear their call to arms and they'll hear ours. Now, Mars, please make us quick at our work, so we can march from here with smoking swords to help our friends in the field! Come on, blow your trumpet.
Tullus Aufidius, is he within your walls?
Is Tullus Aufidius inside your walls?
No, nor a man that fears you less than he, / That's lesser than a little.
No, and there's no one here who fears you less than he does, and that's less than a little.

Hark, our drums / Are bringing forth our youth! we'll break our walls / Rather than they shall pound us up: our gates, / Which yet seem shut, we have but pinn'd with rushes; / They'll open of themselves.

Listen, our drums are calling out our young men! We'll break down our own walls rather than let you pen us in like animals. Our gates, which look shut, are only fastened with reeds; they'll open by themselves.
Hark you far off! / There is Aufidius; list what work he makes / Amongst your cloven army.
Listen out there! That's Aufidius; hear what damage he's doing to your split army.
Their noise be our instruction.—Ladders, ho!
Let their noise be our signal. Ladders, now!

They fear us not, but issue forth their city. / Now put your shields before your hearts, and fight / With hearts more proof than shields.—Advance, brave Titus: / They do disdain us much beyond our thoughts, / Which makes me sweat with wrath.—Come on, my fellows: / He that retires, I'll take him for a Volsce, / And he shall feel mine edge.

They're not afraid of us; they're coming out of their city. Now put your shields in front of your hearts, and fight with hearts tougher than shields. Forward, brave Titus. They scorn us far more than we thought, which makes me sweat with rage. Come on, my men: anyone who retreats I'll treat as a Volscian, and he'll feel my blade.

All the contagion of the south light on you, / You shames of Rome!—you herd of—Boils and plagues / Plaster you o'er, that you may be abhorr'd / Farther than seen, and one infect another / Against the wind a mile! You souls of geese / That bear the shapes of men, how have you run / From slaves that apes would beat! Pluto and hell! / All hurt behind; backs red, and faces pale / With flight and agued fear! Mend, and charge home, / Or, by the fires of heaven, I'll leave the foe / And make my wars on you: look to't: come on; / If you'll stand fast we'll beat them to their wives, / As they us to our trenches.

May all the diseases of the south fall on you, you disgraces to Rome! You herd of— May boils and plagues cover you so people loathe you before they even see you, and you infect each other a mile upwind! You souls of geese in the shape of men, how you've run from slaves that apes could beat! Pluto and hell! All wounded in the back, backs red and faces white with running and shivering fear! Pull yourselves together and charge hard, or by the fires of heaven I'll leave the enemy and make war on you. Watch out! Come on: if you stand firm, we'll beat them back to their wives, as they beat us back to our trenches.
So, now the gates are ope:—now prove good seconds: / 'Tis for the followers fortune widens them, / Not for the fliers: mark me, and do the like.
There, now the gates are open. Now be good backup. Fortune opens them for those who follow, not for those who run away. Watch me, and do the same.
See, they have shut him in.
To th' pot, I warrant him.
He's in the cooking pot, I'll bet.
Following the fliers at the very heels, / With them he enters; who, upon the sudden, / Clapp'd-to their gates: he is himself alone, / To answer all the city.
He was chasing the runaways right at their heels and went in with them, and they suddenly slammed their gates shut. He's all alone, taking on the whole city.

O noble fellow! / Who sensible, outdares his senseless sword, / And when it bows stands up! Thou art left, Marcius: / A carbuncle entire, as big as thou art, / Were not so rich a jewel. Thou wast a soldier / Even to Cato's wish, not fierce and terrible / Only in strokes; but with thy grim looks and / The thunder-like percussion of thy sounds / Thou mad'st thine enemies shake, as if the world / Were feverous and did tremble.

Oh noble man! He can feel, yet he's bolder than his unfeeling sword, and he stands firm when it bends! You're lost, Marcius. A flawless ruby as big as you would not be so rich a jewel. You were a soldier just as Cato would have wished, not only fierce and terrible in your blows, but with your grim looks and the thunderous crash of your voice you made your enemies shake as if the world had a fever and trembled.
O, 'tis Marcius! / Let's fetch him off, or make remain alike.
Oh, it's Marcius! Let's rescue him, or stay there with him.
This will I carry to Rome.
A murrain on't! I took this for silver.
A plague on it! I thought this was silver.

See here these movers that do prize their hours / At a crack'd drachma! Cushions, leaden spoons, / Irons of a doit, doublets that hangmen would / Bury with those that wore them, these base slaves, / Ere yet the fight be done, pack up:—down with them!— / And hark, what noise the general makes!—To him!— / There is the man of my soul's hate, Aufidius, / Piercing our Romans; then, valiant Titus, take / Convenient numbers to make good the city; / Whilst I, with those that have the spirit, will haste / To help Cominius.

Look at these looters, who value their time at a cracked penny! Cushions, lead spoons, iron scraps worth a farthing, jackets a hangman would bury along with the men who wore them: these low slaves are packing up before the fight is even over. Cut them down! And listen to the noise the general's making! Go to him! There's the man my soul hates, Aufidius, cutting through our Romans. So, brave Titus, take enough men to hold the city, while I hurry with those who have the spirit to help Cominius.
Worthy sir, thou bleed'st; / Thy exercise hath been too violent / For a second course of fight.
Worthy sir, you're bleeding. You've worked too hard already to go into a second round of fighting.
Sir, praise me not; / My work hath yet not warm'd me: fare you well; / The blood I drop is rather physical / Than dangerous to me: to Aufidius thus / I will appear, and fight.
Sir, don't praise me. My work hasn't even warmed me up yet. Farewell. The blood I'm losing is more like a healthy bloodletting than a danger to me. This is how I'll show myself to Aufidius and fight.
Now the fair goddess, Fortune, / Fall deep in love with thee; and her great charms / Misguide thy opposers' swords! Bold gentleman, / Prosperity be thy page!
Now may the lovely goddess Fortune fall deeply in love with you, and may her powerful spells turn your enemies' swords aside! Bold gentleman, may success follow you like a page!
Thy friend no less / Than those she placeth highest!—So farewell.
And may she be no less your friend than she is to those she raises highest! So, farewell.
Go, sound thy trumpet in the market-place; / Call thither all the officers o' the town, / Where they shall know our mind: away!
Go and sound your trumpet in the market square. Call all the town's officials there, where they'll learn what we've decided. Go!

Breathe you, my friends: well fought; we are come off / Like Romans, neither foolish in our stands / Nor cowardly in retire: believe me, sirs, / We shall be charg'd again. Whiles we have struck, / By interims and conveying gusts we have heard / The charges of our friends. The Roman gods, / Lead their successes as we wish our own, / That both our powers, with smiling fronts encountering, / May give you thankful sacrifice!—

Catch your breath, my friends. Well fought. We've come out of it like Romans, not foolish in holding our ground or cowardly in retreating. Believe me, sirs, we'll be attacked again. While we were fighting, we heard our friends' charges now and then on the wind. Roman gods, lead them to success as we wish for our own, so both our forces can meet with smiling faces and offer you thankful sacrifice!
The citizens of Corioli have issued, / And given to Lartius and to Marcius battle: / I saw our party to their trenches driven, / And then I came away.
The citizens of Corioli came out and attacked Lartius and Marcius. I saw our side driven back to their trenches, and then I left.
Though thou speak'st truth, / Methinks thou speak'st not well. How long is't since?
Even if you're telling the truth, I don't think you're telling it well. How long ago was it?
More than an hour, my lord.
'Tis not a mile; briefly we heard their drums: / How couldst thou in a mile confound an hour, / And bring thy news so late?
It's not a mile away; we heard their drums a little while ago. How could you waste an hour covering a mile and bring your news so late?
Spies of the Volsces / Held me in chase, that I was forc'd to wheel / Three or four miles about; else had I, sir, / Half an hour since brought my report.
Volscian scouts chased me, so I had to go three or four miles round; otherwise, sir, I'd have brought my report half an hour ago.
Who's yonder, / That does appear as he were flay'd? O gods! / He has the stamp of Marcius; and I have / Before-time seen him thus.
Who's that over there, looking as if he'd been skinned? Oh gods! He has the look of Marcius, and I've seen him like this before.
The shepherd knows not thunder from a tabor / More than I know the sound of Marcius' tongue / From every meaner man.
A shepherd can tell thunder from a drum no better than I can tell Marcius's voice from any lesser man's.
Ay, if you come not in the blood of others, / But mantled in your own.
Yes, if you come covered not in other men's blood but in your own.
O! let me clip ye / In arms as sound as when I woo'd; in heart / As merry as when our nuptial day was done, / And tapers burn'd to bedward.
Oh, let me hug you in arms as strong as when I courted my wife, with a heart as happy as when our wedding day was over and the candles were lit for bed!
Flower of warriors, / How is't with Titus Lartius?
Flower of warriors, how is Titus Lartius doing?

As with a man busied about decrees: / Condemning some to death and some to exile; / Ransoming him or pitying, threat'ning the other; / Holding Corioli in the name of Rome, / Even like a fawning greyhound in the leash, / To let him slip at will.

Like a man busy making decrees: sentencing some to death and some to exile, letting one man pay a ransom or pitying him, threatening another; holding Corioli for Rome like a fawning greyhound on a leash, ready to let it go when he likes.
Where is that slave / Which told me they had beat you to your trenches? / Where's he? call him hither.
Where's that wretch who told me they'd beaten you back to your trenches? Where is he? Call him here.
Let him alone; / He did inform the truth: but for our gentlemen, / The common file,—a plague!—tribunes for them!— / The mouse ne'er shunned the cat as they did budge / From rascals worse than they.

Leave him alone; he was telling the truth. But our gentlemen, the common soldiers (a plague on them! Tribunes for them!), never did a mouse run from a cat the way they ran from scoundrels worse than themselves.
Will the time serve to tell? I do not think. / Where is the enemy? are you lords o' the field? / If not, why cease you till you are so?
Is there time to tell it? I don't think so. Where's the enemy? Are you masters of the field? If not, why stop before you are?
Marcius, / We have at disadvantage fought, and did / Retire, to win our purpose.
Marcius, we fought at a disadvantage and retreated in order to gain our purpose.
How lies their battle? know you on which side / They have placed their men of trust?
How is their army drawn up? Do you know on which side they've put their most trusted men?
As I guess, Marcius, / Their bands in the vaward are the Antiates, / Of their best trust; o'er them Aufidius, / Their very heart of hope.
As I guess, Marcius, the troops in their front line are men of Antium, the ones they trust most, and over them is Aufidius, the very heart of their hope.

I do beseech you, / By all the battles wherein we have fought, / By the blood we have shed together, by the vows / We have made to endure friends, that you directly / Set me against Aufidius and his Antiates; / And that you not delay the present, but, / Filling the air with swords advanc'd and darts, / We prove this very hour.

I beg you, by all the battles we've fought, by the blood we've shed together, by the vows we've made to stay friends forever, put me straight up against Aufidius and his men of Antium. And don't let this moment slip; let's fill the air with raised swords and spears and try our luck this very hour.
Though I could wish / You were conducted to a gentle bath, / And balms applied to you, yet dare I never / Deny your asking: take your choice of those / That best can aid your action.
Though I'd rather you were taken to a soothing bath and had ointment put on your wounds, I'd never dare refuse what you ask. Take your pick of the men who can best help you.

Those are they / That most are willing.—If any such be here,— / As it were sin to doubt,—that love this painting / Wherein you see me smear'd; if any fear / Lesser his person than an ill report; / If any think brave death outweighs bad life, / And that his country's dearer than himself; / Let him alone, or so many so minded, / Wave thus [waving his hand], to express his disposition, / And follow Marcius.

The best men are the most willing. If there are any here (and it would be a sin to doubt it) who love this paint you see me smeared with, if any fear for their bodies less than for a bad reputation, if any think a brave death outweighs a shameful life and their country is dearer than themselves, let him alone, or all who think the same, wave like this (waving his hand) to show their feelings, and follow Marcius.

O, me alone! Make you a sword of me? / If these shows be not outward, which of you / But is four Volsces? none of you but is / Able to bear against the great Aufidius / A shield as hard as his. A certain number, / Though thanks to all, must I select from all: the rest / Shall bear the business in some other fight, / As cause will be obey'd. Please you to march; / And four shall quickly draw out my command, / Which men are best inclin'd.

Oh, me alone! Are you making a sword of me? If this isn't just for show, which of you isn't worth four Volscians? Every one of you can hold up a shield against the great Aufidius as hard as his own. Thanking you all, I must still choose a certain number; the rest will do their part in some other fight, as duty requires. Please march on, and four of you will quickly pick out the men best suited for my command.
March on, my fellows; / Make good this ostentation, and you shall / Divide in all with us.
March on, my comrades. Make good on this show of spirit and you'll share in everything with us.

So, let the ports be guarded: keep your duties / As I have set them down. If I do send, despatch / Those centuries to our aid; the rest will serve / For a short holding: if we lose the field / We cannot keep the town.

So, guard the gates, and carry out your duties as I've set them out. If I send for them, rush those companies to help us; the rest will do for a short defence. If we lose the battle, we can't keep the town.
Don't doubt we'll take care, sir.
Hence, and shut your gates upon's.— / Our guider, come; to the Roman camp conduct us.
Go, and shut your gates behind us. Our guide, come; lead us to the Roman camp.
I'll fight with none but thee, for I do hate thee / Worse than a promise-breaker.
I'll fight no one but you, because I hate you more than a man who breaks his word.
We hate alike: / Not Afric owns a serpent I abhor / More than thy fame and envy. Fix thy foot.
We hate each other equally. There's no snake in Africa I loathe more than your fame, which I envy. Stand your ground.
Let the first budger die the other's slave, / And the gods doom him after!
Let whoever moves first die as the other's slave, and then let the gods damn him!
If I fly, Marcius, / Halloo me like a hare.
If I run, Marcius, hunt me down like a hare.

Within these three hours, Tullus, / Alone I fought in your Corioli walls, / And made what work I pleas'd: 'tis not my blood / Wherein thou seest me mask'd: for thy revenge / Wrench up thy power to the highest.

Within these last three hours, Tullus, I fought alone inside your walls of Corioli and did whatever damage I liked. It's not my own blood you see me covered in. Strain your strength to the highest to get your revenge.
Wert thou the Hector / That was the whip of your bragg'd progeny, / Thou shouldst not scape me here.—
Even if you were Hector, the scourge of the Greeks and pride of your boasted Trojan ancestors, you wouldn't escape me here.
Officious, and not valiant,—you have sham'd me / In your condemned seconds.
Meddling, not brave! You've shamed me with your damned help.

If I should tell thee o'er this thy day's work, / Thou't not believe thy deeds: but I'll report it / Where senators shall mingle tears with smiles; / Where great patricians shall attend, and shrug, / I' the end admire; where ladies shall be frighted / And, gladly quak'd, hear more; where the dull tribunes, / That, with the fusty plebeians, hate thine honours, / Shall say, against their hearts 'We thank the gods / Our Rome hath such a soldier.' / Yet cam'st thou to a morsel of this feast, / Having fully dined before.

If I told you all over again what you did today, you wouldn't believe your own deeds. But I'll report it where senators will mix tears with smiles, where great patricians will listen, shrug, and finally admire; where ladies will be frightened and, happily trembling, ask to hear more; where the dull tribunes, who along with the mouldy plebeians hate your honours, will say against their will, "We thank the gods that our Rome has such a soldier." And yet you came to this feast for just a bite, having already eaten your fill.
O general, / Here is the steed, we the caparison: / Hadst thou beheld,—
Oh general, here's the horse, and we're just its trappings. If you had seen—

Pray now, no more: my mother, / Who has a charter to extol her blood, / When she does praise me grieves me. I have done / As you have done,—that's what I can; induced / As you have been,—that's for my country: / He that has but effected his good will / Hath overta'en mine act.

Please, no more. My mother, who has a right to praise her own child, upsets me when she praises me. I've done what you've done, that is, what I can; driven as you were, that is, by love of my country. Anyone who has carried out his good intentions has done more than I have.

You shall not be / The grave of your deserving; Rome must know / The value of her own: 'twere a concealment / Worse than a theft, no less than a traducement, / To hide your doings; and to silence that / Which, to the spire and top of praises vouch'd, / Would seem but modest: therefore, I beseech you,— / In sign of what you are, not to reward / What you have done,—before our army hear me.

You won't be the grave of your own merit. Rome must know the worth of her own men. It would be a concealment worse than theft, as bad as slander, to hide what you've done and keep quiet about deeds that would seem modestly described even if praised to the skies. So I beg you, as a sign of what you are and not as a reward for what you've done, hear me in front of the army.
I have some wounds upon me, and they smart / To hear themselves remember'd.
I have some wounds on me, and they sting to hear themselves mentioned.

Should they not, / Well might they fester 'gainst ingratitude, / And tent themselves with death. Of all the horses,— / Whereof we have ta'en good, and good store,—of all / The treasure in this field achiev'd and city, / We render you the tenth; to be ta'en forth / Before the common distribution at / Your only choice.

If they didn't hear it, they might well fester from ingratitude and be dressed only by death. Of all the horses we've captured, and there are good ones and plenty, and all the treasure won in this field and in the city, we give you a tenth, to be taken out before the general share-out, entirely your choice.
I thank you, general, / But cannot make my heart consent to take / A bribe to pay my sword: I do refuse it; / And stand upon my common part with those / That have beheld the doing.
Thank you, general, but I can't bring my heart to take a bribe as payment for my sword. I refuse it, and I'll take only my ordinary share with those who saw the fighting.

May these same instruments which you profane / Never sound more! When drums and trumpets shall / I' the field prove flatterers, let courts and cities be / Made all of false-fac'd soothing. / When steel grows soft as the parasite's silk, / Let him be made a coverture for the wars. / No more, I say! for that I have not wash'd / My nose that bled, or foil'd some debile wretch,— / Which, without note, here's many else have done,— / You shout me forth in acclamations hyperbolical; / As if I loved my little should be dieted / In praises sauc'd with lies.

May these same instruments that you're abusing never sound again! When drums and trumpets on the battlefield turn into flatterers, then courts and cities may as well be made entirely of two-faced smooth talk. When steel grows as soft as a flatterer's silk, let silk be made into armour for war. No more, I say! Just because I haven't washed my bleeding nose or have knocked down some feeble wretch, which plenty of others here have done without being noticed, you cheer me with exaggerated shouts, as if I liked my small deeds to be fed on praise flavoured with lies.

Too modest are you; / More cruel to your good report than grateful / To us that give you truly; by your patience, / If 'gainst yourself you be incens'd, we'll put you,— / Like one that means his proper harm,—in manacles, / Then reason safely with you.—Therefore be it known, / As to us, to all the world, that Caius Marcius / Wears this war's garland: in token of the which, / My noble steed, known to the camp, I give him, / With all his trim belonging; and from this time, / For what he did before Corioli, call him, / With all the applause—and clamour of the host, / 'Caius Marcius Coriolanus.'— / Bear the addition nobly ever!

You're too modest, more cruel to your own reputation than grateful to us who are being truthful about you. With your permission, if you're angry with yourself, we'll put you in handcuffs like a man who means to harm himself, and then argue with you safely. So let it be known to the whole world, as it is to us, that Caius Marcius wins this war's garland. As a token of it I give him my noble horse, known throughout the camp, with all its trappings; and from now on, for what he did at Corioli, call him, with all the army's applause and cheering, "Caius Marcius Coriolanus." Wear that title nobly forever!

I will go wash; / And when my face is fair you shall perceive / Whether I blush or no: howbeit, I thank you;— / I mean to stride your steed; and at all times / To undercrest your good addition / To the fairness of my power.

I'll go and wash, and when my face is clean you'll see whether I'm blushing or not. Still, I thank you. I'll ride your horse, and always try to live up to the honourable name you've given me as well as I can.

So, to our tent; / Where, ere we do repose us, we will write / To Rome of our success.—You, Titus Lartius, / Must to Corioli back: send us to Rome / The best, with whom we may articulate / For their own good and ours.

So, to our tent, where before we rest we'll write to Rome about our success. You, Titus Lartius, must go back to Corioli. Send us their leading men to Rome, so we can make terms with them for their good and ours.
The gods begin to mock me. I, that now / Refus'd most princely gifts, am bound to beg / Of my lord general.
The gods are starting to mock me. I've just refused princely gifts, and now I have to beg from my lord general.
Take it, it's yours. What is it?

I sometime lay here in Corioli / At a poor man's house; he used me kindly: / He cried to me; I saw him prisoner; / But then Aufidius was within my view, / And wrath o'erwhelmed my pity: I request you / To give my poor host freedom.

Once, here in Corioli, I stayed at a poor man's house. He treated me kindly. He called out to me; I saw he'd been taken prisoner. But just then I caught sight of Aufidius, and anger swamped my pity. I ask you to set my poor host free.
O, well begg'd! / Were he the butcher of my son, he should / Be free as is the wind. Deliver him, Titus.
Oh, well asked! Even if he had butchered my son, he'd be as free as the wind. Release him, Titus.
By Jupiter, forgot:— / I am weary; yea, my memory is tir'd.— / Have we no wine here?
By Jupiter, I've forgotten. I'm worn out; yes, even my memory's tired. Haven't we any wine here?
Go we to our tent: / The blood upon your visage dries; 'tis time / It should be look'd to: come.
Let's go to our tent. The blood on your face is drying; it's time it was seen to. Come.
'Twill be delivered back on good condition.
We'll get it back on good terms.

Condition! / I would I were a Roman; for I cannot, / Being a Volsce, be that I am.—Condition? / What good condition can a treaty find / I' the part that is at mercy?—Five times, Marcius, / I have fought with thee; so often hast thou beat me; / And wouldst do so, I think, should we encounter / As often as we eat.—By the elements, / If e'er again I meet him beard to beard, / He's mine or I am his: mine emulation / Hath not that honour in't it had; for where / I thought to crush him in an equal force,— / True sword to sword,—I'll potch at him some way, / Or wrath or craft may get him.

Terms! I wish I were a Roman, because as a Volscian I can't be what I really am. Terms? What good terms can a treaty give the side that's at the other's mercy? Five times, Marcius, I've fought you, and every time you've beaten me, and I think you would even if we met as often as we eat. By the elements, if I ever meet him face to face again, either he's mine or I'm his. My rivalry has lost the honour it had, because where I once meant to crush him in a fair fight, sword against sword, now I'll stab at him somehow; either anger or cunning will get him.

Bolder, though not so subtle. My valour's poisoned / With only suffering stain by him; for him / Shall fly out of itself: nor sleep nor sanctuary, / Being naked, sick; nor fane nor Capitol, / The prayers of priests nor times of sacrifice, / Embarquements all of fury, shall lift up / Their rotten privilege and custom 'gainst / My hate to Marcius: where I find him, were it / At home, upon my brother's guard, even there, / Against the hospitable canon, would I / Wash my fierce hand in's heart. Go you to the city; / Learn how 'tis held; and what they are that must / Be hostages for Rome.

Bolder, though not so cunning. My courage is poisoned just by being stained with defeat by him; it will abandon its own nature to get him. Neither sleep nor holy refuge, nor his being unarmed or sick, nor temple nor Capitol, nor priests' prayers or times of sacrifice, all of which hold back fury, shall raise their worn-out rights and customs against my hatred of Marcius. Wherever I find him, even at home under my brother's protection, there, against the laws of hospitality, I'd wash my fierce hand in his heart. Go to the city; find out how it's being held and who must be given as hostages to Rome.
I am attended at the cypress grove: I pray you,— / 'Tis south the city mills,—bring me word thither / How the world goes, that to the pace of it / I may spur on my journey.
I'm expected at the cypress grove. Please (it's south of the city mills) bring me word there of how things stand, so I can set the pace of my journey to match.
The augurer tells me we shall have news tonight.
The fortune-teller says we'll have news tonight.
Not according to the prayer of the people, for they love not / Marcius.
Not the kind the people are praying for, since they don't love Marcius.
Nature teaches beasts to know their friends.
Nature teaches animals to know their friends.
Pray you, who does the wolf love?
Tell me, whom does the wolf love?
Ay, to devour him, as the hungry plebeians would the noble / Marcius.
Yes, to eat it, as the hungry plebeians would like to eat the noble Marcius.
He's a lamb indeed, that baas like a bear.
He's a lamb all right, one that bleats like a bear.
He's a bear indeed, that lives like a lamb. You two are old men: / tell me one thing that I shall ask you.
He's a bear all right, one that lives like a lamb. You two are old men; answer me one question.
In what enormity is Marcius poor in, that you two have not / in abundance?
What vice is Marcius short of that you two don't have plenty of?
He's poor in no one fault, but stored with all.
He's short of no fault at all; he's stocked with every one.
And topping all others in boasting.
And he's ahead of everyone at boasting.
This is strange now: do you two know how you are censured here in / the city, I mean of us o' the right-hand file? Do you?
Now this is odd. Do you two know what people here in the city think of you, I mean people of our upper class? Do you?
Why, what do they think of us?
Because you talk of pride now,—will you not be angry?
Because you're talking about pride now, you won't be angry?

Why, 'tis no great matter; for a very little thief of occasion / will rob you of a great deal of patience: give your dispositions / the reins, and be angry at your pleasures; at the least, if you / take it as a pleasure to you in being so. You blame Marcius for / being proud?

Why, it doesn't matter much, since the smallest excuse will rob you of a great deal of patience. Give your tempers free rein and be angry as much as you like, at least if you enjoy being angry. You blame Marcius for being proud?
We do it not alone, sir.
We're not the only ones, sir.

I know you can do very little alone; for your helps are many, or / else your actions would grow wondrous single: your abilities are / too infant-like for doing much alone. You talk of pride: O that / you could turn your eyes toward the napes of your necks, and make / but an interior survey of your good selves! O that you could!

I know you can do very little on your own; you have plenty of helpers, or else your doings would be remarkably thin. Your abilities are too babyish to do much alone. You talk about pride: oh, if only you could turn your eyes round to the backs of your necks and take a good look inside your own good selves! Oh, if only you could!
Why, then you should discover a brace of unmeriting, proud, / violent, testy magistrates,—alias fools,—as any in Rome.
Why, then you'd find a pair of undeserving, proud, violent, bad-tempered magistrates, otherwise known as fools, as any in Rome.
Menenius, you are known well enough too.
Menenius, you're pretty well known too.

I am known to be a humorous patrician, and one that loves a cup / of hot wine with not a drop of allaying Tiber in't; said to / be something imperfect in favouring the first complaint, hasty / and tinder-like upon too trivial motion; one that converses more / with the buttock of the night than with the forehead of the / morning. What I think I utter, and spend my malice in my breath. / Meeting two such wealsmen as you are,—I cannot call you / Lycurguses,—if the drink you give me touch my palate adversely, / I make a crooked face at it. I cannot say your worships have / delivered the matter well when I find the ass in compound with / the major part of your syllables; and though I must be content to / bear with those that say you are reverend grave men, yet they lie / deadly that tell you have good faces. If you see this in the map / of my microcosm, follows it that I am known well enough too? What / harm can your bisson conspectuities glean out of this character, / if I be known well enough too?

I'm known as a whimsical patrician who loves a cup of hot wine without a drop of Tiber water to dilute it; said to be rather at fault for siding with whoever complains first, quick to flare up like tinder over trifles; one who keeps company with the backside of the night more than the brow of the morning. I say what I think, and use up my spite in talking. When I meet two statesmen like you (I can't call you great lawgivers like Lycurgus), if the drink you give me tastes bad, I pull a face at it. I can't say your worships have argued well when I find most of what you say is asinine; and though I have to put up with people who call you serious, respectable men, those who tell you you have good faces are lying through their teeth. If you can read this in the map of my little world, does it follow that I'm well known too? What harm can your blinkered sight pick out of this description, if I'm well known too?
Come, sir, come, we know you well enough.
Come, sir, come, we know you well enough.

You know neither me, yourselves, nor anything. You are ambitious / for poor knaves' caps and legs; you wear out a good wholesome / forenoon in hearing a cause between an orange-wife and a / fosset-seller, and then rejourn the controversy of threepence / to a second day of audience.—When you are hearing a matter / between party and party, if you chance to be pinched with the / colic, you make faces like mummers, set up the bloody flag / against all patience, and, in roaring for a chamber-pot, dismiss / the controversy bleeding, the more entangled by your hearing: all / the peace you make in their cause is calling both the parties / knaves. You are a pair of strange ones.

You know neither me, nor yourselves, nor anything. You're greedy for poor wretches to doff their caps and bow to you. You waste a whole good morning hearing a case between an orange-seller and a tap-maker, and then adjourn the threepenny dispute to a second day of hearing. When you're hearing a case between two parties, if you happen to get a stomach ache, you pull faces like clowns, raise the red flag of war against all patience, and, bellowing for a chamber pot, dismiss the case still bleeding, more tangled than before you heard it. The only peace you make between them is calling both sides scoundrels. You're a strange pair.
Come, come, you are well understood to be a perfecter giber / for the table than a necessary bencher in the Capitol.
Come, come, everyone knows you're better as a joker at the dinner table than as a useful judge in the Capitol.

Our very priests must become mockers if they shall encounter such / ridiculous subjects as you are. When you speak best unto the / purpose, it is not worth the wagging of your beards; and your / beards deserve not so honourable a grave as to stuff a botcher's / cushion or to be entombed in an ass's pack-saddle. Yet you must / be saying, Marcius is proud; who, in a cheap estimation, is worth / all your predecessors since Deucalion; though peradventure some / of the best of 'em were hereditary hangmen. God-den to your / worships: more of your conversation would infect my brain, being / the herdsmen of the beastly plebeians: I will be bold to take my / leave of you.

Even our priests would have to turn mockers if they met such ridiculous creatures as you. When you speak most to the point, it isn't worth the wagging of your beards, and your beards don't deserve so honourable a grave as stuffing a tailor's cushion or being buried in a donkey's saddle. Yet you have to keep saying Marcius is proud, a man who, at the lowest estimate, is worth all your ancestors since the Flood, though maybe some of the best of them were hangmen by family trade. Good evening to your worships. Any more of your conversation would infect my brain, since you're the herdsmen of those beastly plebeians. I'll make so bold as to take my leave of you.
How now, my as fair as noble ladies,—and the moon, were she / earthly, no nobler,—whither do you follow your eyes so fast?
Well now, my ladies, as beautiful as you are noble (and the moon, if she lived on earth, would be no nobler), where are you hurrying off to so fast?
Honourable Menenius, my boy Marcius approaches; for the love of / Juno, let's go.
Honourable Menenius, my boy Marcius is coming. For the love of Juno, let's go.
Ay, worthy Menenius, and with most prosperous approbation.
Yes, worthy Menenius, and with the greatest success and acclaim.
Take my cap, Jupiter, and I thank thee.—Hoo! Marcius coming / home!
Take my cap, Jupiter, and thank you! Hurrah! Marcius coming home!
Look, here's a letter from him: the state hath another, / his wife another; and I think there's one at home for you.
Look, here's a letter from him. The state has another, his wife another, and I think there's one at home for you.
I will make my very house reel to-night.—A letter for me?
I'll make my whole house shake with celebration tonight. A letter for me?
Yes, certain, there's a letter for you; I saw it.
Yes, certainly, there's a letter for you; I saw it.

A letter for me! It gives me an estate of seven years' / health; in which time I will make a lip at the physician: the / most sovereign prescription in Galen is but empiricutic, and, to / this preservative, of no better report than a horse-drench. Is he / not wounded? he was wont to come home wounded.

A letter for me! It gives me seven years of good health, during which I'll sneer at the doctor. The best prescription in Galen is just quackery and, next to this tonic, no better than horse medicine. Isn't he wounded? He usually comes home wounded.
O, he is wounded, I thank the gods for't.
Oh, he's wounded, and I thank the gods for it.
So do I too, if it be not too much.—Brings a victory in / his pocket?—The wounds become him.
So do I, as long as it's not too badly. Is he bringing a victory in his pocket? The wounds suit him.
On's brows: Menenius, he comes the third time home with the oaken / garland.
On his brows, Menenius. He's coming home for the third time with the oak garland.
Has he taught Aufidius a good lesson?
Titus Lartius writes,—they fought together, but Aufidius / got off.
Titus Lartius writes that they fought each other, but Aufidius got away.

And 'twas time for him too, I'll warrant him that: an he / had stayed by him, I would not have been so fidiused for all the / chests in Corioli and the gold that's in them. Is the Senate / possessed of this?
And it was high time he did, I promise you. If he'd stayed to face him, I wouldn't have wanted to be Aufidius'd like that for all the chests in Corioli and the gold in them. Has the Senate been told?
Good ladies, let's go.—Yes, yes, yes; the Senate has letters / from the general, wherein he gives my son the whole name of the / war: he hath in this action outdone his former deeds doubly.
Good ladies, let's go. Yes, yes, yes; the Senate has letters from the general in which he gives my son full credit for the war. In this campaign he has doubled his earlier deeds.
In troth, there's wondrous things spoke of him.
Honestly, people are saying wonderful things about him.
Wondrous! ay, I warrant you, and not without his true purchasing.
Wonderful! Yes, I'm sure, and not without his having truly earned them.
May the gods make them true!

True! I'll be sworn they are true. Where is he wounded?—[To the / TRIBUNES, who come forward.] God save your good worships! Marcius / is coming home; he has more cause to be proud.—Where is he / wounded?
True! I'll swear they're true. Where is he wounded? (To the Tribunes, who come forward) God save your worships! Marcius is coming home; he has more reason to be proud. Where is he wounded?
I' the shoulder and i' the left arm; there will be large / cicatrices to show the people when he shall stand for his place. / He received in the repulse of Tarquin seven hurts i' the body.
In the shoulder and the left arm. There'll be big scars to show the people when he stands for office. When Tarquin was driven out, he got seven wounds in the body.
One i' the neck and two i' the thigh,—there's nine that I / know.
One in the neck and two in the thigh; that's nine that I know of.
He had, before this last expedition, twenty-five wounds upon him.
Before this last campaign, he had twenty-five wounds on him.
Now it's twenty-seven: every gash was an enemy's grave.
Now it's twenty-seven; every gash was an enemy's grave.

These are the ushers of Marcius: before him / He carries noise, and behind him he leaves tears; / Death, that dark spirit, in's nervy arm doth lie; / Which, being advanc'd, declines, and then men die.
These are Marcius's heralds. He carries noise in front of him and leaves tears behind him. Death, that dark spirit, lies in his muscular arm, which rises, falls, and then men die.

Know, Rome, that all alone Marcius did fight / Within Corioli gates: where he hath won, / With fame, a name to Caius Marcius; these / In honour follows Coriolanus:— / Welcome to Rome, renowned Coriolanus!

Know, Rome, that Marcius fought all alone inside the gates of Corioli, where along with fame he has won a new name for Caius Marcius; in honour, Coriolanus follows those names. Welcome to Rome, famous Coriolanus!
No more of this, it does offend my heart; / Pray now, no more.
No more of this; it hurts my heart. Please, no more.
O, / You have, I know, petition'd all the gods / For my prosperity!
Oh, I know you have begged all the gods for my success!
Nay, my good soldier, up; / My gentle Marcius, worthy Caius, and / By deed-achieving honour newly nam'd,— / What is it?—Coriolanus must I call thee? / But, O, thy wife!
No, my good soldier, get up. My gentle Marcius, worthy Caius, newly named by honour won through deeds— what is it? Must I call you Coriolanus? But oh, your wife!
My gracious silence, hail! / Wouldst thou have laugh'd had I come coffin'd home, / That weep'st to see me triumph? Ah, my dear, / Such eyes the widows in Corioli wear, / And mothers that lack sons.

My dear silent one, greetings! Would you have laughed if I'd come home in a coffin, since you cry to see me in triumph? Ah, my dear, the widows in Corioli have eyes like yours, and so do mothers who have lost their sons.
Now may the gods crown you!
And live you yet? [To VALERIA]—O my sweet lady, pardon.
And you're still alive? (To Valeria) Oh my sweet lady, forgive me.
I know not where to turn.—O, welcome home;—and welcome, / general;—and you are welcome all.
I don't know which way to turn. Oh, welcome home; and welcome, general; and you're all welcome.

A hundred thousand welcomes.—I could weep / And I could laugh; I am light and heavy.—Welcome: / A curse begin at very root on's heart / That is not glad to see thee!—You are three / That Rome should dote on: yet, by the faith of men, / We have some old crab trees here at home that will not / Be grafted to your relish. Yet welcome, warriors. / We call a nettle but a nettle; and / The faults of fools but folly.

A hundred thousand welcomes. I could cry and I could laugh; I'm light-hearted and heavy-hearted. Welcome! May a curse strike right at the root of the heart of anyone who isn't glad to see you!
