You are three men Rome should dote on; and yet, I swear, we have some old crab-apple trees here at home who won't be grafted to your taste. Still, welcome, warriors. We call a nettle just a nettle, and the faults of fools just foolishness.
Give way there, and go on!
Make way there, and move on!

[To his wife and mother] Your hand, and yours: / Ere in our own house I do shade my head, / The good patricians must be visited; / From whom I have receiv'd not only greetings, / But with them change of honours.
(To his wife and mother) Your hand, and yours. Before I rest my head under our own roof, I must visit the good patricians, from whom I've received not only greetings but new honours with them.
I have lived / To see inherited my very wishes, / And the buildings of my fancy; only / There's one thing wanting, which I doubt not but / Our Rome will cast upon thee.
I've lived to see my dearest wishes come true and my imagined castles built. There's only one thing missing, and I'm sure our Rome will give it to you.
Know, good mother, / I had rather be their servant in my way / Than sway with them in theirs.
Understand, good mother, I'd rather be their servant my way than rule with them their way.

All tongues speak of him and the bleared sights / Are spectacled to see him: your prattling nurse / Into a rapture lets her baby cry / While she chats him: the kitchen malkin pins / Her richest lockram 'bout her reechy neck, / Clamb'ring the walls to eye him: stalls, bulks, windows, / Are smother'd up, leads fill'd and ridges hors'd / With variable complexions; all agreeing / In earnestness to see him: seld-shown flamens / Do press among the popular throngs, and puff / To win a vulgar station: our veil'd dames / Commit the war of white and damask, in / Their nicely gawded cheeks, to the wanton spoil / Of Phoebus' burning kisses; such a pother, / As if that whatsoever god who leads him / Were slily crept into his human powers, / And gave him graceful posture.

Everyone's talking about him, and people with bleary eyes put on spectacles to see him. The chattering nurse lets her baby scream itself into fits while she gossips about him. The kitchen maid pins her best linen round her grimy neck and climbs the walls to look at him. Stalls, shop fronts and windows are packed, roofs filled and rooftops straddled by all sorts of people, all equally eager to see him. Priests who rarely show themselves push into the crowds and puff and pant to get a place among the common people. Our veiled ladies let the war of white and red in their carefully made-up cheeks be ruined by the sun's burning kisses. Such a fuss, as if whatever god guides him had slipped secretly into his human body and given him grace.
On the sudden / I warrant him consul.
I'm sure he'll be made consul straight away.
Then our office may / During his power go sleep.
Then our office can go to sleep while he's in power.
He cannot temp'rately transport his honours / From where he should begin and end; but will / Lose those he hath won.
He can't carry his honours calmly from where he starts to where he should finish; he'll lose the ones he's won.

Doubt not the commoners, for whom we stand, / But they, upon their ancient malice will forget, / With the least cause these his new honours; which / That he will give them make as little question / As he is proud to do't.

Don't doubt that the common people we represent, because of their long-standing hatred, will forget these new honours of his at the slightest excuse; and there's as little doubt he'll give them one as there is that he's proud enough to do it.

I heard him swear, / Were he to stand for consul, never would he / Appear i' the market-place, nor on him put / The napless vesture of humility; / Nor, showing, as the manner is, his wounds / To the people, beg their stinking breaths.

I heard him swear that if he stood for consul, he'd never appear in the market square or put on the threadbare gown of humility, or show his wounds to the people, as the custom is, to beg for their stinking breath.
It was his word: O, he would miss it rather / Than carry it but by the suit of the gentry to him, / And the desire of the nobles.
That's what he said. Oh, he'd rather lose it than win it except by the request of the gentry and the wishes of the nobles.
I wish no better / Than have him hold that purpose, and to put it / In execution.
I couldn't wish for anything better than for him to stick to that plan and carry it out.
It shall be to him then, as our good wills, / A sure destruction.
Then it will be what we want: his certain ruin.

So it must fall out / To him or our authorities. For an end, / We must suggest the people in what hatred / He still hath held them; that to's power he would / Have made them mules, silenc'd their pleaders, and / Dispropertied their freedoms; holding them, / In human action and capacity, / Of no more soul nor fitness for the world / Than camels in their war; who have their provand / Only for bearing burdens, and sore blows / For sinking under them.

It has to turn out that way, for him or for our authority. To that end, we must remind the people how much he has always hated them: that if he'd had the power he'd have made them mules, silenced their spokesmen and stripped them of their freedoms; thinking of them, as human beings, as having no more soul or use in the world than camels in war, who get their food only for carrying loads and get hard blows when they sink under them.

This, as you say, suggested / At some time when his soaring insolence / Shall touch the people,—which time shall not want, / If it be put upon't; and that's as easy / As to set dogs on sheep,—will be his fire / To kindle their dry stubble; and their blaze / Shall darken him for ever.

If this is suggested, as you say, at some moment when his soaring arrogance offends the people (and such a moment won't be lacking if he's provoked into it, which is as easy as setting dogs on sheep), it will be the fire that sets their dry stubble alight, and the blaze will blacken him forever.

You are sent for to the Capitol. 'Tis thought / That Marcius shall be consul: / I have seen the dumb men throng to see him, and / The blind to hear him speak: matrons flung gloves, / Ladies and maids their scarfs and handkerchers, / Upon him as he pass'd; the nobles bended / As to Jove's statue; and the commons made / A shower and thunder with their caps and shouts: / I never saw the like.

You're called to the Capitol. They think Marcius will be made consul. I've seen the dumb crowd to see him and the blind to hear him speak. Married women threw gloves at him as he passed, ladies and girls their scarves and handkerchiefs; the nobles bowed as if to Jupiter's statue, and the common people made a storm of thunder with their caps and shouts. I've never seen anything like it.
Let's to the Capitol; / And carry with us ears and eyes for the time, / But hearts for the event.
Let's go to the Capitol, and take ears and eyes for what's happening now, but our hearts set on how it will end.
Come, come; they are almost here. How many stand for consulships?
Come on, come on; they're nearly here. How many are standing for the consulship?
Three, they say; but 'tis thought of every one Coriolanus will / carry it.
Three, they say; but everyone thinks Coriolanus will win it.
That's a brave fellow; but he's vengeance proud and loves not the / common people.
He's a fine fellow, but he's terribly proud and doesn't love the common people.

Faith, there have been many great men that have flattered the / people, who ne'er loved them; and there be many that they have / loved, they know not wherefore; so that, if they love they know / not why, they hate upon no better a ground: therefore, for / Coriolanus neither to care whether they love or hate him / manifests the true knowledge he has in their disposition; and, / out of his noble carelessness, lets them plainly see't.

Well, there have been plenty of great men who flattered the people without ever loving them, and plenty whom the people have loved without knowing why. So if they love without knowing why, they hate for no better reason. So Coriolanus not caring whether they love or hate him shows he truly understands their nature, and his noble indifference lets them see it plainly.

If he did not care whether he had their love or no, he waved / indifferently 'twixt doing them neither good nor harm; but he / seeks their hate with greater devotion than they can render it / him; and leaves nothing undone that may fully discover him their / opposite. Now to seem to affect the malice and displeasure of the / people is as bad as that which he dislikes,—to flatter them for / their love.

If he didn't care whether he had their love or not, he'd sit neutrally between doing them good and doing them harm. But he goes looking for their hatred more eagerly than they can return it, and does everything he can to show he's against them. Seeming to court the people's ill will and anger is as bad as what he dislikes, flattering them for their love.

He hath deserved worthily of his country: and his ascent is not / by such easy degrees as those who, having been supple and / courteous to the people, bonnetted, without any further deed to / have them at all, into their estimation and report: but he hath / so planted his honours in their eyes, and his actions in their / hearts, that for their tongues to be silent, and not confess / so much, were a kind of ingrateful injury; to report otherwise / were a malice that, giving itself the lie, would pluck reproof / and rebuke from every ear that heard it.

He has served his country well, and his rise hasn't come by easy steps like those who were smooth and polite to the people and doffed their caps their way into the people's good opinion without doing anything else. He has planted his honours so firmly in their eyes and his deeds in their hearts that for their tongues to stay silent and not admit it would be an ungrateful wrong. To say otherwise would be malice that proves itself a liar and earns rebuke from everyone who heard it.
No more of him; he is a worthy man: make way, they are coming.
No more about him; he's a worthy man. Make way, they're coming.

Having determined of the Volsces, and / To send for Titus Lartius, it remains, / As the main point of this our after-meeting, / To gratify his noble service that / Hath thus stood for his country: therefore please you, / Most reverend and grave elders, to desire / The present consul, and last general / In our well-found successes, to report / A little of that worthy work perform'd / By Caius Marcius Coriolanus; whom / We met here both to thank and to remember / With honours like himself.

Having settled what to do about the Volscians and to send for Titus Lartius, it remains, as the main point of this further meeting, to reward the noble service of the man who has stood up for his country in this way. So may it please you, most reverend and serious elders, to ask the present consul, our general in these well-won victories, to tell us a little of the worthy work done by Caius Marcius Coriolanus, whom we've met here both to thank and to honour as he deserves.

Speak, good Cominius: / Leave nothing out for length, and make us think / Rather our state's defective for requital / Than we to stretch it out.—Masters o' the people, / We do request your kindest ears; and, after, / Your loving motion toward the common body, / To yield what passes here.

Speak, good Cominius. Leave nothing out to save time, and make us think our state lacks the means to reward him rather than that we lack the will. Representatives of the people, we ask you to listen kindly, and afterwards to use your influence with the common people to agree to what's decided here.
We are convented / Upon a pleasing treaty; and have hearts / Inclinable to honour and advance / The theme of our assembly.
We've been called together for a pleasant purpose, and our hearts are inclined to honour and support the subject of this meeting.
Which the rather / We shall be bless'd to do, if he remember / A kinder value of the people than / He hath hereto priz'd them at.
Which we'll be all the happier to do if he values the people more kindly than he has up to now.
That's off, that's off; / I would you rather had been silent. Please you / To hear Cominius speak?
That's beside the point, beside the point. I wish you'd kept quiet. Will you please hear Cominius speak?
Most willingly. / But yet my caution was more pertinent / Than the rebuke you give it.
Very willingly. But my warning was more to the point than your rebuke.
He loves your people; / But tie him not to be their bedfellow.— / Worthy Cominius, speak.
He loves your people, but don't insist he sleep with them. Worthy Cominius, speak.
Sit, Coriolanus; never shame to hear / What you have nobly done.
Sit down, Coriolanus. Never be ashamed to hear about what you've nobly done.
Your Honours' pardon: / I had rather have my wounds to heal again / Than hear say how I got them.
Forgive me, your honours. I'd rather have my wounds to heal all over again than hear how I got them.
Sir, I hope / My words disbench'd you not.
Sir, I hope my words didn't drive you from your seat.
No, sir; yet oft, / When blows have made me stay, I fled from words. / You sooth'd not, therefore hurt not: but your people, / I love them as they weigh.
No, sir; but often, when blows made me stand my ground, I've run from words. You didn't flatter me, so you didn't hurt me. But your people, I love them as much as they're worth.
I had rather have one scratch my head i' the sun / When the alarum were struck, than idly sit / To hear my nothings monster'd.
I'd rather have someone scratch my head in the sun when the call to arms was sounded than sit idly listening to my trifles blown up into monsters.

Masters o' the people, / Your multiplying spawn how can he flatter,— / That's thousand to one good one,—when you now see / He had rather venture all his limbs for honour / Than one on's ears to hear it?—Proceed, Cominius.

Representatives of the people, how can he flatter your swarming spawn (there's one good one in a thousand) when you see he'd rather risk all his limbs for honour than one of his ears to hear about it? Go on, Cominius.

I shall lack voice: the deeds of Coriolanus / Should not be utter'd feebly.—It is held / That valour is the chiefest virtue, and / Most dignifies the haver: if it be, / The man I speak of cannot in the world / Be singly counterpois'd. At sixteen years, / When Tarquin made a head for Rome, he fought / Beyond the mark of others; our then dictator, / Whom with all praise I point at, saw him fight, / When with his Amazonian chin he drove / The bristled lips before him: he bestrid / An o'erpress'd Roman and i' the consul's view / Slew three opposers: Tarquin's self he met, / And struck him on his knee: in that day's feats, / When he might act the woman in the scene, / He proved best man i' the field, and for his meed / Was brow-bound with the oak. His pupil age / Man-enter'd thus, he waxed like a sea; / And in the brunt of seventeen battles since / He lurch'd all swords of the garland. For this last, / Before and in Corioli, let me say, / I cannot speak him home: he stopp'd the fliers; / And by his rare example made the coward / Turn terror into sport: as weeds before / A vessel under sail, so men obey'd, / And fell below his stem: his sword,—death's stamp,— / Where it did mark, it took; from face to foot / He was a thing of blood, whose every motion / Was timed with dying cries: alone he enter'd / The mortal gate of the city, which he painted / With shunless destiny; aidless came off, / And with a sudden re-enforcement struck / Corioli like a planet. Now all's his: / When, by and by, the din of war 'gan pierce / His ready sense; then straight his doubled spirit / Re-quick'ned what in flesh was fatigate, / And to the battle came he; where he did / Run reeking o'er the lives of men, as if / 'Twere a perpetual spoil: and till we call'd / Both field and city ours he never stood / To ease his breast with panting.

I won't have voice enough; the deeds of Coriolanus shouldn't be told feebly. It's said that courage is the greatest virtue and brings most honour to whoever has it. If so, the man I'm speaking of has no equal in the world. At sixteen, when Tarquin raised an army against Rome, he fought better than anyone. Our dictator then, whom I name with all praise, saw him fight, when with his beardless, Amazon-like chin he drove bearded men before him. He stood over a Roman who'd been knocked down and, in the consul's sight, killed three attackers. He met Tarquin himself and struck him to his knee. In that day's deeds, when he was young enough to play a woman's part on stage, he proved the best man on the field, and as his reward he was crowned with oak leaves. Having entered manhood like that in his boyhood, he grew like a rising sea, and in the shock of seventeen battles since then he has robbed every other sword of the garland. As for this last one, at and in Corioli, let me say I can't praise him enough. He stopped the men who were running away and by his rare example made cowards treat terror as a game. Like weeds before a ship under sail, men gave way and fell beneath his prow. His sword, death's seal, took whatever it marked. From head to foot he was a thing of blood, every movement keeping time with dying cries. Alone he entered the deadly city gate, which he painted with the blood of men who couldn't escape their fate; he got out without help, and with sudden reinforcements struck Corioli like a planet's evil influence. Now it's all his. Then, when the noise of battle reached his alert ears, his doubled spirit revived his tired body, and he came to the battle, where he ran steaming over men's lives as if it would be endless slaughter. Until we could call both field and city ours, he never stopped to let his chest rest from panting.
He cannot but with measure fit the honours / Which we devise him.
He's fully equal to whatever honours we plan for him.

Our spoils he kick'd at; / And looked upon things precious as they were / The common muck of the world: he covets less / Than misery itself would give; rewards / His deeds with doing them; and is content / To spend the time to end it.

He kicked away our loot and looked on precious things as if they were the common dirt of the world. He wants less than poverty itself would give. He rewards his deeds by doing them, and is happy to spend his time just to fill it.
He's right noble: / Let him be call'd for.
He's truly noble. Let him be called in.
The Senate, Coriolanus, are well pleas'd / To make thee consul.
Coriolanus, the Senate is pleased to make you consul.
I do owe them still / My life and services.
I still owe them my life and my services.
It then remains / That you do speak to the people.
Then it only remains for you to speak to the people.
I do beseech you / Let me o'erleap that custom; for I cannot / Put on the gown, stand naked, and entreat them, / For my wounds' sake to give their suffrage: please you / That I may pass this doing.
I beg you, let me skip that custom. I can't put on the gown, stand there bare, and beg them to vote for me because of my wounds. Please let me be spared doing that.
Sir, the people / Must have their voices; neither will they bate / One jot of ceremony.
Sir, the people must have their votes; nor will they give up one bit of the ceremony.
Put them not to't:— / Pray you, go fit you to the custom; and / Take to you, as your predecessors have, / Your honour with your form.
Don't push them on it. Please go and follow the custom, and take your honour together with its formalities, as those before you did.
It is a part / That I shall blush in acting, and might well / Be taken from the people.
It's a part I'll blush to act, and it could well be taken away from the people.
To brag unto them,—thus I did, and thus;— / Show them the unaching scars which I should hide, / As if I had receiv'd them for the hire / Of their breath only!
To boast to them, "I did this, and this"; to show them healed scars I ought to hide, as if I'd got them only to buy their votes!
Do not stand upon't.— / We recommend to you, tribunes of the people, / Our purpose to them;—and to our noble consul / Wish we all joy and honour.
Don't insist on it. Tribunes of the people, we leave our proposal to you to put to them; and to our noble consul we all wish joy and honour.
To Coriolanus come all joy and honour!
May all joy and honour come to Coriolanus!
You see how he intends to use the people.
You see how he means to treat the people.
May they perceive's intent! He will require them / As if he did contemn what he requested / Should be in them to give.
I hope they see what he intends! He'll ask them as if he despised the idea that it's in their power to give what he asks.
Come, we'll inform them / Of our proceedings here: on the market-place / I know they do attend us.
Come, we'll tell them what happened here. I know they're waiting for us in the market square.
Once, if he do require our voices, we ought not to deny him.
Once and for all, if he asks for our votes, we shouldn't refuse him.
We may, sir, if we will.
We can, sir, if we want to.

We have power in ourselves to do it, but it is a power that we / have no power to do: for if he show us his wounds and tell us his / deeds, we are to put our tongues into those wounds and speak for / them; so, if he tell us his noble deeds, we must also tell him / our noble acceptance of them. Ingratitude is monstrous: and for / the multitude to be ingrateful were to make a monster of the / multitude; of the which we being members, should bring ourselves / to be monstrous members.

We have the power to do it in ourselves, but it's a power we have no power to use. If he shows us his wounds and tells us his deeds, we have to put our tongues into those wounds and speak for them. So if he tells us his noble deeds, we must tell him we nobly accept them. Ingratitude is monstrous, and for the crowd to be ungrateful would make a monster of the crowd; and since we're members of it, we'd turn ourselves into monstrous members.
And to make us no better thought of, a little help will serve; / for once we stood up about the corn, he himself stuck not to call / us the many-headed multitude.
And it won't take much to make us thought no better of; because once, when we rose up over the grain, he didn't hesitate to call us the many-headed mob.

We have been called so of many; not that our heads are some / brown, some black, some auburn, some bald, but that our wits are / so diversely coloured; and truly I think if all our wits were to / issue out of one skull, they would fly east, west, north, south; / and their consent of one direct way should be at once to all the / points o' the compass.

Lots of people have called us that, not because some of our heads are brown, some black, some auburn, some bald, but because our wits are so many different colours. And honestly, I think if all our wits came out of one skull, they'd fly east, west, north and south, and the only direction they'd agree on would be all points of the compass at once.
Think you so? Which way do you judge my wit would fly?
You think so? Which way do you reckon my wit would fly?
Nay, your wit will not so soon out as another man's will,—'tis / strongly wedged up in a block-head; but if it were at liberty / 'twould, sure, southward.
Well, your wit wouldn't get out as quickly as another man's; it's jammed tight in a blockhead. But if it were free, it would surely go south.
To lose itself in a fog; where being three parts melted away with / rotten dews, the fourth would return for conscience' sake, to / help to get thee a wife.
To lose itself in a fog, where, once three-quarters of it had melted away in rotten dews, the fourth part would come back out of conscience to help you get a wife.
You are never without your tricks:—you may, you may.
You're always up to your tricks. Go on, go on.

Are you all resolved to give your voices? But that's no matter, / the greater part carries it. I say, if he would incline to the / people, there was never a worthier man. Here he comes, and in the / gown of humility. Mark his behaviour. We are not to stay all / together, but to come by him where he stands, by ones, by twos, / and by threes. He's to make his requests by particulars, wherein / every one of us has a single honour, in giving him our own voices / with our own tongues; therefore follow me, and I'll direct you / how you shall go by him.

Are you all determined to give your votes? But it doesn't matter; the majority decides. I say, if he were well disposed to the people, there was never a worthier man. Here he comes, in the gown of humility. Watch how he behaves. We're not to stay all together but go up to him where he stands in ones, twos and threes. He has to make his requests one by one, so each of us gets the honour of giving him our own vote with our own tongue. So follow me, and I'll show you how to go up to him.
O sir, you are not right; have you not known / The worthiest men have done't!
Oh sir, you've got it wrong. Don't you know the worthiest men have done it?

What must I say?— / 'I pray, sir'—Plague upon't! I cannot bring / My tongue to such a pace.—'Look, sir,—my wounds;— / I got them in my country's service, when / Some certain of your brethren roar'd, and ran / From the noise of our own drums.'

What must I say? "Please, sir"? A plague on it! I can't get my tongue to go at that pace. "Look, sir, my wounds. I got them serving my country, when some of your brothers roared and ran away from the noise of our own drums."
O me, the gods! / You must not speak of that: you must desire them / To think upon you.
Oh my, the gods! You mustn't mention that. You must ask them to think well of you.
Think upon me! Hang 'em! / I would they would forget me, like the virtues / Which our divines lose by 'em.
Think of me! Hang them! I wish they'd forget me, like the moral lessons our priests waste on them.
You'll mar all: / I'll leave you. Pray you speak to 'em, I pray you, / In wholesome manner.
You'll ruin everything. I'll leave you. Please speak to them, I beg you, in a decent way.
Bid them wash their faces / And keep their teeth clean.
Tell them to wash their faces and keep their teeth clean.
You know the cause, sirs, of my standing here.
You know why I'm standing here, sirs.
We do, sir; tell us what hath brought you to't.
We do, sir. Tell us what brought you to it.
No, sir, 'twas never my desire yet to trouble the poor with / begging.
No, sir; it was never my desire to trouble the poor by begging.
You must think, if we give you anything, we hope to gain by you.
You must realize that if we give you anything, we hope to get something from you.
Well then, I pray, your price o' the consulship?
Well then, tell me, what's your price for the consulship?
The price is to ask it kindly.
The price is to ask for it nicely.
Kindly! sir, I pray, let me ha't: I have wounds to show you, / which shall be yours in private.—Your good voice, sir; what / say you?
Nicely! Sir, please, let me have it. I have wounds to show you, which you can see in private. Your good vote, sir; what do you say?
You shall ha' it, worthy sir.
A match, sir.—There's in all two worthy voices begg'd.—I have / your alms: adieu.
It's a deal, sir. That's two worthy votes begged in all. I have your charity. Goodbye.
An 'twere to give again,—but 'tis no matter.
If it were to do over again— but it doesn't matter.
Pray you now, if it may stand with the tune of your voices that I / may be consul, I have here the customary gown.
Please, if it suits the tune of your voices that I should be consul, I have the customary gown on here.
You have deserved nobly of your country, and you have not / deserved nobly.
You've served your country nobly, and you haven't served it nobly.
You have been a scourge to her enemies; you have been a rod to / her friends: you have not indeed loved the common people.
You've been a scourge to her enemies, and a rod to her friends. You haven't really loved the common people.

You should account me the more virtuous, that I have not been / common in my love. I will, sir, flatter my sworn brother, the / people, to earn a dearer estimation of them; 'tis a condition / they account gentle: and since the wisdom of their choice is / rather to have my hat than my heart, I will practise the / insinuating nod and be off to them most counterfeitly: that is, / sir, I will counterfeit the bewitchment of some popular man / and give it bountifully to the desirers. Therefore, beseech you, / I may be consul.

You should think me all the more virtuous for not being common with my love. Sir, I'll flatter my sworn brother, the people, to win a higher opinion from them; that's a quality they think gentlemanly. And since in their wisdom they'd rather have my hat than my heart, I'll practise the ingratiating nod and doff my cap to them as falsely as possible; that is, sir, I'll imitate the charm of some popular man and hand it out generously to those who want it. So I beg you, let me be consul.
We hope to find you our friend; and therefore give you our voices / heartily.
We hope you'll be our friend, so we give you our votes gladly.
You have received many wounds for your country.
You've received many wounds for your country.
I will not seal your knowledge with showing them. I will make / much of your voices, and so trouble you no further.
I won't confirm what you know by showing them. I'll value your votes highly, and so trouble you no further.
The gods give you joy, sir, heartily!
The gods give you joy, sir, truly!

Most sweet voices!— / Better it is to die, better to starve, / Than crave the hire which first we do deserve. / Why in this wolvish toge should I stand here, / To beg of Hob and Dick that do appear, / Their needless vouches? custom calls me to't:— / What custom wills, in all things should we do't, / The dust on antique time would lie unswept, / And mountainous error be too highly heap'd / For truth to o'erpeer. Rather than fool it so, / Let the high office and the honour go / To one that would do thus.—I am half through; / The one part suffer'd, the other will I do. / Here come more voices.

Sweetest voices! It's better to die, better to starve, than beg for the reward we've already earned. Why should I stand here in this wolfish gown begging every Tom, Dick and Harry who comes along for their unnecessary approval? Custom makes me do it. If we did whatever custom wanted in everything, the dust of ancient times would lie unswept, and mountains of error would pile up too high for truth to see over them. Rather than play the fool like this, let the high office and the honour go to someone who would. I'm halfway through; I've suffered one half, I'll do the other. Here come more voices.

Your voices: for your voices I have fought; / Watch'd for your voices; for your voices bear / Of wounds two dozen odd; battles thrice six / I have seen and heard of; for your voices have / Done many things, some less, some more: your voices: / Indeed, I would be consul.

Your votes! For your votes I have fought; for your votes I've kept watch; for your votes I carry two dozen or so wounds; I've seen and heard of eighteen battles; for your votes I've done many things, some small, some great. Your votes! Truly, I'd like to be consul.
He has done nobly, and cannot go without any honest man's voice.
He has acted nobly, and no honest man can refuse him his vote.
Therefore let him be consul: the gods give him joy, and make him / good friend to the people!
So let him be consul. The gods give him joy and make him a good friend to the people!
Amen, amen.—God save thee, noble consul!
Amen, amen. God save you, noble consul!
You have stood your limitation; and the tribunes / Endue you with the people's voice:—remains / That, in the official marks invested, you / Anon do meet the senate.
You've stood the required time, and the tribunes give you the people's vote. All that remains is for you to put on the robes of office and meet the senate shortly.
The custom of request you have discharg'd: / The people do admit you; and are summon'd / To meet anon, upon your approbation.
You've carried out the custom of asking. The people accept you and are called to meet soon to confirm their approval.
That I'll straight do; and, knowing myself again, / Repair to the senate-house.
I'll do that at once, and when I'm myself again, I'll go to the senate house.
I'll keep you company.—Will you along?
I'll go with you. (To the Tribunes) Are you coming?
We stay here for the people.
We're staying here for the people.
He has it now; and by his looks methinks / 'Tis warm at his heart.
He has it now, and from his looks I think he's glowing inside.
With a proud heart he wore his humble weeds. / Will you dismiss the people?
He wore his humble clothes with a proud heart. Will you dismiss the people?
How now, my masters! have you chose this man?
Well, my friends! Have you chosen this man?
We pray the gods he may deserve your loves.
We pray the gods he'll deserve your love.
Amen, sir:—to my poor unworthy notice, / He mocked us when he begg'd our voices.
Amen, sir. In my poor, humble opinion, he was mocking us when he begged for our votes.
Certainly. He openly sneered at us.
No, 'tis his kind of speech,—he did not mock us.
No, it's just his way of talking. He didn't mock us.
Not one amongst us, save yourself, but says / He us'd us scornfully: he should have show'd us / His marks of merit, wounds received for's country.
Not one of us except you doesn't say he treated us with scorn. He should have shown us the marks of his merit, the wounds he got for his country.
Why, so he did, I am sure.

He said he had wounds, which he could show in private; / And with his hat, thus waving it in scorn, / 'I would be consul,' says he; 'aged custom / But by your voices, will not so permit me; / Your voices therefore:' when we granted that, / Here was, 'I thank you for your voices,—thank you,— / Your most sweet voices:—now you have left your voices / I have no further with you:'—was not this mockery?

He said he had wounds he could show in private, and waving his hat scornfully like this, "I'd like to be consul," he says; "ancient custom won't allow me unless I have your votes; so, your votes." When we agreed, it was, "Thank you for your votes, thank you, your sweetest votes. Now that you've handed over your votes, I've nothing more to do with you." Wasn't that mockery?
Why either were you ignorant to see't? / Or, seeing it, of such childish friendliness / To yield your voices?
Why, were you too ignorant to see it? Or, seeing it, so childishly friendly as to give him your votes?

Could you not have told him, / As you were lesson'd,—when he had no power, / But was a petty servant to the state, / He was your enemy; ever spake against / Your liberties, and the charters that you bear / I' the body of the weal: and now, arriving / A place of potency and sway o' the state, / If he should still malignantly remain / Fast foe to the plebeii, your voices might / Be curses to yourselves? You should have said, / That as his worthy deeds did claim no less / Than what he stood for, so his gracious nature / Would think upon you for your voices, and / Translate his malice towards you into love, / Standing your friendly lord.

Couldn't you have told him, as you'd been taught, that when he had no power and was only a minor servant of the state, he was your enemy, always speaking against your liberties and the rights you hold in the commonwealth; and that now he's reaching a position of power and control in the state, if he stayed spitefully your firm enemy, your votes might turn into curses on yourselves? You should have said that, just as his worthy deeds deserved nothing less than what he was asking for, so his gracious nature should remember you for your votes and turn his malice towards you into love, as your friendly lord.

Thus to have said, / As you were fore-advis'd, had touch'd his spirit / And tried his inclination; from him pluck'd / Either his gracious promise, which you might, / As cause had call'd you up, have held him to; / Or else it would have gall'd his surly nature, / Which easily endures not article / Tying him to aught; so, putting him to rage, / You should have ta'en the advantage of his choler / And pass'd him unelected.

Saying that, as you'd been advised, would have tested his spirit and tried his intentions. It would have dragged out of him either a gracious promise, which you could have held him to when the need came, or else it would have irritated his surly nature, which can't easily bear any condition that binds him. Then, having put him in a rage, you could have taken advantage of his anger and left him unelected.

Did you perceive / He did solicit you in free contempt / When he did need your loves; and do you think / That his contempt shall not be bruising to you / When he hath power to crush? Why, had your bodies / No heart among you? Or had you tongues to cry / Against the rectorship of judgment?

Didn't you see that he asked for your votes with open contempt when he needed your love? And don't you think his contempt will crush you when he has the power to crush? Why, didn't your bodies have a single heart among them? Or did you have tongues only to cry out against good sense?
Have you / Ere now denied the asker, and now again, / Of him that did not ask but mock, bestow / Your su'd-for tongues?
Have you refused people who asked before now, and now give your sought-after votes to a man who didn't ask but mocked?
He's not confirm'd: we may deny him yet.
He isn't confirmed yet; we can still refuse him.
And will deny him: / I'll have five hundred voices of that sound.
And we will refuse him. I'll get five hundred votes to say so.
I twice five hundred, and their friends to piece 'em.
I'll get a thousand, and their friends to add to them.

Get you hence instantly; and tell those friends / They have chose a consul that will from them take / Their liberties, make them of no more voice / Than dogs, that are as often beat for barking / As therefore kept to do so.
Go at once and tell those friends they've chosen a consul who'll take their liberties away and give them no more voice than dogs, which are beaten for barking as often as they're kept to bark.

Let them assemble; / And, on a safer judgment, all revoke / Your ignorant election: enforce his pride / And his old hate unto you: besides, forget not / With what contempt he wore the humble weed; / How in his suit he scorn'd you: but your loves, / Thinking upon his services, took from you / Th' apprehension of his present portance, / Which, most gibingly, ungravely, he did fashion / After the inveterate hate he bears you.

Let them assemble and, on second thoughts, all cancel your ignorant choice. Stress his pride and his old hatred of you. And don't forget how scornfully he wore the humble gown, how he despised you while asking. But your love, thinking of his services, stopped you noticing how he was behaving now, which he shaped, in the most mocking and frivolous way, out of his deep-rooted hatred of you.
Lay / A fault on us, your tribunes; that we labour'd,— / No impediment between,—but that you must / Cast your election on him.
Put the blame on us, your tribunes: say that we worked hard, letting nothing stand in the way, to make sure you voted for him.

Say you chose him / More after our commandment than as guided / By your own true affections; and that your minds, / Pre-occupied with what you rather must do / Than what you should, made you against the grain / To voice him consul. Lay the fault on us.

Say you chose him more because we told you to than guided by your own true feelings, and that your minds, full of what you had to do rather than what you should do, made you vote him consul against your will. Put the blame on us.

Ay, spare us not. Say we read lectures to you, / How youngly he began to serve his country, / How long continued: and what stock he springs of— / The noble house o' the Marcians; from whence came / That Ancus Marcius, Numa's daughter's son, / Who, after great Hostilius, here was king; / Of the same house Publius and Quintus were, / That our best water brought by conduits hither; / And Censorinus, darling of the people, / And nobly nam'd so, twice being censor, / Was his great ancestor.

Yes, don't spare us. Say we lectured you on how young he was when he started serving his country, how long he has continued, and what family he comes from: the noble house of the Marcii, which produced that Ancus Marcius, grandson of Numa, who was king here after great Hostilius; Publius and Quintus, who brought our best water here by aqueducts, were of the same house; and Censorinus, the people's darling, so nobly named because he was censor twice, was his great ancestor.

One thus descended, / That hath beside well in his person wrought / To be set high in place, we did commend / To your remembrances: but you have found, / Scaling his present bearing with his past, / That he's your fixed enemy, and revoke / Your sudden approbation.

We recommended to you a man descended like this, who had besides done enough personally to be given high office. But you've found, weighing how he behaves now against his past, that he's your fixed enemy, and so you withdraw your hasty approval.
Say you ne'er had done't,— / Harp on that still,—but by our putting on: / And presently when you have drawn your number, / Repair to the Capitol.
Say you'd never have done it except that we urged you (keep harping on that), and as soon as you've gathered your numbers, go to the Capitol.
We will so; almost all / Repent in their election.
We'll do that. Almost everyone regrets their choice.

Let them go on; / This mutiny were better put in hazard / Than stay, past doubt, for greater: / If, as his nature is, he fall in rage / With their refusal, both observe and answer / The vantage of his anger.

Let them go on. It's better to risk this riot now than wait for a certain greater one later. If, as is his nature, he flies into a rage at their refusal, we must watch for and use the advantage his anger gives us.
To the Capitol, / Come: we will be there before the stream o' the people; / And this shall seem, as partly 'tis, their own, / Which we have goaded onward.
To the Capitol, come. We'll get there before the flood of people, and this will look like their own doing, as it partly is, though we've driven it on.
Tullus Aufidius, then, had made new head?
So Tullus Aufidius had raised a new army?
He had, my lord; and that it was which caus'd / Our swifter composition.
He had, my lord, and that's why we made peace terms so quickly.
So then the Volsces stand but as at first; / Ready, when time shall prompt them, to make road / Upon's again.
So the Volscians are just where they were at first, ready to raid us again when the time's right.
They are worn, lord consul, so / That we shall hardly in our ages see / Their banners wave again.
They're so worn out, lord consul, that we'll hardly see their banners wave again in our lifetimes.
On safeguard he came to me; and did curse / Against the Volsces, for they had so vilely / Yielded the town; he is retir'd to Antium.
He came to me under a safe-conduct and cursed the Volscians for giving up the town so shamefully. He has withdrawn to Antium.

How often he had met you, sword to sword; / That of all things upon the earth he hated / Your person most; that he would pawn his fortunes / To hopeless restitution, so he might / Be call'd your vanquisher.
How often he had met you sword to sword; that of everything on earth he hated you most; that he would pledge all his fortunes beyond hope of recovery just to be called your conqueror.
I wish I had a cause to seek him there, / To oppose his hatred fully.—Welcome home. [To LARTIUS]
I wish I had a reason to go and find him there, to meet his hatred head on. (To Lartius) Welcome home.
Behold! these are the tribunes of the people; / The tongues o' the common mouth. I do despise them, / For they do prank them in authority, / Against all noble sufferance.
Look! These are the tribunes of the people, the tongues of the common mouth. I despise them, because they show off their authority beyond what any noble person can stand.
It will be dangerous to go on: no further.
It will be dangerous to go on. No further.
Hath he not pass'd the noble and the commons?
Hasn't he been approved by the nobles and the commoners?
Tribunes, give way; he shall to the market-place.
Tribunes, make way; he's going to the market square.
The people are incens'd against him.
The people are furious with him.
Stop, / Or all will fall in broil.
Stop, or everything will fall into chaos.

Are these your herd?— / Must these have voices, that can yield them now, / And straight disclaim their tongues?—What are your offices? / You being their mouths, why rule you not their teeth? / Have you not set them on?

Are these your herd? Must these people have votes, who give them one moment and take them back the next? What's your job? Since you're their mouths, why don't you control their teeth? Didn't you set them on?
It is a purpos'd thing, and grows by plot, / To curb the will of the nobility: / Suffer't, and live with such as cannot rule, / Nor ever will be rul'd.
It's deliberate, a growing plot to curb the will of the nobility. Put up with it, and you'll live with people who can't rule and will never be ruled.

Call't not a plot: / The people cry you mock'd them; and of late, / When corn was given them gratis, you repin'd; / Scandal'd the suppliants for the people,—call'd them / Time-pleasers, flatterers, foes to nobleness.

Don't call it a plot. The people say you mocked them, and recently, when grain was given to them free, you complained and slandered the people's representatives, calling them time-servers, flatterers and enemies of nobility.
You are like to do such businesss.
It's just the kind of thing you'd do.
Not unlike, / Each way, to better yours.
Not unlikely; and every way better than you'd do yours.
Why, then, should I be consul? By yond clouds, / Let me deserve so ill as you, and make me / Your fellow tribune.
Then why should I be consul? By those clouds, let me be as worthless as you, and make me your fellow tribune.

You show too much of that / For which the people stir: if you will pass / To where you are bound, you must inquire your way, / Which you are out of, with a gentler spirit; / Or never be so noble as a consul, / Nor yoke with him for tribune.

You're showing too much of what the people are angry about. If you want to get where you're going, you must ask the way, which you've lost, in a gentler spirit; or else you'll never be so noble as a consul, nor even be paired with him as a tribune.
The people are abus'd; set on. This palt'ring / Becomes not Rome; nor has Coriolanus / Deserv'd this so dishonour'd rub, laid falsely / I' the plain way of his merit.
The people have been deceived; they've been stirred up. This trickery doesn't suit Rome, and Coriolanus hasn't deserved this shameful obstacle, falsely placed on the smooth road his merit has earned.
Tell me of corn! / This was my speech, and I will speak't again,—
Talk to me about grain! This was what I said, and I'll say it again—
Not in this heat, sir, now.
Not in this heat, sir, not now.

Now, as I live, I will.—My nobler friends, / I crave their pardons: / For the mutable, rank-scented many, let them / Regard me as I do not flatter, and / Therein behold themselves: I say again, / In soothing them we nourish 'gainst our senate / The cockle of rebellion, insolence, sedition, / Which we ourselves have plough'd for, sow'd, and scatter'd, / By mingling them with us, the honour'd number, / Who lack not virtue, no, nor power, but that / Which they have given to beggars.

Now, as I live, I will. My nobler friends, I ask your pardon. As for the fickle, foul-smelling mob, let them look at me, since I don't flatter, and see themselves in what I say. I say again: by humouring them we're growing the weeds of rebellion, insolence and riot against our senate, which we ourselves ploughed for, sowed and scattered by mixing them with us, the honoured few, who lack no virtue, no, nor power either, except what we've given away to beggars.
No more words, we beseech you.
No more words, we beg you.

How! no more! / As for my country I have shed my blood, / Not fearing outward force, so shall my lungs / Coin words till their decay against those measles / Which we disdain should tetter us, yet sought / The very way to catch them.

What! No more! Just as I've shed my blood for my country, not fearing enemies abroad, so my lungs will keep making words until they give out, against these scabs we'd hate to be covered with, yet we went looking for the very way to catch them.
You speak o' the people / As if you were a god, to punish, not / A man of their infirmity.
You speak of the people as if you were a god sent to punish them, not a man as weak as they are.
'Twere well / We let the people know't.
It would be good to let the people know that.
Choler! / Were I as patient as the midnight sleep, / By Jove, 'twould be my mind!
Temper! If I were as patient as midnight sleep, by Jove, I'd still think the same!
It is a mind / That shall remain a poison where it is, / Not poison any further.
It's a way of thinking that will stay a poison where it is, and poison nothing further.
Shall remain!— / Hear you this Triton of the minnows? mark you / His absolute 'shall'?
"Will stay"! Do you hear this Triton of the minnows? Did you notice his commanding "will"?

'Shall'! / O good, but most unwise patricians! why, / You grave but reckless senators, have you thus / Given Hydra leave to choose an officer, / That with his peremptory 'shall,' being but / The horn and noise o' the monster, wants not spirit / To say he'll turn your current in a ditch, / And make your channel his? If he have power, / Then vail your ignorance: if none, awake / Your dangerous lenity. If you are learn'd, / Be not as common fools; if you are not, / Let them have cushions by you. You are plebeians, / If they be senators: and they are no less / When, both your voices blended, the great'st taste / Most palates theirs. They choose their magistrate; / And such a one as he, who puts his 'shall,' / His popular 'shall,' against a graver bench / Than ever frown'd in Greece. By Jove himself, / It makes the consuls base: and my soul aches / To know, when two authorities are up, / Neither supreme, how soon confusion / May enter 'twixt the gap of both and take / The one by the other.

"Will"! Oh good but most unwise patricians! Why, you serious but careless senators, have you let the many-headed Hydra choose an official who, with his imperious "will", though he's only the horn and noise of the monster, has the nerve to say he'll divert your stream into a ditch and make your channel his own? If he has power, then bow down in your ignorance; if he has none, wake up from your dangerous softness. If you're wise, don't act like common fools; if you're not, let them sit on the senate cushions beside you. You're plebeians if they're senators, and they're no less than senators when, with both your voices mixed, the strongest flavour is theirs. They choose their own magistrate, and one like this, who sets his "will", his mob's "will", against a more dignified senate than ever frowned in Greece. By Jove himself, it makes the consuls worthless, and it pains my soul to know that when two authorities are set up and neither is supreme, chaos can very soon slip into the gap between them and use one to destroy the other.
Well, on to the market square.
Whoever gave that counsel, to give forth / The corn o' the storehouse gratis, as 'twas us'd / Sometime in Greece,—
Whoever gave the advice to hand out the grain from the storehouse free, as they used to do in Greece—
Well, well, no more of that.
Well, well, no more of that.
Though there the people had more absolute power,— / I say they nourish'd disobedience, fed / The ruin of the state.
Even though the people there had more absolute power— I say they nourished disobedience and fed the ruin of the state.
Why shall the people give / One that speaks thus their voice?
Why should the people give their vote to someone who talks like this?

I'll give my reasons, / More worthier than their voices. They know the corn / Was not our recompense, resting well assur'd / They ne'er did service for't; being press'd to the war, / Even when the navel of the state was touch'd, / They would not thread the gates,—this kind of service / Did not deserve corn gratis: being i' the war, / Their mutinies and revolts, wherein they show'd / Most valour, spoke not for them. The accusation / Which they have often made against the senate, / All cause unborn, could never be the motive / Of our so frank donation. Well, what then? / How shall this bisson multitude digest / The senate's courtesy? Let deeds express / What's like to be their words:—'We did request it; / We are the greater poll, and in true fear / They gave us our demands:'—Thus we debase / The nature of our seats, and make the rabble / Call our cares fears; which will in time / Break ope the locks o' the senate and bring in / The crows to peck the eagles.—

I'll give my reasons, which are worth more than their votes. They know the grain wasn't a reward from us, since they're well aware they never did any service for it. When they were called up for war, even when the state was struck at its heart, they wouldn't go out through the gates. That kind of service didn't deserve free grain. In the war, their mutinies and revolts, where they showed most courage, didn't speak well for them. The accusations they've often made against the senate, completely groundless, could never have been the reason for our so generous gift. Well, what then? How will this blind mob take the senate's kindness? Let their actions show what they're likely to say: "We demanded it; we're the majority, and they gave us what we wanted out of real fear." This is how we cheapen the nature of our office and let the rabble call our care fear, which will in time break open the senate's locks and let in the crows to peck at the eagles.

No, take more: / What may be sworn by, both divine and human, / Seal what I end withal!—This double worship,— / Where one part does disdain with cause, the other / Insult without all reason; where gentry, title, wisdom, / Cannot conclude but by the yea and no / Of general ignorance—it must omit / Real necessities, and give way the while / To unstable slightness: purpose so barr'd, it follows, / Nothing is done to purpose. Therefore, beseech you,— / You that will be less fearful than discreet; / That love the fundamental part of state / More than you doubt the change on't; that prefer / A noble life before a long, and wish / To jump a body with a dangerous physic / That's sure of death without it,—at once pluck out / The multitudinous tongue; let them not lick / The sweet which is their poison: your dishonour / Mangles true judgment, and bereaves the state / Of that integrity which should become't; / Not having the power to do the good it would, / For the ill which doth control't.

No, take more. May everything one can swear by, divine and human, confirm what I end with! This divided rule, where one side scorns with reason and the other insults without any reason at all, where birth, title and wisdom can't decide anything without the yes and no of common ignorance, must neglect real needs and give way to fickle trifles. With purpose blocked like that, it follows that nothing purposeful gets done. So I beg you, you who'd rather be wise than fearful, who love the foundations of the state more than you fear changing them, who prefer a noble life to a long one, and would risk a dangerous medicine on a body that will certainly die without it: pull out the mob's tongue at once. Don't let them lick the sweet that is their poison. Your dishonour mangles true judgment and robs the state of the integrity that should belong to it, leaving it without the power to do the good it wants because of the evil that controls it.
Has spoken like a traitor, and shall answer / As traitors do.
He has spoken like a traitor, and he'll answer for it as traitors do.

Thou wretch, despite o'erwhelm thee!— / What should the people do with these bald tribunes? / On whom depending, their obedience fails / To the greater bench: in a rebellion, / When what's not meet, but what must be, was law, / Then were they chosen; in a better hour / Let what is meet be said it must be meet, / And throw their power i' the dust.

You wretch, may contempt crush you! What should the people do with these bald tribunes? By depending on them, they fail to obey the higher authority. They were chosen in a rebellion, when what had to be, not what was right, was law. In a better time, let what's right be declared right, and throw their power into the dust.
The aediles, ho!—Let him be apprehended.
The aediles, here! Let him be arrested.
Go call the people [Exit BRUTUS]; in whose name myself / Attach thee as a traitorous innovator, / A foe to the public weal. Obey, I charge thee, / And follow to thine answer.
Go and call the people. (Exit Brutus) In their name I arrest you myself as a treasonous revolutionary, an enemy of the public good. I order you to obey and come to answer the charge.
Old man, take your hands off.
Hence, rotten thing! or I shall shake thy bones / Out of thy garments.
Get away, you rotten thing, or I'll shake your bones out of your clothes.
Here's he that would take from you all your power.
Here's the man who would take all your power away from you.
Down with him! down with him!
Down with him! Down with him!
Tribunes! patricians! citizens!—What, ho!— / Sicinius, Brutus, Coriolanus, Citizens!
Tribunes! Patricians! Citizens! Stop! Sicinius, Brutus, Coriolanus, citizens!
Peace, peace, peace; stay, hold, peace!
Peace, peace, peace! Stop, hold on, peace!
What is about to be?—I am out of breath; / Confusion's near: I cannot speak.—You tribunes / To the people,—Coriolanus, patience:— / Speak, good Sicinius.
What's about to happen? I'm out of breath. Chaos is close; I can't speak. You tribunes, speak to the people. Coriolanus, be patient. Speak, good Sicinius.
Let's hear our tribune: peace!— / Speak, speak, speak.
Let's hear our tribune. Quiet! Speak, speak, speak.
You are at point to lose your liberties; / Marcius would have all from you; Marcius, / Whom late you have nam'd for consul.
You're about to lose your liberties. Marcius would take everything from you, Marcius, whom you've just named as consul.
Fie, fie, fie! / This is the way to kindle, not to quench.
Shame, shame, shame! This is the way to light the fire, not put it out.
To unbuild the city, and to lay all flat.
To pull the city down and flatten everything.
What is the city but the people?
What is the city but the people?
True, / The people are the city.
True, the people are the city.
By the consent of all, we were establish'd / The people's magistrates.
With everyone's agreement, we were made the people's magistrates.
And so are like to do.
That is the way to lay the city flat; / To bring the roof to the foundation, / And bury all which yet distinctly ranges, / In heaps and piles of ruin.
That's the way to flatten the city, to bring the roof down to the foundations and bury everything that still stands in its proper order under heaps and piles of ruins.
Or let us stand to our authority, / Or let us lose it.—We do here pronounce, / Upon the part o' the people, in whose power / We were elected theirs, Marcius is worthy / Of present death.
Either let's stand by our authority or lose it. We declare here, on behalf of the people, by whose power we were elected their officers, that Marcius deserves immediate death.
Therefore lay hold of him; / Bear him to the rock Tarpeian, and from thence / Into destruction cast him.
So seize him. Take him to the Tarpeian rock and throw him off it to his death.
Hear me one word; / Beseech you, tribunes, hear me but a word.
Let me say one word. I beg you, tribunes, hear just one word.
Be that you seem, truly your country's friends, / And temperately proceed to what you would / Thus violently redress.
Be what you seem to be, true friends of your country, and go about calmly what you want to set right with such violence.
Sir, those cold ways, / That seem like prudent helps, are very poisonous / Where the disease is violent.—Lay hands upon him / And bear him to the rock.
Sir, those cool methods, which look like sensible remedies, are deadly poison when the disease is violent. Seize him and take him to the rock.
No; I'll die here. [Draws his sword] / There's some among you have beheld me fighting; / Come, try upon yourselves what you have seen me.
No; I'll die here. (Draws his sword) Some of you have seen me fighting. Come and try on yourselves what you've seen me do.
Down with that sword!—Tribunes, withdraw awhile.
Put that sword down! Tribunes, step back for a while.
Help Marcius, help, / You that be noble; help him, young and old!
Help Marcius, help, all of you who are noble; help him, young and old!
Down with him, down with him!
Down with him, down with him!
Go, get you to your house; be gone, away! / All will be nought else.
Go, get to your house. Go, away! Otherwise everything will be ruined.
Stand fast; / We have as many friends as enemies.
Stand firm. We have as many friends as enemies.
Shall it be put to that?
The gods forbid: / I pr'ythee, noble friend, home to thy house; / Leave us to cure this cause.
The gods forbid! Please, noble friend, go home to your house. Leave us to heal this matter.
For 'tis a sore upon us / You cannot tent yourself; be gone, beseech you.
Because it's a wound in all of us that you can't treat yourself. Go, I beg you.
I would they were barbarians,—as they are, / Though in Rome litter'd,—not Romans,—as they are not, / Though calv'd i' the porch o' the Capitol.
I wish they were barbarians, which they are, though born in Rome, and not Romans, which they're not, though they were dropped like calves in the doorway of the Capitol.
Be gone; / Put not your worthy rage into your tongue; / One time will owe another.
Go. Don't put your worthy rage into words. There'll be another time to settle this.
On fair ground / I could beat forty of them.
On fair ground I could beat forty of them.
I could myself / Take up a brace o' the best of them; yea, the two tribunes.
I could take on a pair of the best of them myself; yes, the two tribunes.

But now 'tis odds beyond arithmetic; / And manhood is call'd foolery when it stands / Against a falling fabric.—Will you hence, / Before the tag return? whose rage doth rend / Like interrupted waters, and o'erbear / What they are used to bear.

But now the odds are beyond counting, and courage is called foolishness when it stands against a falling building. Will you go before the mob comes back? Their rage tears like water held back by a dam and overwhelms what it usually holds up.
Pray you be gone: / I'll try whether my old wit be in request / With those that have but little: this must be patch'd / With cloth of any colour.
Please go. I'll see if my old wits are in demand with those who have very few. This must be patched up with cloth of any colour.
This man has marr'd his fortune.
This man has ruined his fortune.

His nature is too noble for the world: / He would not flatter Neptune for his trident, / Or Jove for's power to thunder. His heart's his mouth: / What his breast forges, that his tongue must vent; / And, being angry, does forget that ever / He heard the name of death.

His nature is too noble for the world. He wouldn't flatter Neptune for his trident or Jove for his power to thunder. His heart is his mouth: whatever his chest forges, his tongue has to let out; and when he's angry he forgets he ever heard the word death.
I wish they were in bed!
I would they were in Tiber! / What the vengeance, could he not speak 'em fair?
I wish they were in the Tiber! What the devil, couldn't he speak to them politely?
Where is this viper / That would depopulate the city and / Be every man himself?
Where's this snake who would empty the city of people and be every man himself?

He shall be thrown down the Tarpeian rock / With rigorous hands: he hath resisted law, / And therefore law shall scorn him further trial / Than the severity of the public power, / Which he so sets at nought.
He'll be thrown down the Tarpeian rock by stern hands. He has resisted the law, and so the law will deny him any further trial than the severity of the people's power, which he sets at nothing.
He shall well know / The noble tribunes are the people's mouths, / And we their hands.
He'll learn that the noble tribunes are the people's mouths, and we are their hands.
Do not cry havoc, where you should but hunt / With modest warrant.
Don't give the signal for total slaughter when you should only hunt within proper limits.
Sir, how comes't that you / Have holp to make this rescue?
Sir, how is it that you helped him escape?
Hear me speak:— / As I do know the consul's worthiness, / So can I name his faults,—
Let me speak. Just as I know the consul's worth, I can also name his faults—
If, by the tribunes' leave, and yours, good people, / I may be heard, I would crave a word or two; / The which shall turn you to no further harm / Than so much loss of time.
If, with the tribunes' permission and yours, good people, I may be heard, I'd ask for a word or two, which will cost you nothing more than a little lost time.

Speak briefly, then; / For we are peremptory to dispatch / This viperous traitor: to eject him hence / Were but one danger; and to keep him here / Our certain death: therefore it is decreed / He dies to-night.
Speak briefly, then, because we're determined to get rid of this snake of a traitor. Banishing him would be just one danger, and keeping him here our certain death; so it's decided he dies tonight.
Now the good gods forbid / That our renowned Rome, whose gratitude / Towards her deserved children is enroll'd / In Jove's own book, like an unnatural dam / Should now eat up her own!
Now may the good gods forbid that our famous Rome, whose gratitude to her deserving children is written in Jove's own book, should now, like an unnatural mother animal, eat up her own young!
He's a disease that must be cut away.
He's a disease that has to be cut out.

O, he's a limb that has but a disease; / Mortal, to cut it off; to cure it, easy. / What has he done to Rome that's worthy death? / Killing our enemies, the blood he hath lost,— / Which I dare vouch is more than that he hath / By many an ounce,—he dropt it for his country; / And what is left, to lose it by his country / Were to us all, that do't and suffer it / A brand to the end o' the world.

Oh, he's a limb that only has a disease: fatal to cut it off, easy to cure it. What has he done to Rome that deserves death? For killing our enemies? The blood he has lost, which I'd swear is more than he has left by many an ounce, he shed for his country. And if his country made him lose what's left, it would be a brand of shame to the end of the world on all of us who do it or allow it.
Merely awry: when he did love his country, / It honour'd him.
Totally wrong. When he loved his country, it honoured him.
The service of the foot, / Being once gangren'd, is not then respected / For what before it was.
Once a foot has gangrene, its service isn't valued for what it did before.
We'll hear no more.— / Pursue him to his house, and pluck him thence; / Lest his infection, being of catching nature, / Spread further.
We'll hear no more. Go after him to his house and drag him out, in case his infection, which is catching, spreads further.

One word more, one word. / This tiger-footed rage, when it shall find / The harm of unscann'd swiftness, will, too late, / Tie leaden pounds to's heels. Proceed by process; / Lest parties,—as he is belov'd,—break out, / And sack great Rome with Romans.

One more word, just one. This tiger-footed rage, when it sees the harm of rushing ahead without thinking, will tie lead weights to its heels, too late. Proceed by legal process, in case factions break out, since he's loved, and great Rome is sacked by Romans.
What do ye talk? / Have we not had a taste of his obedience? / Our aediles smote? ourselves resisted?—come,—
What are you talking about? Haven't we had a taste of how obedient he is? Our aediles struck, ourselves resisted? Come on—

Consider this:—he has been bred i' the wars / Since 'a could draw a sword, and is ill school'd / In bolted language; meal and bran together / He throws without distinction. Give me leave, / I'll go to him and undertake to bring him / Where he shall answer, by a lawful form, / In peace, to his utmost peril.

Consider this: he has been brought up in the wars since he could draw a sword, and he's badly trained in refined language; he throws out the flour and the bran together without sorting them. Let me go to him, and I'll undertake to bring him where he'll answer peacefully, by lawful procedure, at the risk of the harshest penalty.
Noble tribunes, / It is the humane way: the other course / Will prove too bloody; and the end of it / Unknown to the beginning.
Noble tribunes, that is the humane way. The other course will be too bloody, and how it ends can't be known at the beginning.
Noble Menenius, / Be you then as the people's officer.— / Masters, lay down your weapons.
Noble Menenius, then act as the people's officer. Friends, put down your weapons.
Meet on the market-place.—We'll attend you there: / Where, if you bring not Marcius, we'll proceed / In our first way.
Meet in the market square. We'll wait for you there, and if you don't bring Marcius, we'll proceed as we first intended.
I'll bring him to you.— / [To the SENATORS] Let me desire your company: he must come, / Or what is worst will follow.
I'll bring him to you. (To the Senators) Please come with me. He must come, or the worst will follow.

Let them pull all about mine ears; present me / Death on the wheel, or at wild horses' heels; / Or pile ten hills on the Tarpeian rock, / That the precipitation might down stretch / Below the beam of sight; yet will I still / Be thus to them.

Let them pull everything down around my ears; threaten me with death on the wheel or dragged at wild horses' heels; or pile ten hills on the Tarpeian rock so the drop falls further than the eye can see; I'll still be like this towards them.

I muse my mother / Does not approve me further, who was wont / To call them woollen vassals, things created / To buy and sell with groats; to show bare heads / In congregations, to yawn, be still, and wonder, / When one but of my ordinance stood up / To speak of peace or war.

I'm surprised my mother doesn't approve of me more. She used to call them slaves in wool, creatures made to buy and sell with pennies, to stand bareheaded in meetings and gape, keep quiet and marvel, when a man of my rank stood up to speak about peace or war.
I talk of you: [To Volumnia] / Why did you wish me milder? Would you have me / False to my nature? Rather say, I play / The man I am.
(To Volumnia) I'm talking about you. Why did you want me to be milder? Would you have me false to my own nature? Say rather that I play the man I am.
O, sir, sir, sir, / I would have had you put your power well on / Before you had worn it out.
Oh, sir, sir, sir, I would have liked you to put your power on properly before you wore it out.

You might have been enough the man you are / With striving less to be so: lesser had been / The thwartings of your dispositions, if / You had not show'd them how ye were dispos'd, / Ere they lack'd power to cross you.
You could have been the man you are without trying so hard to be. Your wishes would have been blocked less if you hadn't shown them how you felt before they lost the power to stop you.
Come, come, you have been too rough, something too rough; / You must return and mend it.
Come, come, you've been too rough, rather too rough. You must go back and make amends.
There's no remedy; / Unless, by not so doing, our good city / Cleave in the midst, and perish.
There's no other cure, unless, by not doing it, our good city splits in two and dies.
Pray be counsell'd; / I have a heart as little apt as yours, / But yet a brain that leads my use of anger / To better vantage.
Please take advice. My heart is no more willing than yours, but I have a brain that directs my anger to better advantage.

Well said, noble woman! / Before he should thus stoop to the herd, but that / The violent fit o' the time craves it as physic / For the whole state, I would put mine armour on, / Which I can scarcely bear.

Well said, noble lady! Rather than have him bow like this to the herd, I'd put on my armour, which I can hardly carry, except that the violent sickness of the times needs it as medicine for the whole state.
For them?—I cannot do it to the gods; / Must I then do't to them?
For them? I can't do it for the gods; must I do it for them?

You are too absolute; / Though therein you can never be too noble / But when extremities speak. I have heard you say / Honour and policy, like unsever'd friends, / I' the war do grow together: grant that, and tell me / In peace what each of them by th' other lose / That they combine not there.

You're too unbending, though you could never be too noble in that, except when things are desperate. I've heard you say that honour and cunning grow together in war like inseparable friends. Admit that, and tell me what either of them loses by the other in peace that they shouldn't join together there too.

If it be honour in your wars to seem / The same you are not,—which for your best ends / You adopt your policy,—how is it less or worse / That it shall hold companionship in peace / With honour as in war; since that to both / It stands in like request?

If it's honourable in your wars to seem what you're not, which you adopt as a strategy for your best ends, how is it any less or worse for it to keep company with honour in peace as in war, since it's equally needed in both?

Because that now it lies you on to speak / To the people; not by your own instruction, / Nor by the matter which your heart prompts you, / But with such words that are but rooted in / Your tongue, though but bastards and syllables / Of no allowance, to your bosom's truth. / Now, this no more dishonours you at all / Than to take in a town with gentle words, / Which else would put you to your fortune and / The hazard of much blood. / I would dissemble with my nature where / My fortunes and my friends at stake requir'd / I should do so in honour: I am in this / Your wife, your son, these senators, the nobles; / And you will rather show our general louts / How you can frown, than spend a fawn upon 'em / For the inheritance of their loves and safeguard / Of what that want might ruin.

Because now it's your duty to speak to the people, not as you'd choose yourself or with what your heart prompts, but with words that are rooted only in your tongue, illegitimate syllables that your heart's truth doesn't stand behind. Now this dishonours you no more than capturing a town with gentle words, which otherwise would force you to trust to luck and risk much bloodshed. I'd disguise my true nature if my fortunes and my friends were at stake and honour required it. I speak in this for your wife, your son, these senators, the nobles; and you'd rather show our common oafs how you can frown than give them one fawning look to win their love and protect what lacking it could ruin.
Noble lady!— / Come, go with us; speak fair: you may salve so, / Not what is dangerous present, but the loss / Of what is past.
Noble lady! Come, go with us; speak politely. That way you can heal not just the present danger but the loss of what's already happened.

I pr'ythee now, my son, / Go to them with this bonnet in thy hand; / And thus far having stretch'd it,—here be with them,— / Thy knee bussing the stones,—for in such business / Action is eloquence, and the eyes of the ignorant / More learned than the ears,—waving thy head, / Which often, thus correcting thy stout heart, / Now humble as the ripest mulberry / That will not hold the handling: or say to them / Thou art their soldier, and, being bred in broils, / Hast not the soft way which, thou dost confess, / Were fit for thee to use, as they to claim, / In asking their good loves; but thou wilt frame / Thyself, forsooth, hereafter theirs, so far / As thou hast power and person.

Please now, my son, go to them with this cap in your hand, holding it out this far, like this, be with them; your knee kissing the stones (because in such business action is eloquence, and the eyes of ignorant people are more learned than their ears), nodding your head, and so often correcting your proud heart, which is now as humble as the ripest mulberry that falls apart when it's handled. Or tell them you're their soldier, and being brought up in fighting you don't have the gentle manner which, you admit, it would be right for you to use and for them to expect when you ask for their love; but that from now on you'll make yourself theirs, indeed, as far as you have power and person.
This but done / Even as she speaks, why, their hearts were yours: / For they have pardons, being ask'd, as free / As words to little purpose.
If he only did that, just as she says, their hearts would be yours; because when asked, they give pardons as freely as idle words.
Pr'ythee now, / Go, and be rul'd; although I know thou had'st rather / Follow thine enemy in a fiery gulf / Than flatter him in a bower.
Please now, go, and do as you're told; though I know you'd rather follow your enemy into a fiery pit than flatter him in a garden.
I have been i' the market-place; and, sir, 'tis fit / You make strong party, or defend yourself / By calmness or by absence: all's in anger.
I've been to the market square, and, sir, you'd better raise a strong party or protect yourself by calmness or by going away. Everyone's furious.
I think 'twill serve, if he / Can thereto frame his spirit.
I think that will do, if he can bring his spirit to it.
He must, and will.— / Pr'ythee now, say you will, and go about it.
He must, and he will. Please now, say you will, and get on with it.

Must I go show them my unbarb'd sconce? must I / With my base tongue, give to my noble heart / A lie, that it must bear? Well, I will do't: / Yet, were there but this single plot to lose, / This mould of Marcius, they to dust should grind it, / And throw't against the wind.—To the market-place:— / You have put me now to such a part which never / I shall discharge to the life.

Must I go and show them my bare head? Must I make my base tongue give my noble heart a lie it has to put up with? Well, I'll do it. Yet if there were only this one piece of earth to lose, this body of Marcius, they could grind it to dust and throw it into the wind. To the market square! You've given me a part I'll never play convincingly.
I pr'ythee now, sweet son,—as thou hast said / My praises made thee first a soldier, so, / To have my praise for this, perform a part / Thou hast not done before.
Please now, sweet son: as you've said my praise first made you a soldier, so, to have my praise for this, play a part you've never played before.

Well, I must do't: / Away, my disposition, and possess me / Some harlot's spirit!
