My throat of war be turn'd, / Which quired with my drum, into a pipe / Small as an eunuch, or the virgin voice / That babies lulls asleep! the smiles of knaves / Tent in my cheeks; and school-boys' tears take up / The glasses of my sight! a beggar's tongue / Make motion through my lips; and my arm'd knees, / Who bow'd but in my stirrup, bend like his / That hath receiv'd an alms!—I will not do't; / Lest I surcease to honour mine own truth, / And by my body's action teach my mind / A most inherent baseness.

Well, I have to do it. Away with my true nature, and let some prostitute's spirit possess me! Let my war-trained throat, which sang in chorus with my drum, turn into a pipe as thin as a eunuch's or the girl's voice that lulls babies to sleep! Let villains' smiles camp in my cheeks, and schoolboys' tears fill my eyes! Let a beggar's tongue move between my lips, and my armoured knees, which have only bent in my stirrup, bow like a man who's been given charity! I won't do it, in case I stop honouring my own integrity and, by what my body does, teach my mind a deep-rooted baseness.

At thy choice, then: / To beg of thee, it is my more dishonour / Than thou of them. Come all to ruin: let / Thy mother rather feel thy pride than fear / Thy dangerous stoutness; for I mock at death / With as big heart as thou. Do as thou list. / Thy valiantness was mine, thou suck'dst it from me; / But owe thy pride thyself.

Have it your own way, then. It's more dishonour for me to beg from you than for you to beg from them. Let everything go to ruin. Let your mother suffer your pride rather than fear your dangerous stubbornness, because I laugh at death as boldly as you. Do as you like. Your courage was mine; you sucked it from me. But your pride you owe to yourself.

Pray, be content: / Mother, I am going to the market-place; / Chide me no more. I'll mountebank their loves, / Cog their hearts from them, and come home belov'd / Of all the trades in Rome. Look, I am going. / Commend me to my wife. I'll return consul; / Or never trust to what my tongue can do / I' the way of flattery further.

Please, be calm. Mother, I'm going to the market square. Don't scold me any more. I'll win their love like a quack doctor, cheat their hearts out of them, and come home loved by all the tradesmen in Rome. Look, I'm going. Give my love to my wife. I'll come back consul, or never trust my tongue's skill at flattery again.
Away! The tribunes do attend you: arm yourself / To answer mildly; for they are prepar'd / With accusations, as I hear, more strong / Than are upon you yet.
Come on! The tribunes are waiting for you. Prepare to answer mildly, because I hear they're ready with accusations even stronger than the ones you face already.
The word is, mildly.—Pray you let us go: / Let them accuse me by invention, I / Will answer in mine honour.
The word is "mildly". Please let's go. Let them accuse me with made-up charges; I'll answer honourably.
Well, mildly be it then; mildly.
Well, mildly it is, then. Mildly.
In this point charge him home, that he affects / Tyrannical power: if he evade us there, / Enforce him with his envy to the people; / And that the spoil got on the Antiates / Was ne'er distributed.

Press him hard on this point, that he's aiming at tyrannical power. If he gets out of that, hit him with his hatred of the people and the fact that the loot taken from the men of Antium was never shared out.
With old Menenius, and those senators / That always favour'd him.
Old Menenius, and the senators who have always supported him.
Have you a catalogue / Of all the voices that we have procur'd, / Set down by the poll?
Do you have a list of all the votes we've secured, set down by head?
Have you collected them by tribes?
Have you grouped them by tribes?

Assemble presently the people hither: / And when they hear me say 'It shall be so / I' the right and strength o' the commons,' be it either / For death, for fine, or banishment, then let them, / If I say fine, cry 'Fine!'- if death, cry 'Death;' / Insisting on the old prerogative / And power i' the truth o' the cause.

Gather the people here at once. And when they hear me say, "It shall be so, by the right and power of the commons", whether it's for death, a fine or banishment, then, if I say fine, let them shout "Fine!", if death, "Death!", insisting on their ancient right and their power in the justice of the cause.
And when such time they have begun to cry, / Let them not cease, but with a din confus'd / Enforce the present execution / Of what we chance to sentence.
And once they've started shouting, don't let them stop; let them use the confused din to force the immediate carrying out of whatever sentence we pass.
Make them be strong, and ready for this hint, / When we shall hap to give't them.
Make them steadfast and ready for this cue whenever we give it to them.

Put him to choler straight: he hath been us'd / Ever to conquer, and to have his worth / Of contradiction; being once chaf'd, he cannot / Be rein'd again to temperance; then he speaks / What's in his heart; and that is there which looks / With us to break his neck.

Make him angry straight away. He has always been used to winning and to having his full share of contradicting others. Once he's provoked, he can't be reined back into calm; then he says what's in his heart, and what's there will help us break his neck.

Ay, as an ostler, that for the poorest piece / Will bear the knave by the volume.—The honoured gods / Keep Rome in safety, and the chairs of justice / Supplied with worthy men! plant love among's! / Throng our large temples with the shows of peace, / And not our streets with war!

Yes, like a stable boy who, for the smallest tip, will put up with being called a rogue over and over. May the honoured gods keep Rome safe and the seats of justice filled with worthy men! Plant love among us! Fill our great temples with the ceremonies of peace, and not our streets with war!
List to your tribunes; audience: peace, I say!
Listen to your tribunes. Attention! Quiet, I say!
Shall I be charg'd no further than this present? / Must all determine here?
Will I be charged with nothing beyond what's charged now? Must everything be settled here?
I do demand, / If you submit you to the people's voices, / Allow their officers, and are content / To suffer lawful censure for such faults / As shall be proved upon you.
I ask whether you submit yourself to the people's votes, accept their officers, and are willing to suffer lawful punishment for such faults as are proved against you.
Lo, citizens, he says he is content: / The warlike service he has done, consider; think / Upon the wounds his body bears, which show / Like graves i' the holy churchyard.
Look, citizens, he says he's willing. Consider the service he has done in war; think about the wounds on his body, which look like graves in a holy churchyard.
Scratches with briers, / Scars to move laughter only.
Scratches from brambles, scars that would only make you laugh.

Consider further, / That when he speaks not like a citizen, / You find him like a soldier: do not take / His rougher accents for malicious sounds, / But, as I say, such as become a soldier, / Rather than envy you.
Consider too that when he doesn't speak like a citizen, you'll find he speaks like a soldier. Don't take his rougher tone for malice, but, as I say, as suits a soldier, rather than as hatred of you.
What is the matter, / That being pass'd for consul with full voice, / I am so dishonour'd that the very hour / You take it off again?
What's the matter, that after being passed as consul with full approval, I'm so disgraced that in the same hour you take it away again?
Say then: 'tis true, I ought so.
Go on, then. It's true, I should.
We charge you that you have contriv'd to take / From Rome all season'd office, and to wind / Yourself into a power tyrannical; / For which you are a traitor to the people.
We charge you with having schemed to remove all established offices from Rome and to work your way into tyrannical power, for which you're a traitor to the people.

The fires i' the lowest hell fold in the people! / Call me their traitor!—Thou injurious tribune! / Within thine eyes sat twenty thousand deaths, / In thy hands clutch'd as many millions, in / Thy lying tongue both numbers, I would say, / Thou liest unto thee with a voice as free / As I do pray the gods.

May the fires of deepest hell swallow the people! Call me their traitor! You insulting tribune! If there were twenty thousand deaths sitting in your eyes, as many millions clutched in your hands, and both numbers on your lying tongue, I would still say "You lie" to your face, as freely as I pray to the gods.
To the rock, to the rock, with him!
To the rock, to the rock with him!

Peace! / We need not put new matter to his charge: / What you have seen him do and heard him speak, / Beating your officers, cursing yourselves, / Opposing laws with strokes, and here defying / Those whose great power must try him; even this, / So criminal and in such capital kind, / Deserves the extremest death.

Quiet! We don't need to add new charges. What you've seen him do and heard him say, beating your officers, cursing you, resisting the law with blows, and here defying those whose great power must judge him, this, so criminal and so capital, deserves the harshest death.
But since he hath / Serv'd well for Rome,—
But since he has served Rome well—
What do you prate of service?
What are you chattering about service for?
I talk of that that know it.
I'm talking about what I know.
Is this the promise that you made your mother?
Is this the promise you made your mother?

I'll know no further: / Let them pronounce the steep Tarpeian death, / Vagabond exile, flaying, pent to linger / But with a grain a day, I would not buy / Their mercy at the price of one fair word, / Nor check my courage for what they can give, / To have't with saying Good-morrow.

I'll understand nothing more. Let them sentence me to death from the steep Tarpeian rock, a wanderer's exile, flaying, being locked up to linger on a grain a day; I wouldn't buy their mercy at the price of one polite word, or hold back my spirit for anything they can give, even if all it took was saying "Good morning".

For that he has,— / As much as in him lies,—from time to time / Envied against the people, seeking means / To pluck away their power; as now at last / Given hostile strokes, and that not in the presence / Of dreaded justice, but on the ministers / That do distribute it;—in the name o' the people, / And in the power of us the tribunes, we, / Even from this instant, banish him our city, / In peril of precipitation / From off the rock Tarpeian, never more / To enter our Rome gates: I' the people's name, / I say it shall be so.

Because he has, as far as he could, shown hatred against the people time and again, looking for ways to take away their power, and now at last has struck hostile blows, and not just in the presence of feared justice but against the officers who administer it: in the name of the people and by the power of us, the tribunes, we banish him from our city from this moment, on pain of being thrown off the Tarpeian rock, never to enter Rome's gates again. In the people's name, I say it shall be so.
It shall be so, it shall be so; let him away; / He's banished, and it shall be so.
It shall be so, it shall be so! Let him go! He's banished, and it shall be so.
Hear me, my masters and my common friends,—
Hear me, my masters and my common friends—
He has been sentenced. No more hearing.

Let me speak: / I have been consul, and can show for Rome / Her enemies' marks upon me. I do love / My country's good with a respect more tender, / More holy and profound, than mine own life, / My dear wife's estimate, her womb's increase, / And treasure of my loins; then if I would / Speak that,—

Let me speak. I have been consul, and I can show Rome's enemies' marks on me. I love my country's good with a more tender, holy and deep regard than my own life, my dear wife's honour, her children, the treasure of my body. So if I were to say that—
We know your drift. Speak what?
We know where you're going. Say what?
There's no more to be said, but he is banish'd, / As enemy to the people and his country: / It shall be so.
There's nothing more to say except that he's banished as an enemy of the people and his country. It shall be so.
It shall be so, it shall be so.
It shall be so, it shall be so.

You common cry of curs! whose breath I hate / As reek o' the rotten fens, whose loves I prize / As the dead carcasses of unburied men / That do corrupt my air,—I banish you; / And here remain with your uncertainty! / Let every feeble rumour shake your hearts! / Your enemies, with nodding of their plumes, / Fan you into despair! Have the power still / To banish your defenders; till at length / Your ignorance,—which finds not till it feels,— / Making but reservation of yourselves,— / Still your own foes,—deliver you, as most / Abated captives to some nation / That won you without blows! Despising, / For you, the city, thus I turn my back: / There is a world elsewhere.

You common pack of curs, whose breath I hate like the stink of rotten swamps, whose love I value like the dead bodies of unburied men that poison my air: I banish you! Stay here with your fickleness! May every feeble rumour make your hearts shake! May your enemies, nodding their plumed helmets, fan you into despair! Keep the power to banish your defenders, until at last your ignorance, which understands nothing until it feels it, keeps only yourselves, always your own enemies, and hands you over as the most humbled prisoners to some nation that conquered you without a blow! Despising the city because of you, I turn my back on it like this. There is a world elsewhere.
The people's enemy is gone, is gone!
The people's enemy is gone, he's gone!
Our enemy is banish'd, he is gone! Hoo! hoo!
Our enemy is banished, he's gone! Hurrah! Hurrah!
Go, see him out at gates, and follow him, / As he hath follow'd you, with all despite; / Give him deserv'd vexation. Let a guard / Attend us through the city.
Go and see him out of the gates, and follow him with every insult, as he has pursued you. Give him the torment he deserves. Let a guard go with us through the city.
Come, come, let's see him out at gates; come. / The gods preserve our noble tribunes! Come.
Come on, come on, let's see him out of the gates. Come! The gods preserve our noble tribunes! Come on.

Come, leave your tears; a brief farewell:—the beast / With many heads butts me away.—Nay, mother, / Where is your ancient courage? you were us'd / To say extremities was the trier of spirits; / That common chances common men could bear; / That when the sea was calm all boats alike / Show'd mastership in floating; fortune's blows, / When most struck home, being gentle wounded, craves / A noble cunning; you were us'd to load me / With precepts that would make invincible / The heart that conn'd them.

Come, stop crying; a short goodbye. The beast with many heads butts me out. No, mother, where's your old courage? You used to say extreme trouble tests the spirit; that ordinary men can bear ordinary luck; that when the sea is calm, all boats look equally skilled at floating; that when fortune's blows strike deepest, staying gentle under the wound takes noble skill. You used to load me with rules that would make the heart that learned them unbeatable.
Now the red pestilence strike all trades in Rome, / And occupations perish!
Now may the red plague strike every trade in Rome and all its occupations die!

What, what, what! / I shall be lov'd when I am lack'd. Nay, mother, / Resume that spirit when you were wont to say, / If you had been the wife of Hercules, / Six of his labours you'd have done, and sav'd / Your husband so much sweat.—Cominius, / Droop not; adieu.—Farewell, my wife,—my mother: / I'll do well yet.—Thou old and true Menenius, / Thy tears are salter than a younger man's, / And venomous to thine eyes.—My sometime general, / I have seen thee stern, and thou hast oft beheld / Heart-hard'ning spectacles; tell these sad women / 'Tis fond to wail inevitable strokes, / As 'tis to laugh at 'em.—My mother, you wot well / My hazards still have been your solace: and / Believe't not lightly,—though I go alone, / Like to a lonely dragon, that his fen / Makes fear'd and talk'd of more than seen,—your son / Will or exceed the common or be caught / With cautelous baits and practice.

What, what, what! They'll love me when they miss me. No, mother, take up again the spirit you had when you used to say that if you'd been Hercules's wife, you'd have done six of his labours and saved your husband all that sweat. Cominius, don't be downcast. Goodbye. Farewell, my wife, my mother. I'll do well yet. You old and faithful Menenius, your tears are saltier than a younger man's and poison to your eyes. My former general, I've seen you stern, and you've often seen sights that harden the heart. Tell these sad women it's as foolish to wail at blows that can't be avoided as it is to laugh at them. Mother, you know well my dangers have always been your comfort; and believe me, though I go alone, like a solitary dragon whose swamp is feared and talked about more than seen, your son will either outdo ordinary men or be caught by crafty bait and trickery.
My first son, / Whither wilt thou go? Take good Cominius / With thee awhile: determine on some course / More than a wild exposture to each chance / That starts i' the way before thee.
My first-born son, where will you go? Take good Cominius with you for a while. Decide on some plan, rather than wildly exposing yourself to every chance that springs up in front of you.

I'll follow thee a month, devise with thee / Where thou shalt rest, that thou mayst hear of us, / And we of thee: so, if the time thrust forth / A cause for thy repeal, we shall not send / O'er the vast world to seek a single man; / And lose advantage, which doth ever cool / I' the absence of the needer.

I'll go with you for a month and work out with you where you'll settle, so you can hear from us and we from you. Then, if time brings a reason to recall you, we won't have to send all over the vast world to look for one man and lose our advantage, which always cools when the man who needs it isn't there.

Fare ye well: / Thou hast years upon thee; and thou art too full / Of the wars' surfeits to go rove with one / That's yet unbruis'd: bring me but out at gate.— / Come, my sweet wife, my dearest mother, and / My friends of noble touch; when I am forth, / Bid me farewell, and smile. I pray you, come. / While I remain above the ground, you shall / Hear from me still; and never of me aught / But what is like me formerly.

Farewell. You're old, and you've had too much of war to go wandering with someone who's still unbruised. Just see me out of the gate. Come, my sweet wife, my dearest mother, and my noble friends. When I'm outside, say goodbye to me and smile. Please, come. While I'm still above ground, you'll keep hearing from me, and never anything about me but what's like what I've been before.
That's worthily / As any ear can hear.—Come, let's not weep.— / If I could shake off but one seven years / From these old arms and legs, by the good gods, / I'd with thee every foot.
That's as worthy as anything anyone could hear. Come, let's not cry. If I could shake just seven years off these old arms and legs, by the good gods, I'd go with you every step.
Bid them all home; he's gone, and we'll no further.— / The nobility are vex'd, whom we see have sided / In his behalf.
Send them all home. He's gone, and we'll go no further. The nobility are angry; we can see they've taken his side.
Now we have shown our power, / Let us seem humbler after it is done / Than when it was a-doing.
Now that we've shown our power, let's seem humbler now it's done than while it was being done.
Bid them home: / Say their great enemy is gone, and they / Stand in their ancient strength.
Send them home. Tell them their great enemy is gone, and they keep their old strength.
They have ta'en note of us: keep on your way.
O, you're well met: the hoarded plague o' the gods / Requite your love!
Oh, well met! May the gods' stored-up plagues repay your love!
Peace, peace, be not so loud.
Quiet, quiet, don't be so loud.
If that I could for weeping, you should hear,— / Nay, and you shall hear some.—[To BRUTUS] Will you be gone?
If I could speak for crying, you'd hear— No, you'll hear some anyway. (To Brutus) Are you leaving?
You shall stay too[To SICINIUS]: I would I had the power / To say so to my husband.
(To Sicinius) You'll stay too. I wish I had the power to say that to my husband.
Are you turning into a man?
Ay, fool; is that a shame?—Note but this, fool.— / Was not a man my father? Hadst thou foxship / To banish him that struck more blows for Rome / Than thou hast spoken words?—
Yes, fool; is that shameful? Just note this, fool: wasn't my father a man? Did you have the foxy cunning to banish the man who struck more blows for Rome than you've spoken words?

Moe noble blows than ever thou wise words; / And for Rome's good.—I'll tell thee what;—yet go;— / Nay, but thou shalt stay too:—I would my son / Were in Arabia, and thy tribe before him, / His good sword in his hand.

More noble blows than you've ever spoken wise words, and for Rome's good. I'll tell you what— no, go. No, you'll stay too. I wish my son were in the Arabian desert, and your tribe in front of him, with his good sword in his hand.
What then! / He'd make an end of thy posterity.
What then! He'd wipe out all your descendants.
Bastards and all.— / Good man, the wounds that he does bear for Rome!
Bastards and all. Good man, the wounds he carries for Rome!
I would he had continu'd to his country / As he began, and not unknit himself / The noble knot he made.
I wish he had carried on with his country as he began, and not untied the noble knot he made himself.
I would he had! 'Twas you incens'd the rabble;— / Cats, that can judge as fitly of his worth / As I can of those mysteries which heaven / Will not have earth to know.
"I wish he had"! It was you who stirred up the mob: cats, who can judge his worth as well as I can judge the mysteries heaven won't let earth know.

Now, pray, sir, get you gone: / You have done a brave deed. Ere you go, hear this,— / As far as doth the Capitol exceed / The meanest house in Rome, so far my son,— / This lady's husband here; this, do you see?— / Whom you have banish'd does exceed you all.

Now, please, sir, be off. You've done a fine deed. Before you go, hear this: as far as the Capitol towers above the meanest house in Rome, so far my son, this lady's husband here, do you see, whom you have banished, towers above all of you.
Why stay we to be baited / With one that wants her wits?
Why should we stay to be baited by a woman who's lost her wits?
I would the gods had nothing else to do / But to confirm my curses! Could I meet 'em / But once a day, it would unclog my heart / Of what lies heavy to't.
I wish the gods had nothing else to do but carry out my curses! If I could meet them just once a day, it would unburden my heart of what weighs on it.
You have told them home, / And, by my troth, you have cause. You'll sup with me?
You've told them straight, and honestly, you have reason to. Will you have supper with me?
Anger's my meat; I sup upon myself, / And so shall starve with feeding.—Come, let's go: / Leave this faint puling and lament as I do, / In anger, Juno-like. Come, come, come.
Anger is my food. I feed on myself, and so I'll starve by eating. Come, let's go. (To Virgilia) Stop this feeble whimpering and grieve as I do, in anger, like Juno. Come, come, come.
I know you well, sir, and you know me; your name, I think, / is Adrian.
I know you well, sir, and you know me. Your name, I think, is Adrian.
It is so, sir: truly, I have forgot you.
It is, sir. Honestly, I've forgotten you.
I am a Roman; and my services are, as you are, against 'em: know / you me yet?
I'm a Roman, and I work, as you do, against the Romans. Do you know me now?

You had more beard when I last saw you; but your favour is / well approved by your tongue. What's the news in Rome? I have a / note from the Volscian state, to find you out there; you have / well saved me a day's journey.
You had more beard when I last saw you, but your voice confirms your face. What's the news in Rome? I have orders from the Volscian state to find you there; you've saved me a good day's journey.
There hath been in Rome strange insurrections: the people / against the senators, patricians, and nobles.
There have been strange uprisings in Rome: the people against the senators, patricians and nobles.
Hath been! is it ended, then? Our state thinks not so; / they are in a most warlike preparation, and hope to come upon / them in the heat of their division.
Have been! Is it over, then? Our state doesn't think so. They're preparing hard for war and hope to attack them while they're hotly divided.

The main blaze of it is past, but a small thing would make it / flame again; for the nobles receive so to heart the banishment / of that worthy Coriolanus that they are in a ripe aptness to take / all power from the people, and to pluck from them their tribunes / for ever. This lies glowing, I can tell you, and is almost mature / for the violent breaking out.

The main blaze is past, but a small thing would make it flare up again, because the nobles take the banishment of that worthy Coriolanus so much to heart that they're ripe to take all power away from the people and abolish their tribunes forever. It's glowing under the surface, I can tell you, and almost ready to break out violently.
You will be welcome with this intelligence, Nicanor.
You'll be welcome with this news, Nicanor.

The day serves well for them now. I have heard it said the / fittest time to corrupt a man's wife is when she's fallen out / with her husband. Your noble Tullus Aufidius will appear well in / these wars, his great opposer, Coriolanus, being now in no / request of his country.

The moment's just right for them now. I've heard it said the best time to seduce a man's wife is when she has fallen out with her husband. Your noble Tullus Aufidius will shine in these wars, now that his great opponent, Coriolanus, is no longer wanted by his country.
He cannot choose. I am most fortunate thus accidentally to / encounter you; you have ended my business, and I will merrily / accompany you home.
He's bound to. I'm very lucky to have met you by chance like this. You've finished my business for me, and I'll happily go home with you.
I shall between this and supper tell you most strange things / from Rome; all tending to the good of their adversaries. Have you / an army ready, say you?
Between now and supper I'll tell you the strangest things from Rome, all of them good for Rome's enemies. You have an army ready, you say?
A most royal one; the centurions and their charges, distinctly / billeted, already in the entertainment, and to be on foot at an / hour's warning.
A splendid one. The centurions and their companies, each quartered separately, are already on the payroll and can march at an hour's notice.
I am joyful to hear of their readiness, and am the man, I think, / that shall set them in present action. So, sir, heartily well / met, and most glad of your company.
I'm glad to hear they're ready, and I think I'm the man to set them going at once. So, sir, very well met, and I'm very glad of your company.
You take my part from me, sir; I have the most cause to be / glad of yours.
You're taking my line, sir; I have the most reason to be glad of yours.

A goodly city is this Antium. City, / 'Tis I that made thy widows: many an heir / Of these fair edifices 'fore my wars / Have I heard groan and drop: then know me not. / Lest that thy wives with spits and boys with stones, / In puny battle slay me.

This Antium is a fine city. City, it's I who made your widows. I've heard many an heir of these fine buildings groan and fall in my wars. So don't recognize me, or your wives with roasting spits and your boys with stones will kill me in a petty fight.
Direct me, if it be your will, / Where great Aufidius lies; is he in Antium?
Please tell me, if you will, where the great Aufidius lives. Is he in Antium?
He is, and feasts the nobles of the state / At his house this night.
He is, and he's feasting the nobles of the state at his house tonight.
Which is his house, beseech you?
This one, here, in front of you.

O world, thy slippery turns! Friends now fast sworn, / Whose double bosoms seems to wear one heart, / Whose hours, whose bed, whose meal and exercise / Are still together, who twin, as 'twere, in love / Unseparable, shall within this hour, / On a dissension of a doit, break out / To bitterest enmity; so fellest foes, / Whose passions and whose plots have broke their sleep / To take the one the other, by some chance, / Some trick not worth an egg, shall grow dear friends / And interjoin their issues. So with me:— / My birthplace hate I, and my love's upon / This enemy town.—I'll enter; if he slay me, / He does fair justice; if he give me way, / I'll do his country service.

Oh world, how slippery your turns are! Friends sworn true now, whose two breasts seem to hold one heart, who always spend their hours, their bed, their meals and their exercise together, who are like twins in their inseparable love, will within the hour break out into the bitterest hatred over a quarrel about a penny. In the same way, the deadliest enemies, whose passions and schemes to catch each other have kept them awake, will by some chance, some trick not worth an egg, become dear friends and join their children in marriage. So it is with me. I hate my birthplace, and my love has turned to this enemy town. I'll go in. If he kills me, he does fair justice; if he takes me in, I'll serve his country.
Wine, wine, wine! What service is here! / I think our fellows are asleep.
Wine, wine, wine! What service is this? I think our fellow servants are asleep.
Where's Cotus? my master calls for him.—Cotus!
Where's Cotus? My master's calling for him. Cotus!
A goodly house: the feast smells well; but I / Appear not like a guest.
A fine house. The feast smells good; but I don't look like a guest.
What would you have, friend? whence are you? Here's no place for / you: pray go to the door.
What do you want, friend? Where are you from? There's no place for you here. Please go to the door.
I have deserv'd no better entertainment / In being Coriolanus.
I've deserved no better welcome by being Coriolanus.
Whence are you, sir? Has the porter his eyes in his head that he / gives entrance to such companions? Pray, get you out.
Where are you from, sir? Has the porter got eyes in his head, letting in fellows like this? Please, get out.
Are you so brave? I'll have you talked with anon.
Are you so bold? I'll have someone deal with you soon.
A strange one as ever I looked on: I cannot get him / out o' the house. Pr'ythee call my master to him.
As strange a one as I've ever seen. I can't get him out of the house. Please call the master to him.
What have you to do here, fellow? Pray you avoid the house.
What are you doing here, fellow? Please leave the house.
Let me but stand; I will not hurt your hearth.
Just let me stand here. I won't harm your hearth.
Pray you, poor gentleman, take up some other station; here's no / place for you. Pray you avoid; come.
Please, poor gentleman, find some other place to stand. There's no place for you here. Please leave. Come on.
Follow your function, go, / And batten on cold bits.
Go about your job, go on, and fatten yourself on leftovers.
What, you will not?—Pr'ythee, tell my master what a strange / guest he has here.
What, you won't go? Please tell the master what a strange guest he has here.
I' the city of kites and crows.
In the city of kites and crows.
I' the city of kites and crows!—What an ass it is!—Then thou / dwell'st with daws too?
In the city of kites and crows! What an ass! Then you live with jackdaws too?
No, I serve not thy master.
No, I don't serve your master.
How, sir! Do you meddle with my master?
What, sir! Are you meddling with my master?
Ay; 'tis an honester service than to meddle with thy mistress. / Thou prat'st and prat'st; serve with thy trencher, hence!
Yes; it's more honest work than meddling with your mistress. You chatter and chatter. Go and wait at table with your plate! Get out!
Here, sir; I'd have beaten him like a dog, but for / disturbing the lords within.
Here, sir. I'd have beaten him like a dog, but I didn't want to disturb the lords inside.
Whence com'st thou? what wouldst thou? thy name? / Why speak'st not? speak, man: what's thy name?
Where do you come from? What do you want? Your name? Why don't you speak? Speak, man. What's your name?
[Unmuffling] If, Tullus, / Not yet thou know'st me, and, seeing me, dost not / Think me for the man I am, necessity / Commands me name myself.
(Uncovering his face) If you still don't know me, Tullus, and seeing me, don't take me for the man I am, necessity forces me to name myself.
A name unmusical to the Volscians' ears, / And harsh in sound to thine.
A name that sounds unmusical to Volscian ears and harsh to yours.
Say, what's thy name? / Thou hast a grim appearance, and thy face / Bears a command in't; though thy tackle's torn, / Thou show'st a noble vessel: what's thy name?
Say, what's your name? You look grim, and your face has authority in it. Though your rigging is torn, you look like a noble ship. What's your name?
Prepare thy brow to frown:—know'st thou me yet?
Get ready to frown. Do you know me now?
I don't know you. Your name?

My name is Caius Marcius, who hath done / To thee particularly, and to all the Volsces, / Great hurt and mischief; thereto witness may / My surname, Coriolanus: the painful service, / The extreme dangers, and the drops of blood / Shed for my thankless country, are requited / But with that surname; a good memory, / And witness of the malice and displeasure / Which thou shouldst bear me: only that name remains; / The cruelty and envy of the people, / Permitted by our dastard nobles, who / Have all forsook me, hath devour'd the rest, / And suffer'd me by the voice of slaves to be / Whoop'd out of Rome. Now, this extremity / Hath brought me to thy hearth: not out of hope, / Mistake me not, to save my life; for if / I had fear'd death, of all the men i' the world / I would have 'voided thee; but in mere spite, / To be full quit of those my banishers, / Stand I before thee here. Then if thou hast / A heart of wreak in thee, that wilt revenge / Thine own particular wrongs, and stop those maims / Of shame seen through thy country, speed thee straight / And make my misery serve thy turn: so use it / That my revengeful services may prove / As benefits to thee; for I will fight / Against my canker'd country with the spleen / Of all the under fiends. But if so be / Thou dar'st not this, and that to prove more fortunes / Th'art tir'd, then, in a word, I also am / Longer to live most weary, and present / My throat to thee and to thy ancient malice; / Which not to cut would show thee but a fool, / Since I have ever follow'd thee with hate, / Drawn tuns of blood out of thy country's breast, / And cannot live but to thy shame, unless / It be to do thee service.

My name is Caius Marcius, who has done great harm and damage to you in particular and to all the Volscians; my surname, Coriolanus, is witness to it. The painful service, the extreme dangers and the drops of blood shed for my ungrateful country are repaid only with that surname, a good reminder and proof of the hatred and anger you ought to feel for me. Only the name remains. The cruelty and spite of the people, allowed by our cowardly nobles, who have all abandoned me, has swallowed up the rest and let me be hooted out of Rome by the voices of slaves. Now this desperate state has brought me to your hearth, not in hope of saving my life, don't mistake me, because if I'd feared death, I'd have avoided you more than any man in the world, but out of pure spite, to get even with those who banished me, I stand here before you. So if you have a heart full of vengeance that will avenge your own personal wrongs and stop those shameful wounds seen all over your country, hurry and make my misery serve your purpose. Use it so that my revengeful services prove a benefit to you, because I'll fight against my rotten country with the fury of all the devils in hell. But if you don't dare to do this and you're too tired to try your luck any more, then, in a word, I'm also very tired of living, and I offer my throat to you and your old hatred. Not to cut it would only show you a fool, since I've always pursued you with hatred, drawn barrels of blood from your country's breast, and can only live to your shame, unless it's to serve you.

O Marcius, Marcius! / Each word thou hast spoke hath weeded from my heart / A root of ancient envy. If Jupiter / Should from yond cloud speak divine things, / And say ''Tis true,' I'd not believe them more / Than thee, all noble Marcius.—Let me twine / Mine arms about that body, where against / My grained ash an hundred times hath broke / And scar'd the moon with splinters; here I clip / The anvil of my sword, and do contest / As hotly and as nobly with thy love / As ever in ambitious strength I did / Contend against thy valour. Know thou first, / I lov'd the maid I married; never man / Sighed truer breath; but that I see thee here, / Thou noble thing! more dances my rapt heart / Than when I first my wedded mistress saw / Bestride my threshold. Why, thou Mars! I tell thee / We have a power on foot; and I had purpose / Once more to hew thy target from thy brawn, / Or lose mine arm for't: thou hast beat me out / Twelve several times, and I have nightly since / Dreamt of encounters 'twixt thyself and me; / We have been down together in my sleep, / Unbuckling helms, fisting each other's throat, / And wak'd half dead with nothing. Worthy Marcius, / Had we no other quarrel else to Rome, but that / Thou art thence banish'd, we would muster all / From twelve to seventy; and, pouring war / Into the bowels of ungrateful Rome, / Like a bold flood o'erbear. O, come, go in, / And take our friendly senators by the hands; / Who now are here, taking their leaves of me, / Who am prepar'd against your territories, / Though not for Rome itself.

Oh Marcius, Marcius! Every word you've spoken has rooted out of my heart a root of old hatred. If Jupiter spoke divine things from that cloud and said "It's true", I wouldn't believe him more than you, all-noble Marcius. Let me wind my arms around that body against which my ash-wood spear has broken a hundred times and scared the moon with splinters. Here I hug the anvil of my sword, and I compete as hotly and nobly with your love as I ever fought against your courage in ambitious strength. Know this first: I loved the girl I married; no man ever sighed more truly. But seeing you here, you noble thing, makes my enraptured heart dance more than when I first saw my bride step over my threshold. Why, you Mars! I tell you, we have an army ready, and I intended once more to hack your shield from your arm or lose my own arm trying. You've beaten me twelve separate times, and every night since I've dreamt of fights between us. We've been on the ground together in my sleep, unbuckling helmets, grabbing each other's throats, and I've woken half dead from nothing. Worthy Marcius, if we had no other quarrel with Rome but that you're banished from it, we'd call up every man from twelve to seventy and, pouring war into the guts of ungrateful Rome, overwhelm it like a bold flood. Oh, come in and shake hands with our friendly senators, who are here now taking leave of me; I'm ready to march against your lands, though not against Rome itself.

Therefore, most absolute sir, if thou wilt have / The leading of thine own revenges, take / Th' one half of my commission; and set down,— / As best thou art experienc'd, since thou know'st / Thy country's strength and weakness,—thine own ways; / Whether to knock against the gates of Rome, / Or rudely visit them in parts remote, / To fright them, ere destroy. But come in; / Let me commend thee first to those that shall / Say yea to thy desires. A thousand welcomes! / And more a friend than e'er an enemy; / Yet, Marcius, that was much. Your hand: most welcome!

So, most perfect sir, if you want to lead your own revenge, take half of my command and decide your own course, as you're most experienced and know your country's strengths and weaknesses: whether to knock at the gates of Rome, or roughly attack its outlying parts to frighten them before destroying them. But come in. Let me introduce you first to those who'll agree to what you want. A thousand welcomes! And more a friend than ever an enemy; and yet, Marcius, that was a great deal. Your hand: most welcome!
By my hand, I had thought to have strucken him with a cudgel; and / yet my mind gave me his clothes made a false report of him.
I swear I was going to hit him with a club; and yet I had a feeling his clothes were lying about him.
What an arm he has! He turned me about with his finger and his / thumb, as one would set up a top.
What an arm he has! He spun me round with his finger and thumb like a spinning top.
Nay, I knew by his face that there was something in him; he had, / sir, a kind of face, methought,—I cannot tell how to term it.
Well, I could tell from his face there was something in him. He had, sir, a kind of face, I thought— I can't say how to put it.
He had so, looking as it were,—would I were hanged, but I / thought there was more in him than I could think.
He did, looking as if— hang me, but I thought there was more in him than I could imagine.
So did I, I'll be sworn: he is simply the rarest man i' the / world.
So did I, I swear. He's simply the most remarkable man in the world.
I think he is; but a greater soldier than he you wot on.
I think he is; but there's a greater soldier than him, you know who.
Nay, it's no matter for that.
Nay, not so neither: but I take him to be the greater soldier.
No, not that either; but I think he's the greater soldier.
Faith, look you, one cannot tell how to say that: for the defence / of a town our general is excellent.
Well, look, you can't really say. For defending a town our general is excellent.
Ay, and for an assault too.
Yes, and for attacking one too.
O slaves, I can tell you news,—news, you rascals!
Oh, you slaves, I've got news for you, news, you rascals!
What, what, what? Let's share it.
I would not be a Roman, of all nations; I had as lief be a / condemned man.
I wouldn't be a Roman for anything; I'd as soon be a condemned man.
Why, here's he that was wont to thwack our general,—Caius / Marcius.
Why, here's the man who used to thrash our general: Caius Marcius.
Why do you say, thwack our general?
Why do you say "thrash our general"?
I do not say thwack our general; but he was always good enough / for him.
I don't say "thrash our general"; but he was always more than a match for him.
Come, we are fellows and friends: he was ever too hard for him; I / have heard him say so himself.
Come on, we're comrades and friends. He was always too strong for him; I've heard him say so himself.
He was too hard for him directly, to say the troth on't; before / Corioli he scotched him and notched him like a carbonado.
To tell the truth, he was flatly too much for him. At Corioli he slashed and scored him like a steak for grilling.
An he had been cannibally given, he might have broiled and eaten / him too.
If he'd been a cannibal, he might have grilled and eaten him too.
But what else is your news?

Why, he is so made on here within as if he were son and heir to / Mars; set at upper end o' the table: no question asked him by any / of the senators but they stand bald before him: our general / himself makes a mistress of him, sanctifies himself with's hand, / and turns up the white o' the eye to his discourse. But the / bottom of the news is, our general is cut i' the middle, and but / one half of what he was yesterday; for the other has half, by the / entreaty and grant of the whole table. He'll go, he says, and / sowl the porter of Rome gates by the ears; he will mow all down / before him, and leave his passage polled.

Why, they're making as much of him inside as if he were Mars's son and heir. He's seated at the head of the table; none of the senators asks him a question without standing bareheaded before him. Our general himself treats him like a mistress, touches his hand as if it were holy, and rolls his eyes upward at what he says. But the heart of the news is that our general has been cut in half and is only half of what he was yesterday, because the other man has the other half, at the request and with the consent of the whole table. He says he'll go and drag the porter of Rome's gates by the ears; he'll mow down everything in his way and leave his path cleared.
And he's as like to do't as any man I can imagine.
And he's as likely to do it as any man I can imagine.

Do't! he will do't; for look you, sir, he has as many friends as / enemies; which friends, sir, as it were, durst not, look you, / sir, show themselves, as we term it, his friends, whilst he's in / dejectitude.

Do it! He will do it. Because look, sir, he has as many friends as enemies; and those friends, sir, so to speak, didn't dare, look you, sir, show themselves to be, as we say, his friends while he was in "dejectitude".
But when they shall see, sir, his crest up again, and the man in / blood, they will out of their burrows, like conies after rain, / and revel all with him.
But when they see, sir, his crest raised again and the man in full vigour, they'll come out of their burrows like rabbits after rain and all celebrate with him.
To-morrow; to-day; presently; you shall have the drum struck up / this afternoon: 'tis as it were parcel of their feast, and to be / executed ere they wipe their lips.
Tomorrow; today; right now. You'll hear the drum beaten this afternoon. It's part of their feast, so to speak, and will be carried out before they wipe their lips.
Why, then we shall have a stirring world again. This peace is / nothing but to rust iron, increase tailors, and breed / ballad-makers.
Why, then we'll have a lively world again. This peace does nothing but rust iron, multiply tailors and breed ballad-writers.

Let me have war, say I; it exceeds peace as far as day does / night; it's spritely, waking, audible, and full of vent. Peace is / a very apoplexy, lethargy; mulled, deaf, sleepy, insensible; a / getter of more bastard children than war's a destroyer of men.

Give me war, I say. It beats peace as day beats night. It's lively, wide awake, loud and full of news. Peace is a real paralysis, a coma: flat, deaf, sleepy, senseless; it fathers more bastards than war kills men.
'Tis so: and as war in some sort, may be said to be a ravisher, / so it cannot be denied but peace is a great maker of cuckolds.
That's right. And just as war could be called a rapist in a way, there's no denying peace makes plenty of cuckolds.
Ay, and it makes men hate one another.
Yes, and it makes men hate each other.
Reason: because they then less need one another. The wars for my / money. I hope to see Romans as cheap as Volscians. They are / rising, they are rising.
That's because they need each other less then. Give me war. I hope to see Romans as cheap as Volscians. They're getting up from the table, they're getting up.

We hear not of him, neither need we fear him; / His remedies are tame i' the present peace / And quietness of the people, which before / Were in wild hurry. Here do make his friends / Blush that the world goes well; who rather had, / Though they themselves did suffer by't, behold / Dissentious numbers pestering streets than see / Our tradesmen singing in their shops, and going / About their functions friendly.

We hear nothing of him, and we don't need to fear him. His help is useless now, with the people peaceful and quiet when before they were in wild uproar. This makes his friends blush that everything's going well. They'd rather see quarrelsome crowds plaguing the streets, even if they suffered for it themselves, than see our tradesmen singing in their shops and going about their work in a friendly way.
We stood to't in good time.—Is this Menenius?
We stood firm at the right time. Is this Menenius?
'Tis he, 'tis he. O, he is grown most kind / Of late.
It's him, it's him. Oh, he has become very friendly lately.
Your Coriolanus is not much miss'd / But with his friends: the commonwealth doth stand; / And so would do, were he more angry at it.
Your Coriolanus isn't missed much except by his friends. The state stands firm, and would still stand if he were even angrier with it.
All's well, and might have been much better if / He could have temporiz'd.
All's well, and it might have been much better if he could have compromised.
Have you heard where he is?
Nay, I hear nothing: his mother and his wife / Hear nothing from him.
No, I hear nothing. His mother and his wife hear nothing from him.
God-den to you all, God-den to you all.
Good evening to you all, good evening to you all.
Ourselves, our wives, and children, on our knees, / Are bound to pray for you both.
We, our wives and children are bound to pray for you both on our knees.
Farewell, kind neighbours: we wish'd Coriolanus / Had lov'd you as we did.
Goodbye, kind neighbours. We wish Coriolanus had loved you as we do.
This is a happier and more comely time / Than when these fellows ran about the streets / Crying confusion.
This is a happier and more fitting time than when these fellows ran around the streets shouting for chaos.
Caius Marcius was / A worthy officer i' the war; but insolent, / O'ercome with pride, ambitious past all thinking, / Self-loving,—
Caius Marcius was a worthy officer in war, but arrogant, swollen with pride, ambitious beyond belief, self-loving—
And affecting one sole throne, / Without assistance.
And aiming at sole rule, without anyone to share it.
We should by this, to all our lamentation, / If he had gone forth consul, found it so.
If he'd become consul, we'd all have found it so by now, to our sorrow.
The gods have well prevented it, and Rome / Sits safe and still without him.
The gods have kindly prevented it, and Rome sits safe and quiet without him.

Worthy tribunes, / There is a slave, whom we have put in prison, / Reports,—the Volsces with several powers / Are enter'd in the Roman territories, / And with the deepest malice of the war / Destroy what lies before 'em.

Worthy tribunes, there's a slave we've put in prison who reports that the Volscians, with two separate armies, have entered Roman territory and are destroying everything in their path with the most savage hostility of war.
'Tis Aufidius, / Who, hearing of our Marcius' banishment, / Thrusts forth his horns again into the world; / Which were inshell'd when Marcius stood for Rome, / And durst not once peep out.

It's Aufidius, who, hearing of our Marcius's banishment, is poking his horns out into the world again. They were pulled back into his shell while Marcius stood up for Rome, and he didn't dare peep out once.
Come, what talk you of Marcius?
Come, why are you talking about Marcius?
Go see this rumourer whipp'd.—It cannot be / The Volsces dare break with us.
Have this rumour-monger whipped. It can't be that the Volscians dare break the treaty with us.

Cannot be! / We have record that very well it can; / And three examples of the like hath been / Within my age. But reason with the fellow, / Before you punish him, where he heard this; / Lest you shall chance to whip your information / And beat the messenger who bids beware / Of what is to be dreaded.

Can't be! We have records that show very well it can, and there have been three examples of it in my lifetime. But before you punish the fellow, ask him where he heard this, in case you end up whipping your source of information and beating the messenger who warns you of what you should fear.
Tell not me: / I know this cannot be.
Don't tell me. I know this can't be.
The nobles in great earnestness are going / All to the senate-house: some news is come / That turns their countenances.
The nobles are all going in great seriousness to the senate house. Some news has come that has changed their faces.
'Tis this slave,— / Go whip him fore the people's eyes:—his raising; / Nothing but his report.
It's this slave. Go and whip him in front of the people. It's his stirring, nothing but his report.
Yes, worthy sir, / The slave's report is seconded, and more, / More fearful, is deliver'd.
Yes, worthy sir, the slave's report has been confirmed, and more, more frightening news has been brought.

It is spoke freely out of many mouths,— / How probable I do not know,—that Marcius, / Join'd with Aufidius, leads a power 'gainst Rome, / And vows revenge as spacious as between / The young'st and oldest thing.

Many people are openly saying, how likely it is I don't know, that Marcius has joined Aufidius and is leading an army against Rome, and vows a revenge as wide as the gap between the youngest and the oldest thing.
Rais'd only, that the weaker sort may wish / Good Marcius home again.
Started only so the weaker people will wish good Marcius home again.
This is unlikely: / He and Aufidius can no more atone / Than violentest contrariety.
This is unlikely. He and Aufidius can no more be reconciled than the most violent opposites.

You are sent for to the senate: / A fearful army, led by Caius Marcius / Associated with Aufidius, rages / Upon our territories; and have already / O'erborne their way, consum'd with fire and took / What lay before them.

You're called to the senate. A terrifying army led by Caius Marcius, together with Aufidius, is raging through our territory. They've already forced their way through, burned and taken everything in front of them.
O, you have made good work!
You have holp to ravish your own daughters, and / To melt the city leads upon your pates; / To see your wives dishonour'd to your noses,—
You've helped to rape your own daughters and to melt the city's lead roofs onto your heads, to see your wives disgraced in front of you—
What's the news? what's the news?
What's the news? What's the news?
Your temples burned in their cement; and / Your franchises, whereon you stood, confin'd / Into an auger's bore.
Your temples burned to their foundations, and your rights, which you stood on so firmly, squeezed into a hole the size of a drill bit.
Pray now, your news?— / You have made fair work, I fear me.—Pray, your news. / If Marcius should be join'd wi' the Volscians,—
Please, now, your news? You've done fine work, I'm afraid. Please, your news. If Marcius has joined the Volscians—

If! / He is their god: he leads them like a thing / Made by some other deity than nature, / That shapes man better; and they follow him, / Against us brats, with no less confidence / Than boys pursuing summer butterflies, / Or butchers killing flies.

If! He's their god. He leads them like a being made by some other god than nature, one who shapes men better; and they follow him against us brats as confidently as boys chasing summer butterflies or butchers swatting flies.
You have made good work, / You and your apron men; you that stood so much / Upon the voice of occupation and / The breath of garlic-eaters!
You've done fine work, you and your men in aprons, you who made so much of the votes of workmen and the breath of garlic-eaters!
He'll shake / Your Rome about your ears.
He'll shake your Rome down around your ears.
As Hercules / Did shake down mellow fruit.—You have made fair work!
As Hercules shook down ripe fruit. You've done fine work!

Ay; and you'll look pale / Before you find it other. All the regions / Do smilingly revolt; and who resists / Are mock'd for valiant ignorance, / And perish constant fools. Who is't can blame him? / Your enemies and his find something in him.

Yes, and you'll turn pale before you find it otherwise. All the regions are gladly going over to him, and those who resist are mocked for their brave ignorance and die loyal fools. Who can blame him? Your enemies and his see something in him.
We are all undone unless / The noble man have mercy.
We're all ruined unless the noble man shows mercy.

Who shall ask it? / The tribunes cannot do't for shame; the people / Deserve such pity of him as the wolf / Does of the shepherds: for his best friends, if they / Should say 'Be good to Rome,' they charg'd him even / As those should do that had deserv'd his hate, / And therein show'd like enemies.

Who will ask him for it? The tribunes can't, for shame. The people deserve as much pity from him as the wolf gets from shepherds. As for his best friends, if they said "Be good to Rome", they'd be asking it of him just as those who'd earned his hatred would, and so would look like enemies.

'Tis true: / If he were putting to my house the brand / That should consume it, I have not the face / To say 'Beseech you, cease.'—You have made fair hands, / You and your crafts! You have crafted fair!

That's true. If he were putting the torch to my house to burn it down, I wouldn't have the nerve to say "Please, stop." (To the Tribunes) You've done a fine job, you and your craftsmen! You've crafted it beautifully!
You have brought / A trembling upon Rome, such as was never / So incapable of help.
You've brought a trembling on Rome that was never so far beyond help.
How! Was it we? we lov'd him, but, like beasts, / And cowardly nobles, gave way unto your clusters, / Who did hoot him out o' the city.
What! Was it us? We loved him, but, like beasts and cowardly nobles, we gave way to your mobs, who hooted him out of the city.

But I fear / They'll roar him in again. Tullus Aufidius, / The second name of men, obeys his points / As if he were his officer:—desperation / Is all the policy, strength, and defence, / That Rome can make against them.

But I'm afraid they'll roar him back in again. Tullus Aufidius, the second-best of men, obeys his orders as if he were his officer. Desperation is all the strategy, strength and defence Rome can put up against them.

Here comes the clusters.— / And is Aufidius with him?—You are they / That made the air unwholesome, when you cast / Your stinking greasy caps in hooting at / Coriolanus' exile. Now he's coming; / And not a hair upon a soldier's head / Which will not prove a whip: as many coxcombs / As you threw caps up will he tumble down, / And pay you for your voices. 'Tis no matter; / If he could burn us all into one coal / We have deserv'd it.

Here come the mobs. And is Aufidius with him? You're the ones who poisoned the air when you threw up your stinking greasy caps, hooting at Coriolanus's exile. Now he's coming, and there isn't a hair on any soldier's head that won't be a whip. He'll knock down as many fools' heads as you threw up caps, and pay you back for your votes. It doesn't matter. If he burned us all into one cinder, we'd have deserved it.
For mine own part, / When I said banish him, I said 'twas pity.
For my part, when I said "banish him", I said it was a pity.
And so did I; and, to say the truth, so did very many of us. That / we did, we did for the best; and though we willingly consented to / his banishment, yet it was against our will.
And so did I; and, to tell the truth, so did very many of us. What we did, we did for the best; and though we willingly agreed to his banishment, it was against our will.
You are goodly things, you voices!
You have made / Good work, you and your cry!—Shall's to the Capitol?
You've done good work, you and your pack! Shall we go to the Capitol?
Go, masters, get you home; be not dismay'd; / These are a side that would be glad to have / This true which they so seem to fear. Go home, / And show no sign of fear.
Go home, friends; don't be alarmed. These men are a faction who'd be glad for this to be true, though they seem so afraid of it. Go home and show no sign of fear.
The gods be good to us!—Come, masters, let's home. I / ever said we were i' the wrong when we banished him.
The gods be good to us! Come, friends, let's go home. I always said we were wrong to banish him.
So did we all. But come, let's home.
So did we all. But come, let's go home.
I do not like this news.
Let's to the Capitol:—would half my wealth / Would buy this for a lie!
Let's go to the Capitol. I'd give half my wealth to make this a lie!
Do they still fly to the Roman?
Are they still flocking to the Roman?

I do not know what witchcraft's in him, but / Your soldiers use him as the grace 'fore meat, / Their talk at table, and their thanks at end; / And you are darken'd in this action, sir, / Even by your own.

I don't know what witchcraft is in him, but your soldiers use him as their grace before meat, their talk at dinner, and their thanks at the end. And you're overshadowed in this campaign, sir, even by your own men.

I cannot help it now, / Unless by using means, I lame the foot / Of our design. He bears himself more proudlier, / Even to my person, than I thought he would / When first I did embrace him: yet his nature / In that's no changeling; and I must excuse / What cannot be amended.

I can't help it now, unless I cripple our whole plan by the means I use. He behaves more proudly, even towards me, than I thought he would when I first embraced him. But his nature hasn't changed in that, and I must excuse what can't be put right.
Yet I wish, sir,— / I mean, for your particular,—you had not / Join'd in commission with him; but either / Had borne the action of yourself, or else / To him had left it solely.
Still, I wish, sir, for your own sake, that you hadn't shared the command with him, but had either led the campaign yourself or left it entirely to him.

I understand thee well; and be thou sure, / When he shall come to his account, he knows not / What I can urge against him. Although it seems, / And so he thinks, and is no less apparent / To the vulgar eye, that he bears all things fairly, / And shows good husbandry for the Volscian state, / Fights dragon-like, and does achieve as soon / As draw his sword: yet he hath left undone / That which shall break his neck or hazard mine / Whene'er we come to our account.

I understand you well. And be sure of this: when he comes to account for himself, he doesn't know what I can charge him with. Although it seems, and he thinks so, and it's no less obvious to ordinary eyes, that he conducts everything fairly, manages well for the Volscian state, fights like a dragon and wins as soon as he draws his sword, still he has left something undone that will break his neck or risk mine whenever we come to settle our accounts.
Sir, I beseech you, think you he'll carry Rome?
Sir, please tell me, do you think he'll take Rome?

All places yield to him ere he sits down; / And the nobility of Rome are his; / The senators and patricians love him too: / The tribunes are no soldiers; and their people / Will be as rash in the repeal as hasty / To expel him thence. I think he'll be to Rome / As is the osprey to the fish, who takes it / By sovereignty of nature. First he was / A noble servant to them; but he could not / Carry his honours even: whether 'twas pride, / Which out of daily fortune ever taints / The happy man; whether defect of judgment, / To fail in the disposing of those chances / Which he was lord of; or whether nature, / Not to be other than one thing, not moving / From the casque to the cushion, but commanding peace / Even with the same austerity and garb / As he controll'd the war; but one of these,— / As he hath spices of them all, not all, / For I dare so far free him,—made him fear'd, / So hated, and so banish'd: but he has a merit / To choke it in the utterance. So our virtues / Lie in the interpretation of the time: / And power, unto itself most commendable, / Hath not a tomb so evident as a cheer / To extol what it hath done. / One fire drives out one fire; one nail, one nail; / Rights by rights falter, strengths by strengths do fail. / Come, let's away. When, Caius, Rome is thine, / Thou art poor'st of all; then shortly art thou mine.

Every place surrenders to him before he lays siege. The nobility of Rome are on his side, and the senators and patricians love him too. The tribunes are no soldiers, and their people will be as rash in recalling him as they were hasty in throwing him out. I think he'll be to Rome what the osprey is to the fish, which it takes by natural supremacy. At first he was a noble servant to them, but he couldn't carry his honours steadily. Whether it was pride, which always infects the lucky man who succeeds every day; whether a lack of judgment, failing to make the most of chances he controlled; or whether his nature, not to be anything but one thing, not changing from the helmet to the senate cushion, but ruling in peace with the same harshness and manner as he commanded in war: one of these (he has traces of them all, though not all completely, I'll clear him that far) made him feared, so hated, and so banished. But he has merit enough to choke the charges as they're spoken. So our virtues depend on how the times interpret them, and power, however praiseworthy in itself, has no tomb so certain as a public platform that praises what it has done. One fire drives out another, one nail another; rights give way to rights, strengths fail by strengths. Come, let's go. When Rome is yours, Caius, you'll be the poorest of all; and then you'll soon be mine.

No, I'll not go: you hear what he hath said / Which was sometime his general; who lov'd him / In a most dear particular. He call'd me father: / But what o' that? Go, you that banish'd him; / A mile before his tent fall down, and knee / The way into his mercy: nay, if he coy'd / To hear Cominius speak, I'll keep at home.

No, I won't go. You heard what he said to the man who was once his general and who loved him with a very special affection. He called me father; but what of it? You go, you who banished him. Fall down a mile before his tent and crawl on your knees into his mercy. No, if he was reluctant to hear Cominius speak, I'll stay at home.
He would not seem to know me.
He pretended not to know me.

Yet one time he did call me by my name: / I urged our old acquaintance, and the drops / That we have bled together. Coriolanus / He would not answer to: forbad all names; / He was a kind of nothing, titleless, / Till he had forg'd himself a name i' the fire / Of burning Rome.

Still, once he did call me by my name. I pressed our old friendship and the blood we've shed together. He wouldn't answer to "Coriolanus"; he rejected every name. He was a kind of nothing, without a title, until he had forged himself a name in the fire of burning Rome.
Why, so!—you have made good work! / A pair of tribunes that have rack'd for Rome, / To make coals cheap,—a noble memory!
Why, there you are! You've done good work! A pair of tribunes who've worked so hard for Rome to make coal cheap: a noble memorial!
I minded him how royal 'twas to pardon / When it was less expected: he replied, / It was a bare petition of a state / To one whom they had punish'd.
I reminded him how royal it is to pardon when it's least expected. He replied that it was a feeble petition from a state to a man they had punished.
Very well: / Could he say less?
Very well. Could he say less?

I offer'd to awaken his regard / For's private friends: his answer to me was, / He could not stay to pick them in a pile / Of noisome musty chaff: he said 'twas folly, / For one poor grain or two, to leave unburnt / And still to nose the offence.

I tried to stir his concern for his personal friends. His answer to me was that he couldn't stop to pick them out of a pile of stinking, mouldy chaff. He said it was foolish, for the sake of one or two poor grains, to leave the rest unburnt and go on smelling the stink.

For one poor grain / Or two! I am one of those; his mother, wife, / His child, and this brave fellow too- we are the grains: / You are the musty chaff; and you are smelt / Above the moon: we must be burnt for you.

For one or two poor grains! I'm one of those; his mother, wife, child, and this brave fellow too, we are the grains. You are the mouldy chaff, and you stink higher than the moon. We must be burnt because of you.

Nay, pray be patient: if you refuse your aid / In this so never-needed help, yet do not / Upbraid's with our distress. But, sure, if you / Would be your country's pleader, your good tongue, / More than the instant army we can make, / Might stop our countryman.

No, please be patient. If you refuse your help when it was never needed more, at least don't reproach us in our trouble. But surely if you'd plead for your country, your good tongue might stop our countryman better than any army we could raise right now.
Only make trial what your love can do / For Rome, towards Marcius.
Only try what your love for Marcius can do for Rome.
Well, and say that Marcius / Return me, as Cominius is return'd, / Unheard; what then? / But as a discontented friend, grief-shot / With his unkindness? Say't be so?
Well, and suppose Marcius sends me back unheard, as Cominius was sent back? What then? Just a rejected friend, wounded with grief by his unkindness? Suppose that happens?
Yet your good-will / Must have that thanks from Rome, after the measure / As you intended well.
Still, Rome must thank you for your good will, in proportion to your good intentions.

I'll undertake't; / I think he'll hear me. Yet to bite his lip / And hum at good Cominius much unhearts me. / He was not taken well: he had not din'd; / The veins unfill'd, our blood is cold, and then / We pout upon the morning, are unapt / To give or to forgive; but when we have stuff'd / These pipes and these conveyances of our blood / With wine and feeding, we have suppler souls / Than in our priest-like fasts. Therefore I'll watch him / Till he be dieted to my request, / And then I'll set upon him.

I'll take it on. I think he'll listen to me. Still, his biting his lip and grumbling at good Cominius discourages me a lot. He didn't catch him at the right moment; he hadn't eaten. When our veins aren't filled, our blood is cold, and then we sulk at the morning and aren't inclined to give or forgive. But when we've stuffed these pipes and channels of our blood with wine and food, our spirits are more flexible than when we fast like priests. So I'll wait until he's been fed enough for my request, and then I'll go at him.
You know the very road into his kindness / And cannot lose your way.
You know the very road into his kindness and can't lose your way.
Good faith, I'll prove him, / Speed how it will. I shall ere long have knowledge / Of my success.
Honestly, I'll try him, however it turns out. I'll soon know whether I've succeeded.

I tell you he does sit in gold, his eye / Red as 'twould burn Rome: and his injury / The gaoler to his pity. I kneel'd before him; / 'Twas very faintly he said 'Rise'; dismissed me / Thus, with his speechless hand: what he would do, / He sent in writing after me; what he would not, / Bound with an oath to yield to his conditions: / So that all hope is vain, / Unless his noble mother and his wife; / Who, as I hear, mean to solicit him / For mercy to his country. Therefore, let's hence, / And with our fair entreaties haste them on.

I tell you, he sits on a golden throne, his eye red as if it would burn Rome, and the wrong done to him keeps his pity locked up like a jailer. I knelt before him; he said "Rise" very faintly and dismissed me like this, with a silent wave of his hand. He sent after me in writing what he would do, and what he wouldn't, being bound by an oath to keep to his conditions. So all hope is useless, unless his noble mother and his wife, who I hear mean to beg him to have mercy on his country, can do it. So let's go and hurry them on with our earnest pleas.
You guard like men; 'tis well: but, by your leave, / I am an officer of state, and come / To speak with Coriolanus.
You guard like real men; that's good. But, if you'll excuse me, I'm an officer of state, and I've come to speak to Coriolanus.
You may not pass; you must return: our general / Will no more hear from thence.
You can't pass; you must go back. Our general will hear nothing more from there.
You'll see your Rome embrac'd with fire before / You'll speak with Coriolanus.
You'll see your Rome wrapped in fire before you speak to Coriolanus.
Good my friends, / If you have heard your general talk of Rome / And of his friends there, it is lots to blanks / My name hath touch'd your ears: it is Menenius.
My good friends, if you've heard your general talk about Rome and his friends there, it's a sure bet my name has reached your ears. It's Menenius.
Be it so; go back: the virtue of your name / Is not here passable.
So be it. Go back. Your name's power doesn't get you through here.

I tell thee, fellow, / Thy general is my lover: I have been / The book of his good acts, whence men have read / His fame unparallel'd, haply amplified; / For I have ever verified my friends,— / Of whom he's chief,—with all the size that verity / Would without lapsing suffer: nay, sometimes, / Like to a bowl upon a subtle ground, / I have tumbled past the throw: and in his praise / Have almost stamp'd the leasing: therefore, fellow, / I must have leave to pass.

I tell you, fellow, your general is my dear friend. I've been the book of his good deeds, from which men have read his unequalled fame, perhaps exaggerated, because I've always praised my friends, of whom he's the chief, as fully as truth would allow without slipping; indeed, sometimes, like a bowl on tricky ground, I've rolled past the mark, and in praising him I've almost stamped lies as true. So, fellow, I must be allowed to pass.

Faith, sir, if you had told as many lies in his behalf as you / have uttered words in your own, you should not pass here: no, / though it were as virtuous to lie as to live chastely. / Therefore, go back.
Honestly, sir, if you'd told as many lies on his behalf as you've spoken words on your own, you still wouldn't pass here; no, not even if lying were as virtuous as living chastely. So go back.
Pr'ythee, fellow, remember my name is Menenius, always / factionary on the party of your general.
Please, fellow, remember my name is Menenius, always a supporter of your general's party.
Howsoever you have been his liar,—as you say you have, I am one / that, telling true under him, must say you cannot pass. Therefore / go back.
However much you've been his liar, as you say you have, I'm someone who tells the truth under his command, and I must say you can't pass. So go back.
Has he dined, canst thou tell? For I would not speak with him / till after dinner.
Do you know whether he has eaten? Because I wouldn't want to talk to him until after dinner.
You are a Roman, are you?
I am as thy general is.
I am, as your general is.

Then you should hate Rome, as he does. Can you, when you have / pushed out your gates the very defender of them, and in a violent / popular ignorance, given your enemy your shield, think to front / his revenges with the easy groans of old women, the virginal / palms of your daughters, or with the palsied intercession of such / a decayed dotant as you seem to be? Can you think to blow out the / intended fire your city is ready to flame in, with such weak / breath as this? No, you are deceived; therefore back to Rome, and / prepare for your execution: you are condemned; our general has / sworn you out of reprieve and pardon.

Then you should hate Rome, as he does. When you've pushed the very defender of your gates out of them and, in violent mob ignorance, given your shield to your enemy, can you think you'll face his revenge with old women's feeble groans, your daughters' virgin hands raised in prayer, or the shaky pleading of a worn-out old dodderer like you seem to be? Can you think you'll blow out the fire your city's about to blaze in with such weak breath as this? No, you're mistaken. So go back to Rome and get ready to be executed. You're condemned; our general has sworn you beyond reprieve or pardon.
Sirrah, if thy captain knew I were here he would use me with / estimation.
Fellow, if your captain knew I was here, he'd treat me with respect.
Come, my captain knows you not.
Come on, my captain doesn't know you.
My general cares not for you. Back, I say; go, lest I let forth / your half pint of blood;—back; that's the utmost of your / having:—back.
My general doesn't care about you. Back, I say; go, or I'll let out your half pint of blood. Back; that's all you'll get. Back.

Now, you companion, I'll say an errand for you; you shall know / now that I am in estimation; you shall perceive that a jack / guardant cannot office me from my son Coriolanus: guess but by my / entertainment with him if thou standest not i' the state of / hanging, or of some death more long in spectatorship and crueller / in suffering; behold now presently, and swoon for what's to come / upon thee.—The glorious gods sit in hourly synod about thy / particular prosperity, and love thee no worse than thy old father / Menenius does! O my son! my son! thou art preparing fire for us; / look thee, here's water to quench it. I was hardly moved to come / to thee; but being assured none but myself could move thee, I / have been blown out of your gates with sighs; and conjure thee to / pardon Rome and thy petitionary countrymen. The good gods assuage / thy wrath, and turn the dregs of it upon this varlet here; this, / who, like a block, hath denied my access to thee.

Now, you fellow, I'll put in a word for you. You'll see now that I'm respected; you'll find that a guard dog of a soldier can't keep me from my son Coriolanus. Just judge by how he receives me whether you're not in line for hanging, or some death longer to watch and crueller to suffer. Watch now, and faint at what's coming to you. (To Coriolanus) May the glorious gods sit in council every hour about your personal good fortune, and love you no less than your old father Menenius does! Oh my son, my son! You're preparing fire for us; look, here's water to put it out. I was hard to persuade to come to you; but being assured no one but me could move you, I've been blown out of our gates by sighs, and I beg you to pardon Rome and your pleading countrymen. May the good gods soften your anger and turn the dregs of it on this rascal here, this one who, like a block of wood, has refused to let me through to you.

Wife, mother, child, I know not. My affairs / Are servanted to others: though I owe / My revenge properly, my remission lies / In Volscian breasts. That we have been familiar, / Ingrate forgetfulness shall poison, rather / Than pity note how much.—Therefore be gone. / Mine ears against your suits are stronger than / Your gates against my force. Yet, for I lov'd thee, / Take this along; I writ it for thy sake,

Wife, mother, child, I don't know them. My affairs are now in other men's service. Though the revenge is my own, the power to pardon lies in Volscian hearts. Ungrateful forgetfulness shall poison our past friendship rather than pity remembering how close it was. So go. My ears are stronger against your pleas than your gates are against my force. Still, because I loved you, take this. I wrote it for your sake,
And would have sent it. Another word, Menenius, / I will not hear thee speak.—This man, Aufidius, / Was my beloved in Rome: yet thou behold'st!
