and I would have sent it. Another word, Menenius, I won't listen to. This man, Aufidius, was dear to me in Rome; and yet you see!
Now, sir, is your name Menenius?
Now, sir, is your name Menenius?
'Tis a spell, you see, of much power: you know the way home / again.
It's a spell of great power, you see. You know your way home.
Do you hear how we are shent for keeping your greatness back?
Do you hear how we've been scolded for keeping your greatness out?
What cause, do you think, I have to swoon?
What reason do you think I have to faint?

I neither care for the world nor your general; for such things as / you, I can scarce think there's any, y'are so slight. He that / hath a will to die by himself fears it not from another. Let your / general do his worst. For you, be that you are, long; and your / misery increase with your age! I say to you, as I was said to, / away!

I don't care about the world or your general. As for things like you, I can hardly believe you exist, you're so insignificant. A man who's willing to die by his own hand doesn't fear death from another. Let your general do his worst. As for you, stay what you are for a long time, and may your misery increase as you age! I say to you what was said to me: go away!
A noble fellow, I warrant him.
The worthy fellow is our general: he is the rock, the oak not to / be wind-shaken.
The worthy fellow is our general. He's the rock, the oak no wind can shake.
We will before the walls of Rome to-morrow / Set down our host.—My partner in this action, / You must report to the Volscian lords how plainly / I have borne this business.
Tomorrow we'll set our army down before the walls of Rome. My partner in this campaign, you must tell the Volscian lords how honestly I've conducted this business.
Only their ends / You have respected; stopped your ears against / The general suit of Rome; never admitted / A private whisper, no, not with such friends / That thought them sure of you.
You've considered only their interests, closed your ears to the whole of Rome's plea, and never allowed even a private whisper, not even with friends who thought they were sure of you.

This last old man, / Whom with crack'd heart I have sent to Rome, / Lov'd me above the measure of a father; / Nay, godded me indeed. Their latest refuge / Was to send him; for whose old love I have,— / Though I show'd sourly to him,—once more offer'd / The first conditions, which they did refuse, / And cannot now accept, to grace him only, / That thought he could do more, a very little / I have yielded to: fresh embassies and suits, / Nor from the state nor private friends, hereafter / Will I lend ear to.—

This last old man, whom I've sent back to Rome with a broken heart, loved me more than a father; in fact, he made a god of me. Sending him was their last resort. For the sake of my old love for him, though I was sour to him, I offered the first terms again, which they refused and can't accept now. Only to honour him, who thought he could do more, I've given way a very little. I won't listen to any new embassies or pleas, either from the state or from personal friends, from now on.
Ha! what shout is this? / Shall I be tempted to infringe my vow / In the same time 'tis made? I will not.
Ha! What's that shouting? Will I be tempted to break my vow at the very moment I make it? I won't.

My wife comes foremost; then the honour'd mould / Wherein this trunk was fram'd, and in her hand / The grandchild to her blood. But, out, affection! / All bond and privilege of nature, break! / Let it be virtuous to be obstinate.— / What is that curt'sy worth? or those doves' eyes, / Which can make gods forsworn?—I melt, and am not / Of stronger earth than others.—My mother bows, / As if Olympus to a molehill should / In supplication nod: and my young boy / Hath an aspect of intercession which / Great nature cries 'Deny not.'—Let the Volsces / Plough Rome and harrow Italy: I'll never / Be such a gosling to obey instinct; but stand, / As if a man were author of himself, / And knew no other kin.

My wife comes first; then the honoured mould this body was formed in, and holding her hand, her grandchild. But away, affection! Let every bond and right of nature break! Let it be virtuous to be stubborn. What's that curtsy worth? Or those dove's eyes, which could make gods break their oaths? I'm melting; I'm not made of stronger earth than other men. My mother bows, as if Mount Olympus bowed in pleading to a molehill; and my young boy has a pleading look to which great nature cries, "Don't refuse." Let the Volscians plough Rome and rake over Italy; I'll never be such a gosling as to obey instinct, but stand as if a man were his own creator and had no other family.
These eyes are not the same I wore in Rome.
These eyes aren't the same ones I had in Rome.
The sorrow that delivers us thus chang'd / Makes you think so.
The sorrow that brings us here so changed makes you think so.

Like a dull actor now, / I have forgot my part and I am out, / Even to a full disgrace. Best of my flesh, / Forgive my tyranny; but do not say, / For that, 'Forgive our Romans.'—O, a kiss / Long as my exile, sweet as my revenge; / Now, by the jealous queen of heaven, that kiss / I carried from thee, dear; and my true lip / Hath virgin'd it e'er since.—You gods! I prate, / And the most noble mother of the world / Leave unsaluted: sink, my knee, i' the earth;

Like a bad actor now, I've forgotten my part and lost my lines, to my complete disgrace. Best part of my flesh, forgive my cruelty; but don't say because of that, "Forgive our Romans." Oh, a kiss as long as my exile, as sweet as my revenge! Now, by Juno, jealous queen of heaven, I've carried that kiss from you, dear, and my faithful lip has kept it untouched ever since. You gods! I'm chattering and leaving the most noble mother in the world ungreeted. Sink, my knee, into the earth;
Of thy deep duty more impression show / Than that of common sons.
show a deeper mark of your duty than common sons do.
O, stand up bless'd! / Whilst, with no softer cushion than the flint, / I kneel before thee; and unproperly / Show duty, as mistaken all this while / Between the child and parent.
Oh, stand up, blessed, while I kneel to you with no softer cushion than the flint, and wrongly show the duty that all this time has been mistaken between child and parent.

What is this? / Your knees to me? to your corrected son? / Then let the pebbles on the hungry beach / Fillip the stars; then let the mutinous winds / Strike the proud cedars 'gainst the fiery sun; / Murdering impossibility, to make / What cannot be, slight work.

What's this? Your knees to me? To your rebuked son? Then let the pebbles on the hungry beach flick at the stars; then let the rebellious winds hurl the proud cedars against the fiery sun, murdering impossibility, making what can't be into easy work.
Thou art my warrior; / I holp to frame thee. Do you know this lady?
You're my warrior; I helped make you. Do you know this lady?
The noble sister of Publicola, / The moon of Rome; chaste as the icicle / That's curded by the frost from purest snow, / And hangs on Dian's temple:—dear Valeria!
The noble sister of Publicola, the moon of Rome, as chaste as the icicle frozen by the frost from the purest snow that hangs on Diana's temple. Dear Valeria!
This is a poor epitome of yours, / Which, by the interpretation of full time, / May show like all yourself.
This is a little copy of you, which, when time has filled it out, may look exactly like you.

The god of soldiers, / With the consent of supreme Jove, inform / Thy thoughts with nobleness; that thou mayst prove / To shame unvulnerable, and stick i' the wars / Like a great sea-mark, standing every flaw, / And saving those that eye thee!

May Mars, the god of soldiers, with the consent of supreme Jove, fill your thoughts with nobility, so you prove proof against shame and stand out in the wars like a great landmark for sailors, withstanding every gust and saving those who look to you!
Even he, your wife, this lady, and myself, / Are suitors to you.
He, your wife, this lady and I are all here to ask something of you.

I beseech you, peace: / Or, if you'd ask, remember this before,— / The thing I have forsworn to grant may never / Be held by you denials. Do not bid me / Dismiss my soldiers, or capitulate / Again with Rome's mechanics.—Tell me not / Wherein I seem unnatural: desire not / To allay my rages and revenges with / Your colder reasons.

I beg you, quiet. Or, if you're going to ask, remember this first: you mustn't take it as a refusal of you if I won't grant what I've sworn not to grant. Don't tell me to dismiss my soldiers or negotiate again with Rome's workmen. Don't tell me how I seem unnatural. Don't try to calm my rage and revenge with your cooler reasoning.

O, no more, no more! / You have said you will not grant us anything; / For we have nothing else to ask but that / Which you deny already: yet we will ask; / That, if you fail in our request, the blame / May hang upon your hardness; therefore hear us.

Oh, no more, no more! You've said you won't grant us anything, because we have nothing else to ask except what you've already refused. Still, we will ask, so that if you refuse our request, the blame will rest on your hardness. So hear us.
Aufidius, and you Volsces, mark: for we'll / Hear nought from Rome in private.—Your request?
Aufidius, and you Volscians, take note, because we'll hear nothing from Rome in private. What is your request?

Should we be silent and not speak, our raiment / And state of bodies would bewray what life / We have led since thy exile. Think with thyself, / How more unfortunate than all living women / Are we come hither: since that thy sight, which should / Make our eyes flow with joy, hearts dance with comforts, / Constrains them weep, and shake with fear and sorrow; / Making the mother, wife, and child, to see / The son, the husband, and the father, tearing / His country's bowels out. And to poor we, / Thine enmity's most capital: thou barr'st us / Our prayers to the gods, which is a comfort / That all but we enjoy; for how can we, / Alas, how can we for our country pray, / Whereto we are bound,—together with thy victory, / Whereto we are bound? alack, or we must lose / The country, our dear nurse, or else thy person, / Our comfort in the country. We must find / An evident calamity, though we had / Our wish, which side should win; for either thou / Must, as a foreign recreant, be led / With manacles through our streets, or else / Triumphantly tread on thy country's ruin, / And bear the palm for having bravely shed / Thy wife and children's blood. For myself, son, / I purpose not to wait on fortune till / These wars determine: if I can not persuade thee / Rather to show a noble grace to both parts / Than seek the end of one, thou shalt no sooner / March to assault thy country than to tread,— / Trust to't, thou shalt not,—on thy mother's womb / That brought thee to this world.

Even if we kept silent and didn't speak, our clothes and the state of our bodies would show what life we've led since your exile. Think how much more unfortunate than all living women we are in coming here, since the sight of you, which should make our eyes flow with joy and our hearts dance with comfort, forces them to weep and shake with fear and sorrow, making the mother, wife and child see the son, husband and father tearing out his country's guts. And to poor us your hatred is most deadly. You stop us praying to the gods, a comfort everyone but us enjoys; because how can we, alas, how can we pray for our country, as we're bound to, and also for your victory, as we're bound to? Alas, either we must lose our country, our dear nurse, or else you, our comfort in that country. We're bound to meet obvious disaster even if we had our wish about which side should win; because either you must be led in chains through our streets as a foreign traitor, or else tread in triumph on your country's ruins and win the prize for bravely shedding your wife's and children's blood. As for me, son, I don't intend to wait on fortune until these wars are decided. If I can't persuade you to show noble grace to both sides rather than seek the destruction of one, you won't march to attack your country without treading (believe me, you won't) on your mother's womb that brought you into this world.
Ay, and mine, / That brought you forth this boy, to keep your name / Living to time.
Yes, and on mine, which gave you this boy to keep your name alive through time.
'A shall not tread on me; / I'll run away till I am bigger; but then I'll fight.
He won't tread on me. I'll run away till I'm bigger; but then I'll fight.
Not of a woman's tenderness to be, / Requires nor child nor woman's face to see. / I have sat too long.
Not to be softened by a woman's tenderness, one must not look at a child's or a woman's face. I've sat too long.

Nay, go not from us thus. / If it were so that our request did tend / To save the Romans, thereby to destroy / The Volsces whom you serve, you might condemn us, / As poisonous of your honour: no; our suit / Is that you reconcile them: while the Volsces / May say 'This mercy we have show'd,' the Romans / 'This we receiv'd,' and each in either side / Give the all-hail to thee, and cry, 'Be bless'd / For making up this peace!' Thou know'st, great son, / The end of war's uncertain; but this certain, / That, if thou conquer Rome, the benefit / Which thou shalt thereby reap is such a name / Whose repetition will be dogg'd with curses; / Whose chronicle thus writ:—'The man was noble, / But with his last attempt he wip'd it out; / Destroy'd his country, and his name remains / To the ensuing age abhorr'd.' Speak to me, son: / Thou hast affected the fine strains of honour, / To imitate the graces of the gods, / To tear with thunder the wide cheeks o' the air, / And yet to charge thy sulphur with a bolt / That should but rive an oak. Why dost not speak? / Think'st thou it honourable for a noble man / Still to remember wrongs?—Daughter, speak you: / He cares not for your weeping.—Speak thou, boy: / Perhaps thy childishness will move him more / Than can our reasons.—There's no man in the world / More bound to's mother; yet here he lets me prate / Like one i' the stocks. Thou hast never in thy life / Show'd thy dear mother any courtesy; / When she,—poor hen,—fond of no second brood, / Has cluck'd thee to the wars, and safely home, / Loaden with honour. Say my request's unjust, / And spurn me back: but if it be not so, / Thou art not honest; and the gods will plague thee, / That thou restrain'st from me the duty which / To a mother's part belongs.—He turns away: / Down, ladies: let us shame him with our knees. / To his surname Coriolanus 'longs more pride / Than pity to our prayers. Down: an end; / This is the last.—So we will home to Rome, / And die among our neighbours.—Nay, behold's: / This boy, that cannot tell what he would have / But kneels and holds up hands for fellowship, / Does reason our petition with more strength / Than thou hast to deny't.—Come, let us go: / This fellow had a Volscian to his mother; / His wife is in Corioli, and his child / Like him by chance.—Yet give us our despatch: / I am hush'd until our city be afire, / And then I'll speak a little.

No, don't leave us like this. If our request were meant to save the Romans by destroying the Volscians you serve, you could condemn us as poisoners of your honour. No; our plea is that you reconcile them, so that the Volscians can say, "We showed this mercy", and the Romans, "We received it", and both sides hail you and cry, "Bless you for making this peace!" You know, great son, the outcome of war is uncertain; but this is certain: if you conquer Rome, the reward you'll reap is a name that will be followed by curses whenever it's repeated, whose history will read: "The man was noble, but with his last act he wiped it out, destroyed his country, and his name is hated by the generations that followed." Speak to me, son. You've aimed at the finest heights of honour, to imitate the graces of the gods, to tear the wide cheeks of the sky with thunder, and yet to load your lightning with a bolt that would only split an oak. Why don't you speak? Do you think it's honourable for a noble man to keep remembering wrongs? Daughter, you speak; he doesn't care about your crying. You speak, boy; maybe your childishness will move him more than our reasons can. There's no man in the world who owes more to his mother, yet here he lets me prattle like someone in the stocks. You've never in your life shown your dear mother any kindness, while she, poor hen, wanting no second brood, has clucked you off to the wars and safely home again, loaded with honour. Say my request is unjust and kick me away; but if it isn't, you're not honest, and the gods will punish you for keeping from me the duty owed to a mother. He turns away. Down, ladies; let's shame him with our knees. His surname Coriolanus has more pride in it than pity for our prayers. Down; let's finish. This is the last. Then we'll go home to Rome and die among our neighbours. No, look at us. This boy, who can't say what he wants but kneels and holds up his hands with us, argues our case with more strength than you have to refuse it. Come, let's go. This fellow had a Volscian for a mother; his wife is in Corioli, and his child looks like him by chance. Still, send us away with an answer. I'll be silent until our city is on fire, and then I'll say a little.

O mother, mother! / What have you done? Behold, the heavens do ope, / The gods look down, and this unnatural scene / They laugh at. O my mother, mother! O! / You have won a happy victory to Rome; / But for your son,—believe it, O, believe it, / Most dangerously you have with him prevail'd, / If not most mortal to him. But let it come.— / Aufidius, though I cannot make true wars, / I'll frame convenient peace. Now, good Aufidius, / Were you in my stead, would you have heard / A mother less? or granted less, Aufidius?

Oh mother, mother! What have you done? Look, the heavens open, the gods look down and laugh at this unnatural scene. Oh my mother, mother! Oh! You've won a happy victory for Rome; but for your son, believe it, oh believe it, you've beaten him in a way that's most dangerous to him, if not deadly. But let it come. Aufidius, though I can't fight this war properly, I'll make a suitable peace. Now, good Aufidius, if you were in my place, would you have listened to a mother less? Or granted less, Aufidius?
I was moved by it too.

I dare be sworn you were: / And, sir, it is no little thing to make / Mine eyes to sweat compassion. But, good sir, / What peace you'll make, advise me: for my part, / I'll not to Rome, I'll back with you; and, pray you / Stand to me in this cause.—O mother! wife!

I'd swear you were. And, sir, it's no small thing to make my eyes sweat with pity. But, good sir, advise me what peace you'll make. For my part, I won't go to Rome; I'll go back with you. And please, support me in this. Oh mother! Wife!
[Aside] I am glad thou hast set thy mercy and thy honour / At difference in thee; out of that I'll work / Myself a former fortune.
(Aside) I'm glad you've set your mercy and your honour against each other. Out of that I'll make myself the fortune I had before.

[To VOLUMNIA, VIRGILIA, &c] Ay, by and by; / But we'll drink together; and you shall bear / A better witness back than words, which we, / On like conditions, will have counter-seal'd. / Come, enter with us. Ladies, you deserve / To have a temple built you: all the swords / In Italy, and her confederate arms, / Could not have made this peace.

(To Volumnia, Virgilia and the others) Yes, soon; but first we'll drink together, and you'll carry back a better proof than words, a treaty that we'll have signed on the same terms. Come in with us. Ladies, you deserve to have a temple built for you. All the swords in Italy and its allied armies couldn't have made this peace.
See you yond coign o' the Capitol,—yond corner-stone?
Do you see that corner of the Capitol, that cornerstone?

If it be possible for you to displace it with your little / finger, there is some hope the ladies of Rome, especially his / mother, may prevail with him. But I say there is no hope in't: / our throats are sentenced, and stay upon execution.

If you can shift it with your little finger, there's some hope the ladies of Rome, especially his mother, may win him over. But I say there's no hope in it. Our throats are sentenced and only waiting for the execution.
Is't possible that so short a time can alter the condition of a / man?
Is it possible that so short a time can change a man's nature?
There is differency between a grub and a butterfly; yet your / butterfly was a grub. This Marcius is grown from man to dragon; / he has wings; he's more than a creeping thing.
There's a difference between a grub and a butterfly, yet your butterfly was once a grub. This Marcius has grown from a man into a dragon. He has wings; he's more than a crawling thing.

So did he me: and he no more remembers his mother now than an / eight-year-old horse. The tartness of his face sours ripe grapes: / when he walks, he moves like an engine, and the ground shrinks / before his treading: he is able to pierce a corslet with his eye, / talks like a knell, and his hum is a battery. He sits in his / state as a thing made for Alexander. What he bids be done is / finished with his bidding. He wants nothing of a god but / eternity, and a heaven to throne in.

So he did me; and he remembers his mother now no more than an eight-year-old horse does. The sourness of his face turns ripe grapes sour. When he walks, he moves like a siege engine, and the ground shrinks under his tread. He can pierce armour with his look, he talks like a funeral bell, and his "hm" is a cannon blast. He sits in state like a statue made of Alexander the Great. What he orders is done as soon as he orders it. He lacks nothing of a god except eternity and a heaven to sit enthroned in.
Yes, mercy, if you report him truly.
Yes, and mercy, if you describe him truly.

I paint him in the character. Mark what mercy his mother shall / bring from him. There is no more mercy in him than there is / milk in a male tiger; that shall our poor city find: and all this / is 'long of you.

I paint him true to life. Watch what mercy his mother will bring back from him. There's no more mercy in him than there's milk in a male tiger. Our poor city will find that out, and it's all because of you.
The gods be good unto us!
The gods be good to us!
No, in such a case the gods will not be good unto us. When we / banished him we respected not them; and, he returning to break / our necks, they respect not us.
No, in a case like this the gods won't be good to us. When we banished him we didn't respect them; and now he's coming back to break our necks, they don't respect us.

Sir, if you'd save your life, fly to your house: / The plebeians have got your fellow-tribune / And hale him up and down; all swearing, if / The Roman ladies bring not comfort home / They'll give him death by inches.

Sir, if you want to save your life, run to your house. The plebeians have caught your fellow tribune and are dragging him up and down, all swearing that if the Roman ladies don't bring home good news, they'll kill him inch by inch.
Good news, good news;—the ladies have prevail'd, / The Volscians are dislodg'd, and Marcius gone: / A merrier day did never yet greet Rome, / No, not the expulsion of the Tarquins.
Good news, good news! The ladies have won. The Volscians have broken camp, and Marcius has gone. A happier day never dawned on Rome, no, not even the expulsion of the Tarquins.
Friend, / Art thou certain this is true? is't most certain?
Friend, are you sure this is true? Absolutely sure?
As certain as I know the sun is fire: / Where have you lurk'd, that you make doubt of it? / Ne'er through an arch so hurried the blown tide / As the recomforted through the gates. Why, hark you!

As sure as I know the sun is fire. Where have you been hiding that you doubt it? The swollen tide never rushed through an arch as fast as the comforted people are rushing through the gates. Why, listen!
The trumpets, sackbuts, psalteries, and fifes, / Tabors and cymbals, and the shouting Romans, / Make the sun dance. Hark you!
The trumpets, trombones, harps and fifes, drums and cymbals, and the shouting Romans make the sun dance. Listen!

This is good news. / I will go meet the ladies. This Volumnia / Is worth of consuls, senators, patricians, / A city full: of tribunes such as you, / A sea and land full. You have pray'd well to-day: / This morning for ten thousand of your throats / I'd not have given a doit. Hark, how they joy!

This is good news. I'll go and meet the ladies. This Volumnia is worth a city full of consuls, senators and patricians, and a whole sea and land full of tribunes like you. You've prayed well today. This morning I wouldn't have given a penny for ten thousand of your throats. Listen to how happy they are!
First, the gods bless you for your tidings; next, / Accept my thankfulness.
First, the gods bless you for your news; next, accept my thanks.
Sir, we have all / Great cause to give great thanks.
Sir, we all have great reason to give great thanks.
We'll meet them, / And help the joy.
We'll go and meet them and add to the joy.

Behold our patroness, the life of Rome! / Call all your tribes together, praise the gods, / And make triumphant fires; strew flowers before them: / Unshout the noise that banish'd Marcius, / Repeal him with the welcome of his mother; / Cry, 'Welcome, ladies, welcome!'—

Look at our protector, the life of Rome! Call all your tribes together, praise the gods and light bonfires of triumph; scatter flowers in front of them. Unshout the noise that banished Marcius; call him back by welcoming his mother. Cry, "Welcome, ladies, welcome!"

Go tell the lords o' the city I am here: / Deliver them this paper; having read it, / Bid them repair to the market-place: where I, / Even in theirs and in the commons' ears, / Will vouch the truth of it. Him I accuse / The city ports by this hath enter'd and / Intends t' appear before the people, hoping / To purge himself with words: despatch.

Go and tell the lords of the city I'm here. Give them this paper, and when they've read it, tell them to come to the market square, where I'll swear to its truth in their hearing and the common people's. The man I accuse has entered the city gates by now and means to appear before the people, hoping to clear himself with words. Hurry.
How is it with our general?
How are things with our general?
Even so / As with a man by his own alms empoison'd, / And with his charity slain.
As with a man poisoned by his own charity and killed by his own kindness.
Most noble sir, / If you do hold the same intent wherein / You wish'd us parties, we'll deliver you / Of your great danger.
Most noble sir, if you still have the plan you wanted us to join in, we'll free you from your great danger.
Sir, I cannot tell: / We must proceed as we do find the people.
Sir, I can't say. We must act according to how we find the people.
The people will remain uncertain whilst / 'Twixt you there's difference: but the fall of either / Makes the survivor heir of all.
The people will stay undecided while there's a quarrel between you; but the fall of either one makes the survivor heir to everything.

I know it; / And my pretext to strike at him admits / A good construction. I rais'd him, and I pawn'd / Mine honour for his truth: who being so heighten'd, / He water'd his new plants with dews of flattery, / Seducing so my friends; and to this end / He bow'd his nature, never known before / But to be rough, unswayable, and free.

I know it. And my excuse for striking at him can be presented well. I raised him up, and I pledged my honour for his loyalty. Raised so high, he watered his new plants with the dew of flattery, winning over my friends that way; and to do it he bent his nature, which had never been known to be anything but rough, unbending and outspoken.
Sir, his stoutness / When he did stand for consul, which he lost / By lack of stooping,—
Sir, his stubbornness when he stood for consul, which he lost because he wouldn't stoop—

That I would have spoken of: / Being banish'd for't, he came unto my hearth; / Presented to my knife his throat: I took him; / Made him joint-servant with me; gave him way / In all his own desires; nay, let him choose / Out of my files, his projects to accomplish, / My best and freshest men; serv'd his designments / In mine own person; holp to reap the fame / Which he made all his; and took some pride / To do myself this wrong: till, at the last, / I seem'd his follower, not partner; and / He wag'd me with his countenance as if / I had been mercenary.

I was going to mention that. Banished for it, he came to my hearth and offered his throat to my knife. I took him in, made him my joint commander, let him have his way in everything he wanted; even let him choose my best and freshest troops from my ranks to carry out his plans. I served his schemes in person, helped to reap the fame he made all his own, and took a sort of pride in doing myself this wrong; until in the end I seemed his follower, not his partner, and he paid me with his patronizing looks as if I'd been a hired soldier.
So he did, my lord: / The army marvell'd at it; and, in the last, / When he had carried Rome, and that we look'd / For no less spoil than glory,—
So he did, my lord. The army was amazed at it; and in the end, when he could have taken Rome, and we expected no less loot than glory—

There was it;— / For which my sinews shall be stretch'd upon him. / At a few drops of women's rheum, which are / As cheap as lies, he sold the blood and labour / Of our great action: therefore shall he die, / And I'll renew me in his fall. But, hark!

That was it, the thing for which I'll strain every muscle against him. For a few drops of women's tears, which are as cheap as lies, he sold the blood and toil of our great campaign. So he shall die, and I'll be renewed by his fall. But listen!
Your native town you enter'd like a post, / And had no welcomes home; but he returns / Splitting the air with noise.
You entered your own home town like a messenger, with no welcome home; but he comes back splitting the air with noise.
And patient fools, / Whose children he hath slain, their base throats tear / With giving him glory.
And the long-suffering fools whose children he killed tear their common throats cheering him.

Therefore, at your vantage, / Ere he express himself or move the people / With what he would say, let him feel your sword, / Which we will second. When he lies along, / After your way his tale pronounc'd shall bury / His reasons with his body.

So, at your best moment, before he explains himself or moves the people with what he'd say, let him feel your sword, and we'll back you up. When he's lying flat, your version of his story will bury his reasons along with his body.
Say no more: / Here come the lords.
Say no more. Here come the lords.
I have not deserv'd it. / But, worthy lords, have you with heed perus'd / What I have written to you?
I haven't deserved it. But, worthy lords, have you carefully read what I wrote to you?

And grieve to hear't. / What faults he made before the last, I think / Might have found easy fines: but there to end / Where he was to begin, and give away / The benefit of our levies, answering us / With our own charge: making a treaty where / There was a yielding.—This admits no excuse.

And we're sorry to hear it. The faults he committed before this last one could, I think, have been let off with small fines; but to stop where he should have started, to give away the profit of our war and repay us with nothing but our own costs, to make a treaty where there was a surrender— this can't be excused.
He approaches: you shall hear him.

Hail, lords! I am return'd your soldier; / No more infected with my country's love / Than when I parted hence, but still subsisting / Under your great command. You are to know / That prosperously I have attempted, and / With bloody passage led your wars even to / The gates of Rome. Our spoils we have brought home / Do more than counterpoise a full third part / The charges of the action. We have made peace / With no less honour to the Antiates / Than shame to the Romans: and we here deliver, / Subscribed by the consuls and patricians, / Together with the seal o' the senate, what / We have compounded on.

Greetings, lords! I've come back your soldier, no more infected with love of my country than when I left here, but still serving under your great command. You should know that I've succeeded, and led your wars by a bloody path right up to the gates of Rome. The loot we've brought home more than pays a full third of the cost of the campaign. We've made a peace that brings as much honour to the people of Antium as shame to the Romans; and here we hand over, signed by the consuls and patricians and with the senate's seal, the terms we've agreed.
Read it not, noble lords; / But tell the traitor, in the highest degree / He hath abus'd your powers.
Don't read it, noble lords. Tell the traitor he has abused your power to the highest degree.

Ay, Marcius, Caius Marcius! Dost thou think / I'll grace thee with that robbery, thy stol'n name / Coriolanus, in Corioli?— / You lords and heads o' the state, perfidiously / He has betray'd your business, and given up, / For certain drops of salt, your city Rome,— / I say your city,—to his wife and mother; / Breaking his oath and resolution, like / A twist of rotten silk; never admitting / Counsel o' the war; but at his nurse's tears / He whin'd and roar'd away your victory; / That pages blush'd at him, and men of heart / Look'd wondering each at others.

Yes, Marcius, Caius Marcius! Do you think I'll honour you with that theft, your stolen name Coriolanus, here in Corioli? You lords and leaders of the state, he has treacherously betrayed your cause and given up your city Rome, I say your city, for a few salty drops, to his wife and mother, breaking his oath and his resolve like a strand of rotten silk, never asking the war council's advice. At his nurse's tears he whined and bawled your victory away, so that pageboys blushed at him and brave men looked at each other in amazement.
Name not the god, thou boy of tears,—
Don't name the god, you boy of tears—

Measureless liar, thou hast made my heart / Too great for what contains it. Boy! O slave!— / Pardon me, lords, 'tis the first time that ever / I was forc'd to scold. Your judgments, my grave lords, / Must give this cur the lie: and his own notion,— / Who wears my stripes impress'd upon him; that must bear / My beating to his grave,—shall join to thrust / The lie unto him.

Boundless liar, you've made my heart too big for the body that holds it. Boy! Oh, slave! Forgive me, lords; it's the first time I've ever been forced to brawl with words. Your judgment, my serious lords, must call this cur a liar; and his own memory, since he carries my stripes printed on him and will carry my beating to his grave, will join in throwing the lie back at him.
Peace, both, and hear me speak.
Quiet, both of you, and hear me speak.

Cut me to pieces, Volsces; men and lads, / Stain all your edges on me.—Boy! False hound! / If you have writ your annals true, 'tis there, / That, like an eagle in a dove-cote, I / Flutter'd your Volscians in Corioli: / Alone I did it.—Boy!

Cut me to pieces, Volscians; men and boys, stain all your blades on me. Boy! Lying dog! If you've written your history truthfully, it's recorded there that, like an eagle in a dovecote, I scattered your Volscians in Corioli. I did it alone. Boy!
Why, noble lords, / Will you be put in mind of his blind fortune, / Which was your shame, by this unholy braggart, / 'Fore your own eyes and ears?
Why, noble lords, will you let this godless braggart remind you of his blind luck, which was your shame, in front of your own eyes and ears?
Tear him to pieces, do it presently:—he killed my son; my / daughter; he killed my cousin Marcus; he killed my father,—
Tear him to pieces, do it now! He killed my son! My daughter! He killed my cousin Marcus! He killed my father!
Peace, ho!—no outrage;—peace! / The man is noble, and his fame folds in / This orb o' the earth. His last offences to us / Shall have judicious hearing.—Stand, Aufidius, / And trouble not the peace.

Quiet, there! No violence! Quiet! The man is noble, and his fame wraps around the whole world. His latest offences against us will have a proper hearing. Stand back, Aufidius, and don't disturb the peace.
O that I had him, / With six Aufidiuses, or more, his tribe, / To use my lawful sword!
Oh, if only I had him, and six Aufidiuses or more, his whole tribe, to use my lawful sword on!
Kill, kill, kill, kill, kill him!
Kill, kill, kill, kill, kill him!
My noble masters, hear me speak.
My noble masters, let me speak.
Thou hast done a deed whereat valour will weep.
You've done a deed that will make courage weep.
Tread not upon him.—Masters all, be quiet; / Put up your swords.
Don't stand on him. Everyone, be quiet. Put away your swords.

My lords, when you shall know,—as in this rage, / Provok'd by him, you cannot,—the great danger / Which this man's life did owe you, you'll rejoice / That he is thus cut off. Please it your honours / To call me to your senate, I'll deliver / Myself your loyal servant, or endure / Your heaviest censure.

My lords, when you know (as you can't in this rage he provoked) the great danger this man's life held for you, you'll be glad he has been cut off like this. If your honours will summon me to your senate, I'll show myself your loyal servant or accept your harshest sentence.
Bear from hence his body, / And mourn you for him. Let him be regarded / As the most noble corse that ever herald / Did follow to his urn.
Carry his body away from here, and mourn for him. Let him be honoured as the noblest corpse any herald ever followed to its urn.
His own impatience / Takes from Aufidius a great part of blame. / Let's make the best of it.
His own impatience takes a great part of the blame off Aufidius. Let's make the best of it.

My rage is gone; / And I am struck with sorrow.—Take him up:— / Help, three o' the chiefest soldiers; I'll be one.— / Beat thou the drum, that it speak mournfully; / Trail your steel pikes. Though in this city he / Hath widow'd and unchilded many a one, / Which to this hour bewail the injury, / Yet he shall have a noble memory.— / Assist.

My rage is gone, and I'm struck with sorrow. Lift him up. Help, three of the leading soldiers; I'll be the fourth. Beat the drum so that it sounds mournful. Trail your steel pikes. Though in this city he has made many widows and childless parents, who still grieve over the injury today, he will have a noble memorial. Help me.
